corpus.headline: The existing KPI doc has a defensible north star and input tree, but it skips the one step the canonical literature says teams always skip (Goals→Signals→Metrics), states point-estimate predictions that Kohavi's own data says are implausible for 9 of 9 changes, and defines TTFA as an unwinsorized, client-anchored time-to-success metric — the exact metric shape Microsoft found needs truncation and server anchoring before it can be trusted.

findings.claim: Amplitude's own playbook says never try to move the North Star directly — and "Weekly Proven Agents" as currently written invites exactly that.
findings.detail: The North Star Playbook is explicit: "Inputs are independent variables. The North Star Metric is an outcome, a dependent variable... Never try to influence the North Star directly." John Cutler's line in the same document: "If you can move your North Star directly, it's probably not a good North Star." The playbook's tree has four layers — Mid/long-term business results (lagging) at the bottom, North Star, 3–5 Input Metrics, then "The Work" (lagging→leading, bottom to top). The current doc's formula `WPA = new agents deployed × AR7` is a decomposition, not an input tree: it collapses four inputs into two.
findings.soWhat: Redraw §1 as the literal four-layer tree: Work (tracker rows 01–11) → Inputs (TTFA, TTFD, TCR, AR7) → WPA → billable minutes / retained accounts. Delete the `WPA = new agents deployed × AR7` formula from the headline position; it reads as a lever and it is an outcome. Keep it as a sanity identity in an appendix.
findings.source: Amplitude, The North Star Playbook (John Cutler et al.), pp. 6–9

findings.claim: The playbook's input template asks you to assert independence between inputs — and TTFA and TTFD are not independent, because TTFD's start event is TTFA's stop event.
findings.detail: The fill-in-the-blank template is: "I believe that [NORTH STAR METRIC] is a function of [X, Y, AND Z]. I also believe that there is some independence between [X, Y, AND Z] (e.g. movements in one aren't immediately felt in the others)." In the current doc, TTFD starts at "first successful test (the TTFA stop)," so any change to the TTFA stop definition mechanically moves TTFD. Worse, the TTFA stop condition is still an open question (§8.2: does a simulation count?), which means both clocks are undefined until it is settled.
findings.soWhat: Either (a) re-anchor TTFD on `agent_create` too, so the two clocks share an origin and are genuinely comparable, or (b) keep the sequential definition but state plainly in §1 that TTFA and TTFD are serial, not independent, and that the pair should be read as one cumulative curve (time-to-first-answer, time-to-first-deploy) rather than two levers. Settle §8.2 before W0 ships — both clocks are undefined until it is settled, and it changes the meaning of A2 and A9.
findings.source: Amplitude, The North Star Playbook, p. 27 (input template)

findings.claim: The Goals→Signals→Metrics step is missing from the doc, and that middle step is the entire contribution of the HEART paper — the authors' first tip is that different team members disagree about goals, and the process exists to force that out.
findings.detail: Rodden, Hutchinson and Fu (CHI 2010): "No matter how user-centered a metric is, it is unlikely to be useful in practice unless it explicitly relates to a goal." Their Signals step carries the load-bearing rule: "Choose signals that are sensitive and specific to the goal — they should move only when the user experience is better or worse, not for other, unrelated reasons." They also note "Sometimes failure is easier to identify than success (e.g. abandonment of a task, 'undo' events, frustration)." The current doc jumps from the goal ("fastest platform") straight to metrics (dwell budgets, funnels) with no signals column.
findings.soWhat: Add a one-page GSM grid to §2 before the budget table: one row per builder section, three columns (Goal for that section / Signals that it went well or badly / Metric). The failure-is-easier-than-success tip is free money here: a dedicated `agent_config_reverted` and `sheet_abandoned_without_save` signal will be more sensitive than dwell time, which moves for a dozen unrelated reasons.
findings.source: Rodden, Hutchinson & Fu, "Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale," CHI 2010, Google

findings.claim: The "struggle index" fails HEART's sensitivity-and-specificity test and will generate false alarms — it is a composite of four signals that each move for unrelated reasons.
findings.detail: The doc defines it as "doc links + failed saves + sheet re-entries + config churn, by section." `doc_link_viewed` rises if the docs get better or if a new link is added; `operation_failed` rises on a backend incident; sheet re-entry rises if a user is comparing two voices deliberately. HEART's rule is that a signal should move only when the experience is better or worse. Rodden and Fu also warn that raw counts grow with the user base and must be normalised — the struggle index as written is a sum of counts.
findings.soWhat: Do not build "Struggle index" as a single PostHog trend in §6.4. Split it into four separately-owned rates, each normalised per builder session (not per person, not raw), and only ever read them together next to an over-budget dwell row. If you need one number, make it a count of sessions with ≥2 of the four signals firing in the same section — a conjunction is far more specific than a sum.
findings.source: Rodden, Hutchinson & Fu, CHI 2010 (Signals tips; "Raw counts will go up as your user base grows, and need to be normalized")

findings.claim: TTFA is a time-to-success metric — the exact metric shape Microsoft measured as needing truncation before it is usable, and untruncated it needs ~1,550 users per arm just to be normally distributed.
findings.detail: Kohavi's Rule #7 gives a lower bound on sample size of 355 × skewness². His published table for Bing: TimeToSuccess has skewness² = 4.4, minimum sample 1,550, detectable effect 12.3% at 80% power; truncated, skewness² drops to 0.15 and minimum sample to ~50. Bing itself uses Time-To-Success as a key metric, "where success is defined as clicking on a result and not returning back in less than 30 seconds" — a stop condition with a built-in quality bar, exactly analogous to a test session with turnCount ≥ 1.
findings.soWhat: Promote the doc's "hard ceiling 10 min" from prose into the metric definition as a winsorization rule: TTFA is computed with all values truncated at 600 s, and sessions exceeding it are counted separately as a failure rate, not as a long success. Report median and p75 only — never mean. Do the same for TTFD (truncate at 24h, per its own definition). Without this, a handful of users who left a tab open will dominate the number.
findings.source: Kohavi, Deng, Longbotham & Xu, "Seven Rules of Thumb for Web Site Experimenters," KDD 2014 (Rule #7 and Rule #4 slides)

findings.claim: The assumptions ledger predicts a positive, quantified win for 9 out of 9 changes; Microsoft's measured base rate is roughly one in three experiments moving metrics, and 10–20% at Bing.
findings.detail: Kohavi's Rule #2 is literally titled "Changes Rarely have a Big Positive Impact to Key Metrics": "Most progress is made by small continuous improvements: 0.1%-1% after a lot of work." He applies Bayes' rule with π = 1/3 ("the average across multiple experiments at Microsoft") and notes Bing's own idea success rate is "about 10-20%." He also warns about dilution: "A 10% improvement to a 1% segment has an overall impact of approximately 0.1%" — directly relevant to A7 (import), which only reaches migrators.
findings.soWhat: Add an expected-value column to the A1–A9 table: predicted delta × a stated prior (start at 0.33 unless there is evidence). Then re-sum: the doc claims A1 −45 s and A2 −60 s against a 3-minute median target — that is 58% of the whole budget from two rows. Discounted, the ledger no longer reaches 3 minutes on UI changes alone, which is the honest read and points the work at defaults (A11) and import (A7) instead. Also dilute A7 and A4 by their reachable population before quoting the effect.
findings.source: Kohavi et al., "Seven Rules of Thumb for Web Site Experimenters," KDD 2014 (Rules #2, #3; Bayes slide)

findings.claim: Most of the ledger's stated effects are local feature metrics, and Microsoft's Xbox experiment is the canonical case of a big local win with zero global movement.
findings.detail: Dmitriev et al.'s pitfall 5.11 (Incomplete Funnel Metrics): Xbox promotion changes "have large positive impacts on the number of users who click through to the sale... In some of these experiments we did not see any corresponding revenue increase even when it had sufficient power... it cost our users wasted time and effort." Kohavi's Rule #5 puts it as: "local improvements are easy; Global improvements are much harder" — he lists an ad-background-colour change that moved revenue 12% (≈$150M/yr) while abandonment rate did not move at p=0.83. A4's "backup attach rate 15% → 35%" and A6's "speech-section completion +15pp" are pure local metrics.
findings.soWhat: Enforce rule §5.1 of the doc harder: every A-row must print its local metric AND its named input metric on the same scorecard line, and a row may not be closed on the local metric alone. Concretely, A4 does not close on attach rate; it closes on attach rate plus TCR or a failover-survival number. Also follow 5.11's instruction to measure both conditional (of those who started the step) and unconditional (of all who entered the builder) success rates at each funnel step — the PostHog funnel in §6.4 gives you conditional for free and unconditional only if you ask for it.
findings.source: Dmitriev, Gupta, Kim & Vaz, "A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls in Online Controlled Experiments," KDD 2017 §5.11; Kohavi KDD 2014 Rule #5

findings.claim: TTFA's stop event is client-side, which exposes the whole metric to telemetry-loss bias — the pitfall that invalidated every client-event metric in a Microsoft mobile experiment.
findings.detail: Pitfall 5.3 (Telemetry Loss Bias): "Since the new events that make it (or events that are lost) are typically a highly biased set, telemetry loss bias practically invalidates any metrics that are based on the affected events... Metrics based on the server-side events, however, remained valid." Their prescription is specific: "for every client event used in metrics, a Data Quality metric measuring the rate of event loss should be created," preferably by comparing to a corresponding server event, and "As much as possible metrics should be based on more reliable server-side events." A test panel that holds a live voice session is precisely where a client will drop its last beacon.
findings.soWhat: Change the 2.2.0 spec: anchor `agent_test_session` succeeded on a server-side signal (the runtime's first `turn-finished` for that agent, which `src/lib/latency-metrics.ts` already parses) and keep the client event only as a secondary. Add a data-quality metric to §6.4 comparing client `agent_test_session_succeeded` count to the server turn count — this is the single highest-leverage line in the whole telemetry plan, because without it W0's two-week baseline is uninterpretable.
findings.source: Dmitriev et al., KDD 2017 §5.3

findings.claim: Several of the doc's rate metrics have denominators the changes themselves move — the "metric sample ratio mismatch" that makes a metric's delta arbitrary in direction.
findings.detail: Pitfall 5.1: a one-line change at MSN showed an 8.32% Page Load Time increase; the cause was that treatment had 7.8% fewer homepage loads, i.e. the denominator changed. "In a situation like this the metric value cannot be trusted... the treatment-control delta may change in an arbitrary direction." Their fix: "two separate metrics at user level could be created for numerator and denominator... it is a good idea to always have such a decomposition on the scorecard." A2 ("test available from the first section") deliberately changes who tests — so "tested-before-live rate" and "simulation coverage" both have moving denominators under A2.
findings.soWhat: For every rate in §2.4 (preflight pass rate, first-publish failure rate, TCR, tested-before-live, simulation coverage, failover exercised), put the numerator and the denominator on the dashboard as their own series. Also adopt method A (average of per-user ratios) not method B (ratio of totals) where a per-user ratio makes sense — the paper says it is more sensitive, more resilient to outliers, and less likely to suffer a metric-level SRM because its denominator is the randomisation unit.
findings.source: Dmitriev et al., KDD 2017 §5.1 and §5.2

findings.claim: The guardrails in §1 are written as "must not rise," which is statistically unfalsifiable at the volumes this console will see — guardrails are routinely underpowered by an order of magnitude relative to the primary metric.
findings.detail: Statsig's guidance is blunt: a test powered to detect a 1% primary-metric effect "might only detect 10-30% changes in guardrail metrics, resulting in wide confidence intervals." Dmitriev's pitfall 5.4 is the same failure at Microsoft: a 0.5% page-views change was called "no impact" when the experiment could only detect 7.8% or larger at 80% power — "we cannot assume that we did not impact the underpowered metric." Their recommendation: "at least 80% power to detect small enough changes in success and guardrail metrics," established by a priori power analysis.
findings.soWhat: Rewrite each guardrail as a non-inferiority statement with a declared margin and an honest MDE, e.g. "24h rollback rate: we will ship if the upper bound of the 95% CI is below baseline + 2pp; at current volume our MDE is X pp, so below that threshold this guardrail is a monitor, not a test." Compute X during W0 from the real baseline. Otherwise §5.4's "counter-metric on every claim" is theatre — the guardrail will read "flat" for every change regardless of truth.
findings.source: Statsig, "What are guardrail metrics in A/B tests?"; Dmitriev et al., KDD 2017 §5.4

findings.claim: Name which Goodhart variant each guardrail defends against — the four-variant taxonomy turns "don't game the metric" into a checkable list, and TTFA is exposed to at least two of them.
findings.detail: Manheim & Garrabrant (arXiv 1803.04585) split Goodhart into: regressional (proxy ≠ goal, and you select for the gap), extremal (the proxy/goal relationship breaks at the extreme), causal (intervening on the proxy doesn't move the goal), and adversarial (someone games it). Applied to TTFA: the extremal failure is a builder stripped to a "Create agent" button that publishes a canned demo — TTFA falls to 20 seconds and AR7 collapses. The causal failure is A11's assumption itself: maybe defaults cut TTFA without cutting the thing that actually blocks deployment (confidence). Adversarial is internal — solutions engineers creating agents on customers' behalf inflate WPA.
findings.soWhat: Add a one-line "defends against" tag on each guardrail in §1: AR7 defends TTFA against extremal Goodhart; TCR defends it against causal Goodhart; a new guardrail — agents per account, and internal-vs-external traffic kept as its own series (the doc already refuses to exclude internal traffic, which is right) — defends WPA against adversarial Goodhart. This is four words per line and it makes the guardrail set auditable rather than assertive.
findings.source: Manheim & Garrabrant, "Categorizing Variants of Goodhart's Law," arXiv:1803.04585 (MIRI)

findings.claim: Amazon's own history says the first version of an input metric gets gamed and needs three or four refinement passes — plan TTFA v2 now rather than defending v1 later.
findings.detail: Amazon measured retail selection as "number of detail pages created." Teams responded by adding tens of thousands of low-demand items; sales did not move. The metric was refined to detail page *views* ("you don't get credit for a new detail page if customers don't view it"), then to the percentage of detail page views where the product was in stock, then to the percentage in stock *and* ready for two-day shipping — ultimately "Fast Track In Stock." Each refinement added a quality qualifier to a volume count. Amazon's framing throughout is "controllable input metrics" — things the team directly controls — reviewed weekly at the WBR.
findings.soWhat: Write the expected refinement path into §3 as a dated commitment, not a footnote: TTFA v1 (time to a test session with turnCount ≥ 1) → v2 (turnCount ≥ 3, i.e. the user actually had a conversation) → v3 (test session whose e2eLatencyBucket was acceptable, i.e. they heard a *good* agent). The doc's own `turnCount` and `e2eLatencyBucket` dimensions already make v2 and v3 computable from day one — log them now so the refinement is a redefinition, not a re-instrumentation.
findings.source: Holistics, "How Amazon Uses Input Metrics" (drawing on Bryar & Carr, Working Backwards)

findings.claim: Activation should be a three-moment ladder with a window on each — the doc has the Aha moment (TTFA) but no Setup moment and its Habit moment is measured on the wrong unit.
findings.detail: Reforge's activation model is Setup → Aha → Habit: setup is when the user has done the actions that give them "a high probability at experiencing the value prop for the first time"; aha is "the first time a user experiences the core value... and within a time window where it can stick," ideally first session or 24–48h; habit is "the core action multiple times within some initial time period" (their example: "User pinned 4 days out of the first 28 days"). The doc's AR7 counts *agents* with production sessions in week 0 and week 1 — that is agent survival, not human habit. A person can have one surviving agent and never return.
findings.soWhat: Add a Setup metric to the input tree (share of new accounts that reach a saved agent with a stack + voice within the first session) and split AR7 into two: AR7-agent (as written, keep it) and a person-level habit metric such as "share of first-agent builders who create or meaningfully edit a second agent within 28 days." The second is what actually predicts account retention and it is currently invisible. Both need a stated window; unbounded activation cannot be compared week to week.
findings.source: Reforge, Retention + Engagement series — Setup / Aha / Habit moments (Casey Winters, Brian Balfour)

findings.claim: A metric definition two people can compute the same way needs eight fields, and Airbnb enforces them in version control — the current doc has about half of them for TTFA and fewer for the rest.
findings.detail: Airbnb's Minerva makes metrics "defined in Git repositories using declarative syntax, version-controlled with full history, peer reviews, and automated testing, deployed via CI/CD" and requires "self-describing metadata, such as ownership, lineage, and metric description" before a metric can be certified. Amplitude's naming rule adds the human half: "Our North Star Metric is called X, which we define as Y," with the name "pithy and punchy" and the definition "precise and clear, explaining exactly how you'll measure it" — their own example is "Weekly Learning Users (WLUs): the count of active Amplitude users who have shared a learning that is consumed by at least two other people in the previous seven days."
findings.soWhat: Add `docs/observability/metric-definitions.md` (or better, a typed file next to `src/lib/observability/types.ts` so CI can check it) with one block per metric carrying all eight fields: name · definition sentence · formula with numerator and denominator named · population · window · exclusions · owner · cadence · target · guardrail. The exclusions line is the one the doc is missing everywhere: bots, internal `cid`s, duplicated agents, imported agents, and resumed sessions all need an explicit in-or-out ruling, or two people will compute two different TTFAs in the first week.
findings.source: Airbnb Engineering, Minerva metric platform (Robert Chang, Amit Pahwa); Amplitude North Star Playbook pp. 24–26

findings.claim: Don't over-engineer the thresholds — Amplitude publicly admits the "two other people" in its own north star was a judgement call, and the criterion is "aspirational and achievable," not optimal.
findings.detail: The playbook: "You might wonder how we came up with exactly two or more users. Did we just pull that out of thin air?... The reality is that these numbers aren't magic. Learning consumed by two other people is great; three is even better; one is better than zero... The important thing is to identify thresholds that are both aspirational and achievable." Cutler's line in the same document: "Powerful ideas imperfectly measured are better than perfect measures for less powerful ideas." The doc's own §8 lists three open questions that are all threshold questions.
findings.soWhat: Stop treating §8's open decisions 1–3 as blockers. Ship WPA with the thresholds as written, add a one-line "why this threshold, and how confident we are" note under each (3-min median TTFA is a sum of the dwell budgets, not a round number — say so, the doc already earns this), and put a revisit date on them. The playbook's own checklist asks "What will be your signal to revisit this metric?" — answer it once, in writing, rather than holding W0 for a perfect number.
findings.source: Amplitude, The North Star Playbook, pp. 25–26

findings.claim: Predicted effects should be ranges with stated assumptions, not point estimates — Shopify's opportunity-sizing template is a sentence the ledger can adopt verbatim.
findings.detail: Shopify frames every sizing as: "if we build feature X, we will acquire MM (+/- delta) new active users in T timeframe under DD assumptions," and requires all estimates "in ranges with an upper and lower bound." Their three methods are t-shirt sizing (early ideation and sanity-checking only), bottom-up from comparables (their worked example: France's 5% localized-email CTR → 3% active-user lift → 100,000 Italian leads × 3% = 3,000 users/yr), and top-down for genuinely new work, which they explicitly test against historical initiative performance because "we're biased to believe that our initiatives will have a positive impact."
findings.soWhat: Rewrite each A-row's "Expected effect" cell in that sentence form with a range: A1 becomes "−30 to −60 s median TTFA over 8 weeks, assuming 70% of first agents never open manual config and preset dwell holds at 45 s p75." This does two things the current table can't: it makes the assumption falsifiable separately from the effect, and it lets you compare A1 against A7 on the same scale even though they reach different populations.
findings.source: Shopify Engineering, "Shopify Data's Guide To Opportunity Sizing"

findings.claim: RICE, scored with Reach taken from the real funnel, is the missing link between the tracker rows and the input metrics — and its exact scales stop the scoring becoming false precision.
findings.detail: Sean McBride's original scales at Intercom: Reach = "how many people each project will affect within a given period," from "real measurements from product metrics instead of pulling numbers from a hat"; Impact = 3 massive / 2 high / 1 medium / 0.5 low / 0.25 minimal; Confidence = 100% high / 80% medium / 50% low, and below 50% is a "total moonshot"; Effort in whole person-months (0.5 for anything well under a month); score = (R × I × C) / E. His caveat: "RICE scores shouldn't be used as a hard and fast rule" — deviate for dependencies and table stakes, but "clearly identify when you're making these trade-offs."
findings.soWhat: Add R/I/C/E columns to the ClickUp Design Tracker and populate Reach from the W0 funnel (how many first-agent builders reach §1 per month), not from intuition. This immediately re-ranks the ledger honestly: A7 (import) has small Reach but huge Impact; A1 (preset) has full Reach with medium Impact; A9 (simulations) has low Confidence (50% — the doc itself says "if TCR does not move, simulations are theatre"). Use Confidence 50% for every row whose assumption has not yet survived a baseline read — that is most of them today.
findings.source: Sean McBride, Intercom — "RICE: Simple prioritization for product managers"

findings.claim: A metric with no named owner and no action threshold is a vanity metric by Cutler's own test — the doc's §8.6 ("who owns the weekly read") is the failure mode, not an open question.
findings.detail: Cutler's ten-statement vanity test includes: the team understands the rationale for tracking it; calculations are "inspectable and decomposable by those with domain knowledge"; the team holds "a working theory about what changes in the metric indicate"; and — the one that matters here — there are "clear action thresholds where metric declines inspire investigation." His summary of the failure: a metric is vanity "when no one can act in a meaningful way" or when movements don't "inspire inspection/action." Elsewhere he names the root cause: "Metrics are too wrapped up in performance, optics, and scrutiny to be useful," and prescribes shifting from "measuring to control and manage" to "measuring to learn."
findings.soWhat: Put a named human against each of the four input metrics and each guardrail in §1, plus an action threshold that triggers investigation (not a target — a trigger: "if p75 TTFA crosses 8 min for two consecutive weeks, the §1 owner opens an investigation"). Close §8.6 by choosing: the weekly read belongs in `docs/observability/weekly-report.md` where a cadence already exists, with the design board consuming it. The general guidance across KPI practice is 3–5 owned metrics per team and no more than about three per individual — four inputs plus four guardrails is already at the ceiling, so nothing new gets added without something leaving.
findings.source: John Cutler, "What Are Vanity Metrics and How to Stop Using Them" (Amplitude) and "TBM 50/53: The Curse of 'Success' Metrics"

findings.claim: Don't force all five HEART categories, and note that with Session Replay disabled the Happiness row has no signal source at all — the paper's own answer is a survey.
findings.detail: Rodden et al. say explicitly that a team "may not find it necessary to use metrics from every category... For example, Engagement may not be meaningful" for some products, and that some may "choose to focus more on Happiness or Task Success." Their two signal sources are "logs and surveys," with attitudinal signals gathered by "deploy[ing] a survey on a regular basis." The practitioner critique adds the counterweight to a single north star: no single metric adequately represents user experience, and optimising one "can render it useless per Goodhart's Law."
findings.soWhat: Declare in §2 which HEART categories are in scope — for a builder, Task Success and Adoption carry it, Retention is AR7, Engagement is deliberately out (more time in the builder is bad, not good) — and say so, so nobody adds an engagement metric later. For Happiness, the privacy policy rules out replay, so add the only remaining instrument: a two-question post-deploy micro-survey ("did the agent behave as you expected?" + free text) gated to first deploys. Without it, §2.4's "confidence in production" is entirely behavioural inference with no attitudinal check.
findings.source: Rodden, Hutchinson & Fu, CHI 2010; QuantUX, "How to make HEART metrics work in practice"

findings.claim: Pre-register Twyman's law: an implausibly large TTFA win should trigger an instrumentation investigation, not a ship decision.
findings.detail: Kohavi: "Twyman: Any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong!" His worked case — Sessions/User at Bing is distributed roughly Normal(0, 0.25%²) across thousands of experiments, so a claimed +2.0% is eight standard deviations out, probability ~1e-15, and gets sent for bug-hunting rather than celebration. His example list is almost entirely instrumentation artefacts: a JavaScript addition that "improved" clicks-per-user because the web beacon had more time to reach the servers; an Office redesign showing a 56% click decline because the new variant listed the price.
findings.soWhat: After W0's two-week baseline, write down the observed week-to-week standard deviation of median TTFA and put it in the ledger. Then add one line to §6.5: any variant claiming more than 3 standard deviations of TTFA improvement is investigated for telemetry loss or a changed stop condition before it is read as a win. Given that the doc's own A2 changes when the test event can fire, this is not hypothetical — A2 is the most likely row to produce a fake win.
findings.source: Kohavi et al., "Seven Rules of Thumb for Web Site Experimenters," KDD 2014 (Twyman's Law slides)

findings.claim: Agora's entire international paying customer base is ~1,880 accounts and total active customers grew 0.4% year-on-year — the console's first-agent population is in the tens per week, not the thousands.
findings.detail: Agora reports Active Customers = "an organization or individual developer from which the Company generated more than $100 of revenue during the preceding 12 months." Q2 2026: 3,892 total, +0.4% YoY from 3,877. Q1 2026: 3,946, +3.8% YoY. The last disclosed split (Q2 2025) was 1,880 for the international Agora business (+12.4% YoY) and 1,997 for Shengwang in China. Studio X serves the international side, so the ceiling on accounts that could ever touch this builder is ~2,000, and new-logo growth is roughly zero. Even if every international account created a first agent once a year, that is ~36 first-agent sessions per week across the entire company.
findings.soWhat: Closes the first pass's gap 1 with an external upper bound. §6.5 must be rewritten as staged rollout + before/after against a pre-declared baseline, with feature flags used for exposure control and rollback, not for causal inference. The A1–A9 ledger should be re-scoped so that A-rows are read as a group against the aggregate TTFA curve plus qualitative evidence, not individually A/B tested. Only TTFA itself has any chance of a powered flag test.
findings.source: Agora, Inc. Q2 2026 results (GlobeNewswire 13 Aug 2026); Q1 2026 results; Bamboo Works on the Agora/Shengwang split

findings.claim: Applying PostHog's own published sample-size formula to the doc's own metrics shows every guardrail is out of reach: ~1,216 users per arm for the rollback guardrail and ~816 for tested-before-live.
findings.detail: PostHog gives N = (16 × variance) / d² per variant, with variance = p(1−p) for funnel metrics, 2 × baseline for counts, and 0.25 × baseline² for sum/avg metrics; default MDE is 30%. Computed against the doc's targets: detecting a 24h rollback rate rising from 5% to 7.5% needs 16 × 0.0475 / 0.025² = 1,216 per arm. Moving tested-before-live from 85% to 90% needs 16 × 0.1275 / 0.05² = 816 per arm. TTFA at a 10-minute baseline needs only ~100 per arm under PostHog's assumed variance (0.25 × baseline², i.e. CV = 0.5), but ~900 per arm at a realistic CV of 1.5 for a time-to-success distribution. PostHog also refuses to show an estimate below 100 exposures and 1 day of runtime.
findings.soWhat: Put this table in §6.5 verbatim. It makes the volume argument unarguable: TTFA is the only input metric with any prospect of a powered experiment, and the four §1 guardrails must be read as monitoring, not as tests that can fail. It also sets an exposure floor per flag — below 100 exposures PostHog will not even produce a number.
findings.source: PostHog docs, Sample size and running time (formula and variance table); arithmetic computed here

findings.claim: Spotify's published decision framework fixes the doc's unfalsifiable "must not rise" guardrails — and shows that each guardrail you add costs power on the primary metric via β* = β/(G+1).
findings.detail: Schultzberg, Ankargren & Frånberg (Spotify, arXiv 2402.11609 / Spotify Engineering, Mar 2024) define four metric types: success (superiority tests), guardrail ("metrics that we don't expect to improve, but we want evidence that they're not deteriorating by more than a certain margin" — non-inferiority tests), deterioration (inferiority tests), and quality (SRM, pre-exposure bias). Two results: "if guardrail metrics with non-inferiority tests are used, the significance level does not need to be multiplicity-adjusted for those tests" — α* = α/S applies only to the S success metrics; but "the type II error rate must be corrected," each metric powered for β* = β/(G+1). With the doc's four guardrails and β = 0.2, β* = 0.04 → 96% power per test → (1.96+1.751)²/(1.96+0.842)² = 1.75× the sample per arm versus a single 80%-powered test.
findings.soWhat: Rewrite §1's guardrails as non-inferiority tests with explicit margins (e.g. "rollback rate non-inferior within +1.5pp") instead of "must not rise." Then cut the guardrail count: at this volume, four guardrails inflate the required sample by ~75% before a single extra user is available. Two guardrails (rollback, publish failure) is the defensible set; the rest become monitored trends.
findings.source: Mårten Schultzberg, Sebastian Ankargren, Mattias Frånberg — "Risk-aware product decisions in A/B tests with multiple metrics" (Spotify)

findings.claim: Spotify's four-clause ship rule is a drop-in replacement for the doc's §5 "kill rule" and is checkable by someone who was not in the room.
findings.detail: Ship if and only if: the treatment is significantly superior to control on at least one success metric; the treatment is significantly non-inferior on all guardrail metrics; no success, guardrail or deterioration metric shows evidence of deterioration; and no quality test significantly invalidates the experiment. The fourth clause is the one the doc has no equivalent of — it names sample ratio mismatch and pre-exposure bias as *tests that must pass before the result counts*, not as caveats.
findings.soWhat: Adopt the four clauses as the header of §6.5 and add a quality-test row to the §6.4 PostHog objects (SRM check on flag exposure, and an isFirstAgent-share check). The doc's existing "Data quality" trend is close but is not wired into the ship decision.
findings.source: Spotify Engineering, Risk-Aware Product Decisions in A/B Tests with Multiple Metrics

findings.claim: The doc's guardrail vocabulary is missing the deterioration tier, and it is currently mis-classifying rollback rate.
findings.detail: Spotify's taxonomy separates guardrails — where a bounded regression is acceptable and you test non-inferiority against a margin — from deterioration metrics, where no margin is acceptable and you run an inferiority test. The doc's §1 lists four items under one heading: publish failure rate, 24h rollback/disable rate, support contacts per new agent, and median production latency. Rollback and publish failure are deterioration metrics (no acceptable margin — a rise is a revert trigger). Support contacts and latency are true guardrails (a small, bounded rise in exchange for a large speed win is a trade the owner might take).
findings.soWhat: Split §1's guardrail block into two named tiers with different decision rules, and state the margin for each guardrail. This is also the mechanism that makes A10 ("speed vs trust, TCR is the tiebreaker") operational rather than rhetorical.
findings.source: Schultzberg et al., Spotify

findings.claim: Time-to-first-answer should be reported as a geometric mean with log-transformed confidence intervals below n≈25, not as a median — which contradicts the first pass's truncation recommendation.
findings.detail: Sauro & Lewis (CHI 2010, "Average task times in usability tests: what to report?") and MeasuringU's small-sample guidance: task time is positively skewed with a floor at zero, "it's not uncommon for some users to take 10 to 20 times longer than other users," and below about n = 25 "the geometric mean (average of the log values transformed back) tends to be a better measure of the middle"; above 25 "the median works fine." Secondary summaries put the geometric mean at ~13% less error and ~22% less bias than the sample median, with the sample median carrying ~7% bias at n = 10. The prescribed CI method is to log-transform, compute the interval on the logs, and transform back.
findings.soWhat: Write the central-tendency rule into the TTFA metric definition itself: geometric mean + log-CI for any cell under 25 (every moderated study, every early flag cell, every per-cid breakdown), median/p75 only when n ≥ 25. This is a better answer than truncating, because truncation discards exactly the slow sessions the dwell budgets exist to find.
findings.source: Jeff Sauro & James Lewis, CHI 2010; MeasuringU, "Best practices for using statistics on small sample sizes"

findings.claim: A 20–30 participant moderated benchmark is the only instrument that can actually measure a TTFA change at Agora's volume, and it can resolve roughly the size of change the ledger predicts.
findings.detail: MeasuringU: "sample sizes of 20–30 seem to provide the most gain in measurement precision for the smallest recruiting pain"; at n = 20 a task time has a margin of error under 20% at 95% confidence, and you have "at least a 90% chance of seeing problems that affect 10% or more of the user population." NN/g's parallel guidance: 40 participants is the standard for quantitative studies (15% margin of error, 95% confidence), 28 at 90%/15%, 15 at 90%/20%, and 19–47 for continuous metrics like task time. A1+A2 together claim −105 s off a ~3–10 min TTFA, i.e. roughly a 20–30% reduction — inside what n = 20 can see.
findings.soWhat: Add a W0 line item the doc currently lacks: a 20-participant moderated first-agent benchmark run against today's console, timed the same way TTFA is defined, reported as a geometric mean with a log-CI. It gives A0 a real baseline in a week instead of two weeks of telemetry that may never accumulate 100 exposures, and it is the measurement that survives the volume problem.
findings.source: MeasuringU, Sample size recommendations for benchmark studies; NN/g, How many participants for quantitative usability studies

findings.claim: Every major competitor publishes a time-to-first-agent claim, and the best of them is three minutes — so the doc's ≤3-minute median target is parity with a marketing claim, not a lead.
findings.detail: Retell: "launch a production voice agent in about three minutes," "Go live in minutes, not sprints," "most customers are live and running test calls the same day they sign up." Vapi docs: "Build your first voice agent in 5 minutes using our dashboard." ElevenLabs: "build your first conversational agent in as little as 5 minutes" and "Deploy AI Agents in Minutes, Not Months." LiveKit docs: "Build and deploy a simple voice assistant with Python or Node.js in less than 10 minutes." Synthflow: "Build and launch AI voice agents in minutes," with one independent review timing a working appointment-booking agent at 11 minutes. Bland's "minutes" applies to prototypes; its enterprise insurance page says "live in 30 days."
findings.soWhat: Closes gap 4, the first pass's highest-value open item. "Fastest platform" cannot be claimed against a 3-minute target alone. Either the target moves (a sub-90-second first answer would be genuinely differentiated, and A7's importer target is already ≤90 s), or the claim shifts to a dimension the others do not compete on — time to a *trusted* deploy, where nobody publishes anything.
findings.source: Retell AI comparison page; Vapi docs quickstart; ElevenLabs Agents; LiveKit Agents docs; Synthflow

findings.claim: No competitor publishes a *measured* TTFA — every number is a scripted-happy-path documentation claim — which makes publishing our measured distribution the actual differentiator.
findings.detail: Across Vapi, Retell, ElevenLabs, LiveKit, Synthflow and Bland, none of the time claims is accompanied by a definition, a population, a window, a sample size or a percentile. They are tutorial-completion times, measured on a user who already knows the steps, not medians across real first-time builders. The only competitor numbers with methodology anywhere in this space are third-party latency benchmarks — the same pattern §4 of the doc already exploits for TTFAB.
findings.soWhat: Treat the published TTFA methodology as a deliverable, not just an internal metric. §4 already forbids printing vendor component latency as an end-to-end number; apply the same discipline to onboarding speed and publish median/p75/p90 with n and the event definitions. A measured p75 with a stated method beats an unmeasured "3 minutes" in any technical buyer's evaluation, and it is defensible when a competitor disputes it.
findings.source: Synthesis across Vapi, Retell, ElevenLabs, LiveKit, Synthflow and Bland public docs and marketing

findings.claim: The "no vendor API keys needed" advantage is not unusual — it is table stakes across the competitive set, which undermines A2's stated blocker.
findings.detail: LiveKit Inference "provides access to many of the best models and providers for voice agents, including models from OpenAI, Google, AssemblyAI, Deepgram, Cartesia, Inworld, and more," is "included in LiveKit Cloud," and "does not require any additional plugins" — explicitly contrasted with plugins, which need "your own account with the provider, as well as an API key." Vapi's provider-keys page frames BYOK purely as a billing switch: "Once your API key is validated, you won't be charged when using that provider through Vapi. Instead, you'll be charged directly by the provider" — i.e. Vapi works without your keys by default. Retell gives $10 of free credits (~60 minutes of calls) on signup. ElevenLabs' dashboard path needs no API key at all; keys are only for CLI/API creation.
findings.soWhat: Directly contradicts the product-context premise. Do not build positioning or the §1 preset story on "zero keys." More consequentially, A2's fallback ("if attempts rise but success does not, the blocker is credentials/quota") is probably testing a blocker that does not exist for the default path; rewrite A2's failure branch around draft-state and quota instead. The real bundled-stack advantage, if there is one, is Agora's own measured end-to-end latency (§4), not credential avoidance.
findings.source: LiveKit docs (LiveKit Inference); Vapi docs (provider keys); Retell AI free credits; ElevenLabs Agents quickstart

findings.claim: PostHog group analytics is a paid add-on whose billing applies to every identified event in the project — so the `cid` breakdowns §6.4 assumes are a budget decision, not a free property.
findings.detail: PostHog docs: "Billing starts when you enable group analytics from your billing page, not when you add group analytics code to your application," and "billing applies to all identified events in your project, not just events with group properties attached." The cap is five group types per project. Group analytics is not in the free-tier bundle (which covers 1M analytics events, 5K replays, 1M flag requests, 100K exceptions, 1.5K survey responses).
findings.soWhat: Closes half of gap 6. Open decision §8.4 must expand from "is VITE_POSTHOG_KEY set" to "is group analytics enabled and funded" — every account-level cut in §6.4 (breakdown by cid, per-company TTFA, internal-traffic series) depends on it, and turning it on re-prices the whole project's identified-event volume, not just the builder's.
findings.source: PostHog docs, Group analytics; PostHog pricing

findings.claim: PostHog's native time-to-convert insight does not expose p75/p90 — the TTFA and TTFD objects have to be SQL insights, or the doc's percentile targets are uncomputable as written.
findings.detail: PostHog's funnels documentation describes the time-to-convert graph only as showing "steps with the highest friction. Steps with a long time to convert are likely much harder than steps with a short time" — it does not state which statistics are reported. PostHog's own conversion-modelling guidance points to HogQL with windowFunnel for time-to-convert, and warns that pre-aggregated numbers lock you out of asking later for the median, the 90th percentile or the distribution if they were not pre-computed.
findings.soWhat: Closes the other half of gap 6. Rewrite the TTFA and TTFD rows in §6.4 from "Funnel, time-to-convert" to "SQL insight: windowFunnel + quantile(0.5/0.75/0.9)", and ship the query alongside the schema-2.2.0 change so the dashboard promise in §6.3 clause 4 is actually met. Otherwise §2.1's p75 ≤ 6 min and §2.2's p75 ≤ 45 min are targets nobody can read off the tool.
findings.source: PostHog docs, Funnels; PostHog conversion-metrics guidance

findings.claim: Amplitude's 2025 benchmark of 2,600+ companies supplies the external evidence for the activation→retention leg the doc only assumes — but it is measured on user day-7 return, not on agent survival.
findings.detail: "When at least 7% of your original cohort of users return on day seven, your product has demonstrated early value that correlates strongly with long-term success" — 7% D7 puts a product in the top 25% for activation; the 90th-percentile day-14 rate is about 9%; "69% of top day seven performers were also top three-month performers"; in enterprise, the top 10% reach 12.4% D7 against a 2.1% median, nearly six times less.
findings.soWhat: Closes gap 5 with a number and a published bar. Add a user-level D7 return metric beside AR7 with 7% as the initial target, and use the 69% figure as the stated basis for the tree's activation→retention link rather than leaving it as an unsourced assumption. It also confirms the first pass's point that the Habit moment is measured on the wrong unit — agents cannot be compared to any published benchmark; users can.
findings.source: Amplitude, "The 7% retention rule," from the 2025 Product Benchmark Report (2,600+ companies)

findings.claim: The formal name for the doc's largest untested assumption is the Prentice surrogacy criterion, and there is a published method to validate it on data Agora already has.
findings.detail: The surrogate-index literature (Athey, Chetty, Imbens & Kang, NBER w26463; Review of Economic Studies, 2025) combines short-term proxies into an index whose treatment effect equals the long-term effect "under the Prentice surrogacy assumption, which requires that the primary outcome is independent of the treatment conditional on the surrogates," and the paper "provides simple methods to validate these assumptions using additional observed outcomes." Their demonstration uses six quarters of short-run data to estimate effects that would otherwise take nine years to observe.
findings.soWhat: Gives §3's A0 a testable prerequisite. Before W1, run the surrogacy check on existing agent_create / agent_publish history: does create→publish elapsed time predict 90-day agent survival conditional on account size and source? If elapsed time carries no signal once account is conditioned on, the whole TTFA→WPA tree is decoration and the work should re-point at TCR/AR7 — which is exactly the decision rule A0 already promises but currently has no method for.
findings.source: Susan Athey, Raj Chetty, Guido Imbens & Hyunseung Kang — The Surrogate Index

findings.claim: CUPED — the standard rescue for low-traffic experiments — cannot help TTFA, because first-agent builders have no pre-experiment period.
findings.detail: CUPED (Deng, Xu, Kohavi & Walker, WSDM 2013) reduced variance by about 50% on Bing and typically delivers 30–50%, shortening tests proportionally. But the reduction is proportional to the correlation between a pre-experiment covariate and the metric, and the doc's primary metric is defined on first agents by definition new users. Statsig's implementation "uses stratification alongside CUPED to account for users who may not have pre-experiment data," which "retains users with missing pre-experiment data while still providing variance reduction where applicable" — i.e. it keeps them in the analysis but gives them no variance reduction.
findings.soWhat: Pre-empts the obvious reviewer question "why not just use CUPED?" in §6.5. State that it is unavailable for TTFA and available only for second-agent and existing-account metrics. If the volume problem becomes binding, the branch to read is Deng et al., KDD 2023, on in-experiment variance reduction, which was written for exactly this case.
findings.source: Deng, Xu, Kohavi & Walker (Microsoft, WSDM 2013); Statsig docs on variance reduction

findings.claim: The voice-agent eval vendors define production readiness at the conversation level with bars the doc has no equivalent of — and their sample-size figure independently corroborates A12.
findings.detail: Hamming's production-reliability framework: goal completion rate baseline >85% with ±2% drift before alerting; first call resolution >75% with ±3%; hallucination rate <5% with ±1% (exceeding it is "critical"); word error rate <10% with ±2%; error rate <0.1% excellent, >1% critical; time-to-first-word <300ms excellent, >800ms critical failure; turn latency p95 <800ms. On experimentation: "approximately 1,000 calls per variant for 95% statistical confidence" on goal completion, 500+ minimum for goal completion, 1,000+ for FCR, 200+ for latency p95; stop early when error rate exceeds 2% in either variant; declare a winner only when secondary metrics have not regressed more than 5%. A separate readiness checklist puts task completion above 95%, compliance at 100% and average latency under 500ms, with deployment blocked if any threshold is breached.
findings.soWhat: Closes gap 7. TCR ≥95% measures publishes surviving 24h — it says nothing about whether the conversations were any good, so it is not comparable to these bars and on its own it is a low bar. Add a conversation-level row to §2.4 (goal completion ≥85%, hallucination <5%) sourced from the runtime path, and note that the 200-sample floor for latency p95 is the one eval bar Agora's volume can actually clear. The ~1,000 calls/variant figure is independent corroboration of A12 from a second source.
findings.source: Hamming AI, Testing voice agents: load, regression and A/B evaluation for production reliability

findings.claim: Agora's own financials argue the north star is pointed at the part of the business that is not growing — expansion, not new logos, is producing the revenue.
findings.detail: Q2 2026: revenue $40.4M, +18% YoY, third consecutive quarter of accelerating growth; dollar-based net retention 104%, up from 94% a year earlier; GAAP net profit $2.2M, +50%. Against that, active customers moved +0.4% YoY (3,892 vs 3,877). Revenue growth is coming from existing accounts spending more, not from new accounts arriving. The earnings commentary attributes it to conversational AI agents in market surveying, buyer-interest capture and customer service.
findings.soWhat: Weekly Proven Agents as written counts first agents from new builders — the thinnest part of the funnel. Split WPA into a new-account series and an existing-account series and report both, and make isFirstAgent the primary breakdown on every §6.4 object. It also re-prioritises the ledger: if expansion is where the money is, A7 (import), templates and the second-agent path are the rows that touch the growing half of the business, and they currently sit in W3, last.
findings.source: Agora, Inc. Q2 2026 financial results

findings.claim: Airbnb's guardrails post is still unreadable, but Spotify's paper supersedes it — it is peer-reviewed, gives the statistical treatment firsthand, and Kohavi himself amplified the Airbnb original, so citing Spotify loses nothing.
findings.detail: The Medium original (Xifara, Andersen, Yang & Rauh, Airbnb Tech Blog) returned 403 on a second route and the InfoQ write-up returned HTTP 405; freedium is dead. The Airbnb framework as described secondhand is a "Stat Sig Negative Guardrail" that escalates an experiment showing a statistically significant negative impact on a metric owned by another team, with escalation severity tuned per metric. That is a governance mechanism. The Spotify paper supplies what the first pass actually wanted: the non-inferiority formulation, the multiplicity result, and the power correction, with Monte Carlo validation.
findings.soWhat: Stop chasing the Airbnb post. Cite Spotify for the statistics and Airbnb (via the secondary description) only for the cross-team escalation idea — which is worth one line in §8.6: a guardrail breach should escalate to the metric's owner, which presupposes the doc names one, and it currently does not.
findings.source: Airbnb Tech Blog (inaccessible); InfoQ summary (inaccessible); Spotify paper as substitute

numbers.label: Recommended number of North Star input metrics
numbers.value: 3–5 ("a small set of influential, complementary factors")
numbers.caveat: The doc's four (TTFA, TTFD, TCR, AR7) sits correctly in range, but two of them are serial rather than independent.

numbers.label: North Star checklist
numbers.value: 7 questions: expresses customer value · represents vision and strategy · leading indicator · actionable · understandable to non-technical partners · measurable · not a vanity metric
numbers.source: Amplitude, The North Star Playbook, p. 14
numbers.caveat: WPA passes 6; "understandable to non-technical partners" needs the name doing more work than the formula.

numbers.label: Amplitude's own north star threshold
numbers.value: Weekly Learning Users = shared a learning consumed by ≥2 other people in the previous 7 days
numbers.source: Amplitude, The North Star Playbook, p. 26
numbers.caveat: Amplitude states in print that the "2" was not rigorously derived — precedent for not agonising over Agora's 3-minute target.

numbers.label: Netflix's 2005 north star
numbers.value: % of customers placing 3 or more DVDs in their queue during their first session
numbers.source: Amplitude, The North Star Playbook, p. 8
numbers.caveat: A first-session, time-boxed, threshold-count metric — structurally the closest published analogue to a TTFA-style activation metric.

numbers.label: Named vanity metrics to avoid as a north star
numbers.value: DAU · registered users · ad impressions · story points delivered · downloads · time on page · page views
numbers.source: Amplitude, The North Star Playbook, p. 18
numbers.caveat: "Time on page" being on this list is a direct warning about how the dwell budgets are framed — they are design contracts, not success metrics.

numbers.label: Minimum sample size rule for a skewed metric
numbers.value: 355 × skewness²
numbers.caveat: Applies to the normality of the mean; percentile targets (the doc's p75) have their own, generally larger, requirements.

numbers.label: Bing TimeToSuccess — untruncated
numbers.value: skewness² = 4.4 · min sample 1,550/arm · 12.3% detectable at 80% power
numbers.source: Kohavi et al., KDD 2014, Rule #7 table
numbers.caveat: Bing's own time-to-success metric; TTFA is the same metric shape.

numbers.label: Bing TimeToSuccess — truncated
numbers.value: skewness² = 0.15 · min sample ~50/arm · 27.9% detectable at 80% power
numbers.source: Kohavi et al., KDD 2014, Rule #7 table
numbers.caveat: Truncation cuts the sample requirement ~30x at the cost of sensitivity — the trade Agora should take at console volumes.

numbers.label: Bing Sessions/User (their north star)
numbers.value: skewness² = 13.2 · min sample 4,700/arm · 5.4% detectable at 80% power
numbers.source: Kohavi et al., KDD 2014, Rule #7 table
numbers.caveat: Sets the scale for how much traffic an agent-builder A/B test needs; if Agora is below this, flags in the console are for staged rollout, not for causal claims.

numbers.label: Base rate of experiments that actually move metrics
numbers.value: π ≈ 1/3 across Microsoft; 10–20% success rate on ideas at Bing
numbers.source: Kohavi et al., KDD 2014, Rule #3 / Bayes slide
numbers.caveat: Prior for discounting the A1–A9 predicted effects; a well-optimised surface sits at the low end, a neglected one higher.

numbers.label: Typical size of a real win on a key metric
numbers.value: 0.1%–1% after a lot of work; 10% revenue wins are "rare" (2 in Kohavi's career at Bing)
numbers.caveat: Applies to key organizational metrics, not feature metrics — a −45s TTFA change may be plausible precisely because the builder is not yet optimised.

numbers.label: Dilution rule
numbers.value: A 10% improvement to a 1% segment ≈ 0.1% overall impact
numbers.caveat: Directly applies to A7 (import from Vapi/Retell) and A4 (backup providers).

numbers.label: Server speed sensitivity (why latency is a real guardrail)
numbers.value: Bing: every 100 ms speedup ≈ +0.6% revenue; a 10 ms server improvement pays an engineer's fully-loaded annual cost
numbers.caveat: Search-engine economics, not voice — but it is the canonical published justification for keeping latency as a hard guardrail.

numbers.label: Perceived vs measured latency
numbers.value: Slowing Bing's right pane by 250 ms produced no significant change in key metrics
numbers.caveat: Where the latency lands matters more than the number — supports the doc's rule that vendor component latency must never be printed as end-to-end.

numbers.label: Underpowered guardrails
numbers.value: A test powered for a 1% primary effect may only detect 10–30% changes in guardrail metrics
numbers.source: Statsig, "What are guardrail metrics in A/B tests?"
numbers.caveat: Vendor blog, but consistent with Dmitriev §5.4's measured case (0.5% observed vs 7.8% MDE).

numbers.label: Multiple-comparison cost of many guardrails
numbers.value: 5% false-positive rate per metric at α=0.05; hundreds of false positives expected across 5,000 experiments/yr
numbers.source: Statsig; Kohavi et al., KDD 2014, Rule #2
numbers.caveat: Argues for 4 guardrails, not 10 — the doc's current four is the right number.

numbers.label: Power recommendation for success and guardrail metrics
numbers.value: ≥80% power, established by a priori power analysis
numbers.caveat: Their simplified house rule at Bing US was ≥10% of users for one week for a feature affecting most users.

numbers.label: RICE Impact scale
numbers.value: 3 massive · 2 high · 1 medium · 0.5 low · 0.25 minimal
numbers.caveat: Fixed ordinal scale by design — resist inventing intermediate values.

numbers.label: RICE Confidence scale
numbers.value: 100% high · 80% medium · 50% low · below 50% = "total moonshot"
numbers.caveat: Every A-row whose assumption has not survived a baseline read should be scored at 50%.

numbers.label: Activation time window for the aha moment
numbers.value: First session, or within 24–48 hours
numbers.caveat: Agora's 3-minute TTFA target is far inside this, which is the right ambition; the missing piece is the habit window (Reforge example: 4 days out of the first 28).

numbers.label: Recommended KPI count
numbers.value: 3–5 per team; ~3 per individual owner; no more than ~8–9 total
numbers.source: Stacey Barr / PuMP and general KPI practice
numbers.caveat: Practitioner consensus, not research; the doc's 4 inputs + 4 guardrails is already at the ceiling.

numbers.label: PostHog's own north star definition
numbers.value: "Discoveries": analysing any insight or session recording for ≥10 seconds; chosen because it "retained 2.3x more users than the alternative metric"
numbers.source: PostHog, "Finding your North Star metric and why it matters"
numbers.caveat: Useful precedent for a duration-thresholded definition, and for how to justify a threshold with retention data.

numbers.label: Twyman's law trigger at Bing
numbers.value: Sessions/User ~ Normal(0, 0.25%²); a claimed +2.0% is 8σ, p ≈ 1e-15 → investigate, don't ship
numbers.caveat: Requires a measured baseline variance first — which is exactly what W0 produces.

numbers.label: Real-world funnel conversion floor
numbers.value: "final success rates of less than 1% are not uncommon" in sign-up and shopping funnels
numbers.caveat: Cited to argue that every funnel step needs its own power check, not that Agora's funnel will be this bad.

numbers.label: Agora total Active Customers, Q2 2026
numbers.caveat: Definition: >$100 of revenue in the preceding 12 months. Includes both Agora international and Shengwang China.

numbers.label: Agora Active Customers, Q1 2026
numbers.caveat: Sequentially down to 3,892 in Q2.

numbers.label: Agora international vs Shengwang active-customer split (last disclosed)
numbers.value: 1,880 international (+12.4% YoY) vs 1,997 China (+1.4%)
numbers.caveat: Q2 2025 figures; 2026 releases no longer disclose the split. 1,880 is the practical ceiling on accounts that could use Studio X.

numbers.label: Agora Q2 2026 revenue / DBNRR / net profit
numbers.caveat: Growth is expansion-led: revenue +18% against customer count +0.4%.

numbers.label: PostHog sample-size formula
numbers.value: N = (16 × variance) / d² per variant; variance = p(1−p) funnel, 2×baseline count, 0.25×baseline² sum/avg; default MDE 30%
numbers.source: PostHog docs, Sample size and running time
numbers.caveat: The 0.25×baseline² heuristic assumes CV = 0.5, optimistic for time-to-success data.

numbers.label: Users per arm to detect 24h rollback rising 5% → 7.5%
numbers.caveat: Absolute MDE 2.5pp. Unreachable at Agora's volume.

numbers.label: Users per arm to move tested-before-live 85% → 90%
numbers.caveat: Absolute MDE 5pp.

numbers.label: Users per arm to detect −2 min on a 10-min TTFA
numbers.value: ~100 (PostHog's assumed variance, CV 0.5) vs ~900 (CV 1.5)
numbers.caveat: The 9× spread is the whole argument for measuring TTFA's variance in W0 before promising any experiment.

numbers.label: PostHog experiment minimum before an estimate appears
numbers.value: 100 exposures and 1 day of runtime
numbers.source: PostHog docs, Sample size and running time
numbers.caveat: An exposure floor per flag, independent of power.

numbers.label: Spotify power correction for guardrails
numbers.value: β* = β/(G+1); α* = α/S for success metrics only
numbers.caveat: G = number of guardrails, S = number of success metrics.

numbers.label: Sample inflation from the doc's four guardrails
numbers.caveat: Argues for cutting four guardrails to two.

numbers.label: Geometric-mean threshold for task times
numbers.value: Use geometric mean below n≈25; median fine at n≥25
numbers.caveat: Reported advantage over the sample median (~13% less error, ~22% less bias; ~7% median bias at n=10) is from secondary summaries — the CHI PDF would not parse.

numbers.label: Benchmark usability study sample size
numbers.value: 20–30 participants; at n=20, task-time margin of error <20% at 95% confidence, 90% chance of catching problems affecting ≥10% of users
numbers.source: MeasuringU, Sample size recommendations for benchmark studies
numbers.caveat: Between-subjects comparisons need more than within-subjects.

numbers.label: NN/g quantitative study sample sizes
numbers.value: 40 standard (15% MoE, 95% conf); 28 at 90%/15%; 15 at 90%/20%; 19–47 for continuous metrics
numbers.source: NN/g, How many participants for quantitative usability studies
numbers.caveat: Derived for binary success metrics; task time sits in the 19–47 band.

numbers.label: Competitor published time-to-first-agent claims
numbers.value: Retell ~3 min · Vapi 5 min · ElevenLabs "as little as 5 minutes" · LiveKit <10 min · Synthflow "minutes" (11 min in one independent test) · Bland "minutes" (prototype), 30 days (enterprise)
numbers.source: Retell, Vapi docs, ElevenLabs, LiveKit docs, Synthflow
numbers.caveat: All are scripted-happy-path documentation claims. None states a definition, population, window, sample size or percentile.

numbers.label: Retell free starting credit
numbers.value: $10 ≈ 60 minutes of calls, no vendor API keys required
numbers.caveat: Comparable managed-key defaults exist at Vapi, ElevenLabs and LiveKit Inference.

numbers.label: PostHog group analytics
numbers.value: Paid add-on; billing applies to all identified events in the project; max 5 group types
numbers.caveat: Not included in the free tier's 1M analytics events.

numbers.label: Amplitude day-7 retention benchmark
numbers.value: 7% D7 = top 25% for activation; ~9% D14 at the 90th percentile; enterprise top 10% 12.4% D7 vs 2.1% median
numbers.caveat: Measured on user return, not agent survival.

numbers.label: Activation→retention persistence
numbers.value: 69% of top day-7 performers were also top three-month performers
numbers.caveat: A persistence rate across quartiles, not a correlation coefficient, despite being reported as one elsewhere.

numbers.label: Hamming production-readiness bars
numbers.value: Goal completion >85% (±2% drift) · FCR >75% (±3%) · hallucination <5% (±1%) · WER <10% (±2%) · error rate <0.1% excellent / >1% critical · TTFW <300ms excellent / >800ms critical · turn latency p95 <800ms
numbers.source: Hamming AI, Testing voice agents for production reliability
numbers.caveat: Vendor-published, not independently audited.

numbers.label: Hamming experiment sample sizes for voice agents
numbers.value: ~1,000 calls per variant for 95% confidence on goal completion; 500+ minimum; 1,000+ for FCR; 200+ for latency p95; stop early above 2% error rate
numbers.caveat: Independently corroborates the doc's A12 figure from a second source.

numbers.label: CUPED variance reduction
numbers.value: ~50% at Bing; typically 30–50%
numbers.source: Deng, Xu, Kohavi & Walker, WSDM 2013; Statsig docs
numbers.caveat: Proportional to pre-period correlation — effectively zero for first-time users, who have no pre-period.

numbers.label: Low-traffic A/B threshold
numbers.value: "Tens of thousands of users" minimum; ~200,000 users to detect a 5% improvement
numbers.source: Kohavi, via secondary summaries of his low-traffic guidance
numbers.caveat: Secondary; the LinkedIn primary was not retrievable. Directionally consistent with the computed PostHog numbers.

gaps: Agora's own console traffic is still unmeasured. The 1,880 international active-customer figure is a ceiling on *accounts*, not a count of weekly first-agent builders — the ratio between them (what share of accounts open the AI console, how many distinct builders per account, how many create a first agent) exists only in PostHog and nobody has pulled it. W0 should report this number in week one, before any target in §2 is signed off.

The Airbnb "Designing Experimentation Guardrails" post is still unread firsthand — Medium 403 on a second route, the InfoQ write-up returns HTTP 405, freedium's domain is dead. Their actual non-inferiority margins and false-alarm handling remain unverified. Spotify's paper covers the statistics better, so this is now a low-value gap.

The Sauro & Lewis CHI 2010 PDF would not parse, so the specific 13%-less-error / 22%-less-bias / 7%-median-bias figures for the geometric mean come from secondary MeasuringU summaries. The n<25 recommendation itself is confirmed firsthand.

PostHog's time-to-convert UI could not be confirmed to show or omit a median — the docs page describes the graph's purpose only. Someone with the project open should check in five minutes whether p75/p90 are available natively before §6.4 is rewritten as SQL insights.

Vapi's default-key behaviour is inferred, not confirmed: their provider-keys page only says BYOK shifts billing to the provider, and never states whether Vapi supplies default keys or how much free credit a new account gets. Retell's $10/60-minute figure is from secondary coverage, not Retell's own pricing page.

No competitor's *internal* onboarding funnel data was found, and it almost certainly is not public. The claim that nobody measures TTFA is an absence-of-evidence argument; a conference talk or a careers-page metric could contradict it.

The Amplitude benchmark numbers come from the blog summary of the 2025 Product Benchmark Report, not the report itself — the category breakdown (is there a developer-tools or API-infrastructure band?) is unread, and the widely-repeated "developer tools 18–28% activation" figure traces to Userpilot's report, which I could not open.

Nothing was found on what a "trusted change rate" equivalent looks like at any other developer console, so TCR ≥95% still has no external calibration. The Hamming and Coval bars measure conversations, not publishes, so they inform §2.4 but do not benchmark TCR itself.

corpus.headline: The defensible target set is: every control responds under 400ms, no single step blocks past 10s without a labour-illusion progress state, the whole zero-key path to hearing the agent talk (TTFA) lands under 5 minutes to beat Vapi and ElevenLabs, a deployed agent under 15 minutes to beat Retell, and the total first session must fit inside the 2–4 minute page-visit norm extended to at most ~28 minutes of engaged work — because published research says attention on a screen now averages 47 seconds and any wait over ~10s hands the user to another tab they may not come back from.

findings.claim: Nielsen's 10-second limit is the hard ceiling for any single blocking step in the builder — past it, users leave the tab, and that is the abandonment event, not the wait itself.
findings.detail: Nielsen's three limits (published 1993, still NN/g's canonical article) are 0.1s for the feeling of instantaneous reaction, 1.0s for uninterrupted flow of thought, and 10s as "the limit for keeping the user's attention focused on the dialogue." Beyond 10s Nielsen says users will want to perform other tasks while waiting, so the system must show a percent-done indicator and "a clearly signposted way for the user to interrupt the operation." This maps directly onto Studio X's slow operations: deploying, provisioning a SIP number, indexing a knowledge base, and the first connection of the Voice call test panel.
findings.soWhat: Set a hard engineering budget: any Studio X action that can exceed 10s (deploy, SIP provisioning, KB indexing, first test-call connect) must ship with a determinate progress state and a cancel affordance, and must fire a PostHog timing event so you can see the p50/p90/p99 of each. Anything that can be made non-blocking (KB indexing, number provisioning) should be moved to a background job with the user free to keep configuring.
findings.source: Jakob Nielsen / Nielsen Norman Group, "Response Time Limits" (1 Jan 1993)

findings.claim: NN/g's own guidance says a simple task should be completable in about one minute and the average site visit runs 2–4 minutes — so the accordion section a user opens must each be finishable inside roughly a minute.
findings.detail: NN/g's "Powers of 10" time-scale article extends Nielsen's limits upward: at 10s "the average attention span is maxed out"; at 1 minute, "users should be able to complete simple tasks in about 1 minute"; the average site visit is 2–4 minutes; at 1 hour, the typical usability-study duration, "people tire beyond this"; and half of e-commerce purchases happen within 28 minutes of arrival. That 28-minute figure is the closest published proxy for how long an engaged, motivated user will sustain a committed multi-step task in one sitting.
findings.soWhat: Budget each of the five Studio X sections at ≤1 minute of active work for the default path, and the whole first session at ≤28 minutes to a deployed agent. Instrument per-section dwell time in PostHog (section_opened → section_completed) and treat any section whose p50 exceeds 60s as a defect, not a design choice. The Voice & Models section, with the latency-vs-cost slider as the only required input, should be well under that; the Prompt section is the one at risk.
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group, "Powers of 10: Time Scales in User Experience"

findings.claim: Attention on a screen now averages 47 seconds before a task switch, down from 2.5 minutes in 2004 — so the builder must be designed to survive interruption, not to hold uninterrupted attention.
findings.detail: Gloria Mark's longitudinal observational work (stopwatch-clicked task switches in real workplaces) recorded an average focus duration on a screen of about 2.5 minutes in 2004, 75 seconds by 2012, and 47 seconds by 2016, with a median of 40 seconds — half of all observations were 40 seconds or shorter. Her related finding is that it can take up to ~25 minutes to return attention to an interrupted project. This is population-level knowledge-worker data, not builder-specific, but it bounds the realistic assumption: the user will leave mid-flow.
findings.soWhat: Assume the user will tab away mid-configuration and design Studio X to be resumable rather than continuous: autosave every field on change, persist accordion open/closed state and scroll position, and on return surface a "you were here" resume affordance pointing at the next unfinished step. Instrument a PostHog `builder_session_resumed` event with time-since-last-interaction so you can measure how many sessions are actually multi-sitting — that number will likely justify the resume work on its own.
findings.source: Gloria Mark (UC Irvine), "Attention Span" research, via Dropbox Blog / Steelcase interview

findings.claim: The Doherty Threshold of 400ms is the right budget for every interactive control in the builder — slider drag, sheet open, voice preview, model switch.
findings.detail: Doherty and Thadani (IBM Systems Journal, 1982) argued systems should respond within 400ms rather than the then-standard 2 seconds, and reported that when the machine and user interact without either waiting on the other, "productivity soars" and work quality improves. Secondary summaries cite participants completing 25–30% more transactions per hour on sub-400ms systems, though that specific figure is repeated in UX blogs rather than quoted from the original paper and should be treated as indicative.
findings.soWhat: Give Studio X a 400ms interaction budget for everything that is not a network round-trip: the latency-vs-cost slider re-rendering its bundled stack, the Configure sheet opening, the Select voice dialog opening and playing a preview sample. Voice preview samples in particular should be pre-cached or pre-warmed — a voice that takes 2s to preview will make the user audition fewer voices and pick worse. Track a PostHog `interaction_latency_ms` on these and alarm above 400ms p90.
findings.source: Walter J. Doherty & Ahrvind J. Thadani, IBM Systems Journal (1982), via Laws of UX

findings.claim: Three named competitors publish explicit setup-time claims, which sets the number Agora has to beat: Vapi "under 5 minutes" to a phone agent, Retell "15 minutes", ElevenLabs ~7 dashboard steps with no API key.
findings.detail: Vapi's phone quickstart states "in under 5 minutes, you'll create a voice assistant and start talking to it" and requires roughly 7 distinct decisions (template, first message, system prompt, number type, area code, inbound assistant assignment, then dialling). Retell's quickstart is titled "Build your first Retell AI phone agent in 15 minutes" and — importantly — puts a free browser test at step 3, explicitly "free and doesn't need a phone number or payment method," deferring the payment method and number purchase ($2–$5/month) to step 4. ElevenLabs' dashboard path is 7 steps with 5 distinct decisions (name, first message, system prompt, knowledge base, voice) and needs no API key.
findings.soWhat: Two targets fall straight out. TTFA (hearing the agent talk) must beat 5 minutes — ideally land near 60–90 seconds, because Agora Managed Key removes the credential step every competitor still has somewhere. Time-to-deployed-agent must beat 15 minutes. Also copy Retell's structural move: the in-browser/web-widget test must come before any phone number, payment, or SIP step in the Studio X flow, so the Test section is reachable without touching Deployment.
findings.source: Vapi docs, Retell AI docs, ElevenLabs docs (fetched Sep 2026)

findings.claim: The published KPI for time-to-hello-world in API programs is under 30 minutes, with a graded scale — and 30 minutes is treated as ambitious, not easy.
findings.detail: Axway's API-program guidance names 30 minutes as the "Time to First Hello, World!" KPI, defined end-to-end as signup + access + reading the instructions + getting a first response, and cites a record of 8 minutes for one developer integrating an SMS API. Ably's published rubric (reported via Nordic APIs) grades it: 5/5 under 30 minutes; 4/5 30–60 minutes; 3/5 1–2 hours; 2/5 2–4 hours; 1/5 over 4 hours. Twilio's long-stated goal is to get developers "up and running in 5 minutes or less."
findings.soWhat: Adopt the Ably rubric as the internal scoring scale for Studio X and aim at 5/5 (under 30 min) for the full journey landing → deployed agent, with TTFA as a separate, much tighter sub-metric. This gives the product owner a defensible external grading scale rather than an invented one. Note the definition includes signup and docs-reading, so the measurement must start at first page view, not at first click inside the builder.
findings.source: Axway "Time to First Hello, World!" and Ably's TTHW rubric via Nordic APIs

findings.claim: Twilio published the only hard before/after numbers on developer-onboarding redesign found in this sweep: 62% improvement in first-message activation and 33% improvement in production launches within 7 days.
findings.detail: Twilio's engineering blog on its onboarding redesign attributes those gains to three changes: a Virtual Phone that lets developers prototype and send messages without waiting on compliance registration; a short survey that personalises the path by role, code preference and use case; and a single-screen configuration surface with embedded code samples and message logs. The pattern is deferral of every gate that isn't needed to see the thing work — exactly the shape of Agora's Managed Key advantage.
findings.soWhat: This is the closest published analogue to Studio X's thesis and worth citing to the product owner directly. The three moves map onto: (1) let the user test the agent in the browser before any SIP/phone/credential step; (2) use the latency-vs-cost slider as the personalisation survey rather than adding a separate one; (3) keep the five sections on one page with the test panel always visible. Also mirror Twilio's second metric — "production launches within 7 days" — as a Studio X counterpart: `agent_deployed` within 7 days of `first_builder_view`.
findings.source: Twilio Engineering Blog, "Twilio's New Onboarding: Fast, Personalized, and Developer-Friendly"

findings.claim: Cross-industry SaaS median time-to-value is a day and a half, and average activation is only 37.5% — so a builder that reaches a working agent in one session is an order-of-magnitude outlier, and worth measuring as such.
findings.detail: Userpilot's Product Metrics Benchmark Report, drawn from first-party data across 547 SaaS companies, puts median time to value at 1 day, 12 hours, 23 minutes (PLG 1d12h, SLG 1d11h) and average user activation at 37.5% (PLG 34.6%, SLG 41.6%). Onboarding-checklist completion averages just 19.2%. The 1-month retention split is PLG 48.4% vs SLG 39.1%. These are cross-vertical SaaS numbers, not developer-tool-specific, so they set a floor rather than a peer benchmark.
findings.soWhat: Two things. First, the checklist completion number (19.2%) is an argument against adding a separate onboarding checklist to Studio X — the five accordion sections with completion state are already the checklist, so don't stack another one on top.
