Second, set the activation-rate target well above 37.5%: with zero required credentials, the honest target for `reached_first_agent_test` among users who open the builder should be 60%+, and if it isn't, the flow has a gate that shouldn't be there.
findings.source: Userpilot, Product Metrics Benchmark Report (547 SaaS companies)

findings.claim: Requiring an account or credential before value is a measured 18-point abandonment cause — which is the strongest external evidence for keeping Agora Managed Key as the default and never gating the first test on a key.
findings.detail: Baymard Institute's aggregated cart-abandonment data (70.22% average abandonment across 50 studies) breaks down reasons, excluding the 42% "just browsing" segment: extra costs too high 40%, delivery too slow 20%, didn't trust the site with card details 19%, site required account creation 18%, checkout process too long/complicated 17%, website errors 17%. The account-creation and too-long-checkout figures are the two that transfer cleanly to a configuration flow.
findings.soWhat: Keep the zero-key path absolutely clean: no vendor API key, no payment method, no phone number anywhere on the route to hearing the agent talk. Every Configure sheet (vendor, credential, model, backup vendor, backup credential) must stay behind the "Or configure models manually" expander and never appear in the default path. Instrument each credential field with a PostHog `field_focused`/`field_abandoned` pair so you can see whether anyone is being pulled into BYOK unintentionally.
findings.source: Baymard Institute, cart abandonment statistics (updated Sep 2025)

findings.claim: Real-world form benchmarks put completion at ~52% across 93 million sessions, with software the second-worst vertical at 50.6% — half of everyone who starts a configuration form does not finish it.
findings.detail: Zuko Analytics' benchmarking, based on 93,022,997 tracked form sessions, reports 51.71% view-to-completion overall: desktop 54.48%, mobile 47.53%, tablet 49.31%. By industry, Forex Trading tops at 67.35% and Software sits at 50.61%. Field-level, the password field has the highest mean drop-off at 10.5%, with email at 6.4% and phone at 6.3%. Average field counts range from 10.7 (media) to 54.3 (insurance). Autofill materially improves completion.
findings.soWhat: Use 50% as the pessimistic baseline for any Studio X form-shaped surface and measure per-field drop-off, not just per-section. The password/credential finding matters specifically: credential entry is the single highest-drop field type known, which is another argument that the Configure sheets must be optional and off the default path. Instrument `field_drop` per field id so the worst offender in Studio X is visible rather than inferred.
findings.source: Zuko Analytics, Form Conversion Benchmarking (93,022,997 sessions)

findings.claim: "Fewer fields" is not reliably true — the evidence supports fewer *required decisions* and better *perceived* effort, and multi-step beats single-step even with more questions.
findings.detail: The famous 11→4 fields = +120% result (attributed variously to Experian or Imagescape) is widely cited but poorly sourced. Against it: a MarketingExperiments test where going from 11 to 15 fields produced a 109% uplift and a 10-field variant produced 87%; an Unbounce client whose conversions fell 14% when fields were cut, then rose 19.21% after the right fields were restored; and modern CRO reporting that field-removal tests now mostly land under 5% lift. Meanwhile multi-step formats consistently win: BrokerNotes +35%, Vendio +59%, and a 30+ question four-step form converting at 53%.
findings.soWhat: This directly validates the Studio X accordion structure — chunking the work into five named, progressively-disclosed sections is the intervention that pays, not stripping fields out of each section. It also means the right optimisation target is the count of *required* decisions on the default path (currently: the slider position, and arguably nothing else), while optional depth in Advanced Speech Settings, MCP servers, and structured outputs costs nothing as long as it is collapsed. Measure `required_decisions_made` before first test, and keep it ≤3.
findings.source: Venture Harbour, "5 Studies on How Form Length Impacts Conversion Rates"; CXL

findings.claim: The labour illusion is real and quantified: with a progress readout naming the work being done, 62–63% of people chose a service that made them wait 30 or 60 seconds over an instant one; without it, only 42% and 23% did.
findings.detail: Buell & Norton (Management Science 57:9, 2011) ran a 2 (transparent vs blind) × 6 (10/20/30/40/50/60s wait) design on a simulated flight search, with an identical progress bar in every non-zero condition to control for uncertainty. Transparency raised perceived value (M=5.36, SD=0.79 vs M=4.96, SD=0.91 on a 7-point scale; F(1,212)=10.68, p<0.01), and value with transparency compared favourably even against the instant-results condition. The critical caveat: there was still a main effect of wait time (F(5,212)=4.47, p<0.01) with value trending down over time — transparency lifts the whole curve, it does not flatten it.
findings.soWhat: For Studio X's genuinely slow operations — deploy, SIP provisioning, KB indexing, first test-call connect — show named work, not a spinner: "reserving SIP trunk… warming ASR… loading voice… connecting." That will make a 20-second deploy feel better than a silent 8-second one. But do not use it as licence to stop optimising: the downward trend means a transparent 60s deploy is still worse than a transparent 15s deploy.
findings.source: Ryan W. Buell & Michael I. Norton, "The Labor Illusion," Management Science 57(9), 1564–1579 (2011)

findings.claim: Progress-bar shape buys about 11% of perceived duration for free — accelerating bars that finish fast are perceived as faster, and any pause near the end is perceived as slowest.
findings.detail: Harrison et al. (UIST 2007, "Rethinking the Progress Bar") held actual duration constant at 5.5s across nine progress functions and found the two exponential/accelerating functions (Power, Fast Power) perceived as significantly faster than linear, while the three with pauses near the end (Slow Wavy, Fast Wavy, Late Pause) were perceived as slowest — a peak-and-end effect. The follow-up (CHI 2010, "Faster Progress Bars") found backwards-moving, decelerating ribbing reduced perceived duration by 11%: participants rated a 16.75s augmented bar (SE=0.45) equal to a 15s standard one, an 11.7% actual-time increase absorbed for free.
findings.soWhat: Specify the Studio X deploy and test-connect progress indicators as accelerating (front-load the slow work, finish fast) with a subtle backwards-moving texture, and never let them stall near 90% — which is exactly where a real deploy tends to stall. Practically: cache visible progress early so a late backend pause does not surface as a visible freeze. This is cheap perceived-speed that costs no backend work.
findings.source: Harrison, Amento, Kuznetsov & Bell, UIST 2007; Harrison, Yeo & Hudson, CHI 2010

findings.claim: Endowed progress is worth a third of completion time: a 12-stamp card pre-stamped twice was completed in a median of 10 days versus 15 days for an equivalent 10-stamp card.
findings.detail: Kivetz, Urminsky & Zheng (Journal of Marketing Research, 2006) showed that customers given a 12-stamp coffee card with two "bonus" stamps already filled completed the same 10 required purchases in a median of 10 days, against 15 days for a plain 10-stamp card — a 33% reduction in time to goal from an illusion of progress alone. They also found inter-purchase time fell roughly 20% as customers neared the reward.
findings.soWhat: Studio X's left rail should show the five sections as already partially complete on first load, because they genuinely are — Agora Managed Key, the default bundled stack, the default voice and the default opening are all pre-filled. Render that as "3 of 5 ready" rather than an empty checklist. This is honest (the defaults really are working values) and is the single cheapest intervention in this sweep for reducing time-to-deploy. Instrument it as an A/B once PostHog lands.
findings.source: Kivetz, Urminsky & Zheng, "The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected," JMR 43(1), 39–58 (2006)

findings.claim: Defaults are the highest-leverage speed intervention available, and the canonical evidence is a roughly sixfold difference in outcome from changing nothing but the default.
findings.detail: Johnson & Goldstein (Science 302, 2003) found countries with opt-out organ-donation defaults show on average about six times higher registration than opt-in countries, with the choice architecture — not the underlying preference — doing the work. Their cross-country and experimental data are the standard citation for default power. I was unable to verify the precise lab-experiment percentages from a primary source in this sweep, so treat the 6× country-level figure as the quotable number.
findings.soWhat: Every decision Studio X can make on the user's behalf should be pre-made and visibly reversible, not presented as an open question: the latency-vs-cost slider should land on a specific recommended position with the resulting stack named; Agent Voice and Spoken Language should be pre-selected; the Opening greeting, AI disclosure and failure message should be pre-written; hosting region should be pre-picked from the user's locale. The design rule is that a default is not the absence of a decision — it is a decision the product made, shown as made.
findings.source: Eric J. Johnson & Daniel G. Goldstein, "Do Defaults Save Lives?", Science 302 (2003)

findings.claim: Do not justify cutting configuration options with Hick's Law or the jam study — both fail for exactly the kind of scanning-and-reading choices Studio X presents, and a meta-analysis of 50 experiments found the choice-overload effect is on average zero.
findings.detail: Hick's Law describes simple stimulus-response choice and "does not apply to complex menus or hierarchies of options," because finding a named item in a list requires linear scanning rather than logarithmic subdivision — it applies only when the list is ordered and the user already knows what they want. The Iyengar & Lepper jam study (24 vs 6 jams; roughly 3% vs 30% purchase in the popular retelling) did not survive meta-analysis: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd (JCR, Oct 2010) pooled 63 conditions from 50 experiments (N=5,036) and found "a mean effect size of virtually zero" with large between-study variance and no identified sufficient conditions.
findings.soWhat: The argument for Studio X's collapsed vendor sheets and voice dialog is progressive disclosure and default quality — not "too many choices paralyse people." Practically this means the Select voice dialog can carry a long voice list without harm as long as it is searchable, filterable and has a recommended default pre-selected; the cost is scanning time, which search fixes, not decision paralysis, which hiding options would not fix. Don't spend design effort pruning the voice catalogue.
findings.source: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd, JCR 37(3), 409–425 (2010); Hick's law critique via Wikipedia/NN/g

findings.claim: The first 10 seconds of the page decide whether the user stays at all, and past 30 seconds the leave-rate flattens sharply — so the builder's first screen must communicate the whole deal in 10 seconds.
findings.detail: NN/g's dwell-time analysis of 205,873 web pages (each with 10,000+ visits, over 2 billion dwell times, measured via a browser plug-in) found the average page visit lasts a little under a minute, that "the first 10 seconds of the page visit are critical," and that after roughly 30 seconds the survival curve flattens — people keep leaving, but far more slowly, and those who stay often stay 2+ minutes. 99% of pages showed negative aging: the longer someone stays, the more likely they are to keep staying.
findings.soWhat: The first paint of /agents/agt_default/edit has to make three things legible within 10 seconds: that an agent already exists and is configured, that no API keys are needed, and where the test button is. The right-hand test panel being visible on load is doing real work here and should not be collapsed by default. Instrument `time_to_first_meaningful_interaction` in PostHog and watch the 0–10s and 10–30s bounce buckets separately — they have different causes and different fixes.
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group, "How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?"

findings.claim: Perceived-speed tricks have a narrow working range — skeleton screens only help between roughly 400ms and 3 seconds, so below and above that band you must fix the actual speed.
findings.detail: Reporting on NN/g's skeleton-screen guidance states the technique improves perceived performance only when actual load time falls between 400ms and 3s: below 400ms there is nothing to mask and the skeleton adds a flash of noise; above ~3s the skeleton stops reading as progress and starts reading as a stall, at which point a determinate progress indicator with named work is required. This dovetails with Google's finding that 53% of mobile visits are abandoned if a page takes over 3 seconds to load, and SOASTA's finding that one second faster yielded up to a 27% conversion increase.
findings.soWhat: Gives Studio X a three-band rule to implement literally. Under 400ms: no indicator at all, just swap the content. 400ms–3s: skeleton. Over 3s: determinate progress with named operational transparency and a cancel. Encode this as a shared loading component with a duration-aware state machine rather than leaving each surface to choose, so the Configure sheets, voice dialog, KB indexing and deploy all behave consistently.
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group skeleton-screen guidance (via secondary reporting); Google Mobile Site Speed Playbook / Think with Google

findings.claim: Only 10% of real programming sessions resume editing within a minute, and about 30% take more than 30 minutes to the first edit — the developer resumption cost is minutes, not seconds.
findings.detail: Parnin & Rugaber instrumented 85 programmers across 9,899 sessions and 4.5 million IDE events (Eclipse + Visual Studio, 2005). They measured 'edit lag' — time from returning to a task to the first edit. In 10% of sessions edit lag was under a minute; in ~30% it exceeded 30 minutes. Even when the developer resumed work in the very same method they last edited, they managed it within a minute only 35% of the time. Sessions were segmented at 15-minute activity breaks; 98% of the 4.5M inter-event gaps were under a minute, so the clustering is clean.
findings.soWhat: Studio X's builder must treat any return to the page as a cold start, not a warm one. The section a user left must show, without being asked, what was already set and what is still missing — the 'ongoing review' Baymard found accordions destroy. And the PostHog TTFA clock needs the idle-stripped variant (TTFA_active) as the primary design metric, because wall-clock TTFA will be dominated by resumption lag the builder cannot control.
findings.source: Chris Parnin & Spencer Rugaber, 'Resumption Strategies for Interrupted Programming Tasks', ICPC 2009 (primary PDF, verified)

findings.claim: A working developer's day is made of 1–3 blocks of 15 minutes, 1–2 of 30 minutes, 1–2 of an hour, and one 2-hour block — so the honest budget for a first agent build is one 15–30 minute block, not one sitting.
findings.detail: Parnin & Rugaber's Table 2 characterises a typical day directly from the instrumented sessions: 1–3 sessions of 15 minutes, 1–2 of 30 minutes, 1–2 of one hour, one of two hours, 0–1 of four hours, and rarely eight. This is the population pass 1 said was missing — professional developers at work in their own IDE, not consumer web visitors. It replaces both the 28-minute e-commerce figure and the 47-second attention figure as the right proxy.
findings.soWhat: Set the TTFA target against the 15-minute modal block, not against a 47-second attention span or a 28-minute e-commerce session. A sub-3-minute TTFA fits comfortably inside the smallest natural block, which is the defensible framing for the owner: 'a first talking agent inside the shortest block a developer ever has'. Deployment (TTFD) can be allowed to spill into the second block, and should be designed to be resumable across one.
findings.source: Parnin & Rugaber, ICPC 2009, Table 2 (primary PDF, verified)

findings.claim: 40% of interrupted tasks are never resumed at all — so same-session completion is the wrong denominator for the builder funnel.
findings.detail: O'Conaill & Frohlich's observational finding, cited in Parnin & Rugaber's related work, is that 40% of interrupted tasks are not resumed at all. Alongside it: Czerwinski found resumed tasks took twice as long and were harder; Mark et al. observed 57% of tasks were interrupted; van Solingen measured an hour a day spent managing interruptions with ~15 minutes to recover from each; a Microsoft survey found 62% of developers considered recovering from interruptions a serious problem.
findings.soWhat: The PostHog builder funnel must be measured over a 24-hour and 7-day window per person, not per session, or roughly 40% of the people who genuinely wanted an agent will be scored as abandonment. It also justifies a concrete feature: a resumable draft with a deep link back into the exact section (the repo already has ?designFocus= anchors — the same mechanism should carry a 'resume where you left off' email or in-app return path).
findings.source: O'Conaill & Frohlich, and Czerwinski/Mark/van Solingen, as cited in Parnin & Rugaber ICPC 2009 §1

findings.claim: Interrupted people finish tasks FASTER with no quality loss — but with significantly more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort — so a falling TTFA can coexist with a worsening experience.
findings.detail: Mark, Gudith & Klocke (CHI 2008) ran a controlled simulated-office experiment with periodic interruptions. Interrupted participants completed the task in less time, with no difference in quality, but reported higher stress, frustration, time pressure and effort. The mechanism is compensation: people adopt a faster, more stressful working style. This cuts directly against the naive reading that interruption always shows up as slower completion.
findings.soWhat: TTFA alone can improve while the builder becomes more punishing. The measurement plan needs a paired effort counter-metric that a speed win cannot cannibalise — a single-question SEQ ('How easy was setting up this agent?') fired once at first successful test, plus support/Concierge contacts per new agent. The existing KPI doc has guardrails on failure and rollback but nothing on perceived effort; this is the missing one.
findings.source: Gloria Mark, Daniel Gudith & Ulrich Klocke, 'The Cost of Interrupted Work: More Speed and Stress', CHI 2008

findings.claim: CONTRADICTS PASS 1 — the labour illusion reverses: its benefit starts declining after 30 seconds in one context and after just 15 seconds in another, and when the outcome is bad, showing the work actively lowers perceived value.
findings.detail: Pulled from the Buell & Norton primary (Management Science 57(9), 2011). Experiment 1 crossed transparency against waits of 10/20/30/40/50/60s; there was a main effect of wait time such that value perceptions trended downward throughout. The authors state plainly in §4.1 that in the travel simulation the benefits began to decline after 30 seconds, while in the Experiment 5 dating simulation the decline began at 15 seconds — and they attribute the difference to user expectations of how long that particular service should take, explicitly noting Google has trained users to expect fractions of a second. Experiment 5 further showed that when service outcomes are subjectively unfavourable, increasing operational transparency has negative effects on value perceptions. Their own conclusion: 'If wait times are lengthy, reducing them may be more beneficial than implementing operational transparency.'
findings.soWhat: Two hard rules for Studio X. First, the expectation anchor for 'make my agent talk' is ChatGPT voice mode and Siri — sub-second — so the labour-illusion window here is nearer 15 seconds than 30, and a narrated progress readout is licensed only for genuinely slow steps (knowledge-base ingestion, SIP number provisioning), never for a model switch or a voice preview. Second, and more important: never pair a rich 'here is everything we are doing' readout with a step that can fail. A detailed provisioning narration followed by a failed test call is measurably worse than a bare spinner followed by the same failure.
findings.source: Ryan W. Buell & Michael I. Norton, 'The Labor Illusion: How Operational Transparency Increases Perceived Value', Management Science 57(9):1564–1579, 2011 (primary PDF, §4.1 and Experiment 5)

findings.claim: GAP 4 CLOSED with a correction — the Johnson & Goldstein numbers are 42% opt-in / 79% neutral / 82% opt-out on 161 respondents, and the neutral no-default condition was statistically indistinguishable from the best default.
findings.detail: Retrieved the Science 2003 paper itself. The online experiment used 161 respondents in three conditions. Effective consent was 42% (opt-in), 79% (neutral — forced choice, no default at all) and 82% (opt-out). The paper's own wording: the opt-out condition did not differ significantly from the neutral condition, and only the opt-in condition was significantly lower. Respondents could change their choice with a single mouse click, which the authors say largely eliminates effort as the explanation. Separately, the cross-country field data shows nearly 60 percentage points separating the four opt-in from the six opt-out countries with no overlap in the distributions — larger than the lab effect precisely because changing the default in the field costs forms, phone calls and mail.
findings.soWhat: The commonly quoted pair is accurate but the missing middle number changes the design conclusion for Studio X. A well-made forced choice performs as well as a good default; what destroys completion is a BAD default. So the Agora Managed Key default is safe, but so is asking the user to pick — the risk is never 'we asked', it is 'we pre-selected the wrong thing and they had to undo it'. Concretely: the latency-vs-cost slider may legitimately start unselected with a clear choice, provided the options read in the user's own terms; what it must not do is default to a stack most first agents will have to change. Instrument the change-away-from-default rate per control as the direct test — the repo's A1 assumption (manual config under 30%) is exactly this measurement.
findings.source: Eric J. Johnson & Daniel Goldstein, 'Do Defaults Save Lives?', Science 302:1338–1339, 21 Nov 2003 (primary PDF, verified)

findings.claim: GAP 5 CLOSED and CONTRADICTS PASS 1 — NN/g never gave a 400ms–3s window for skeleton screens; their actual rule is nothing under 1s, spinners and skeletons for 2–10s, progress bars above 10s, and skeletons for full-page loads only.
findings.detail: Read the NN/g article directly. Their guidance: below 1 second, neither skeleton nor spinner is needed; wait animations/spinners suit 2–10 second loads; skeleton screens are for waits under 10 seconds; progress bars are strongly recommended for anything over 10 seconds. Crucially they scope by SURFACE, not just duration — spinners belong on a single module (a card, a video), skeleton screens are for full-screen loads. Two caveats pass 1 did not have: animated skeletons can be distracting, annoying or an accessibility problem; and a skeleton on a fast-loading page is actively annoying because the flash makes users feel they cannot keep up. The perceived-speed claim rests on Mejtoft et al. (2018), not on NN/g data of their own.
findings.soWhat: Rewrite the loading-state rule in the design kit. For Studio X the mapping is: the voice preview and model switch (target sub-400ms) get NO loading state at all; a Configure sheet opening gets none; a test-call connection gets a spinner scoped to the test panel, not a page skeleton; only a full builder cold-load gets a skeleton, and only if it exceeds ~1s. The 'skeleton on a fast page is annoying' caveat matters most — if the builder hits its Doherty targets, adding skeletons will make it feel worse, not better.
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Skeleton Screens 101' (article read directly)

findings.claim: GAP 6 PARTIALLY CLOSED — Baymard's data does NOT support accordions outperforming multi-step or single-page layouts, and 75% of accordion implementations carry major usability problems from two specific causes.
findings.detail: Baymard tested accordion-style checkouts (their use rose from 14% of the top 100 US e-commerce sites in 2012 to 32% by 2016). They explicitly found the claim that accordions consistently outperform multi-page or one-step checkouts unsupported by their data — concluding that the format matters far less than what users are asked to do and how they are asked to do it. 75% of accordion flows had major usability problems, from two causes: (1) depriving the user of the ongoing review that is the accordion's main advantage in the first place, and (2) breaking back-button expectations, often with data loss. Both were observed as direct causes of abandonment in testing, the back-button issue especially.
findings.soWhat: This is the closest external evidence to Studio X's exact pattern — five accordion sections on one page — and it says the section count is not the lever. The two named failure modes are, and both are checkable today: does a collapsed section still show a readable summary of what is set inside it (ongoing review), and does browser back, or collapsing a section, ever lose entered configuration? Test both before spending any design effort on whether five sections should be three. Note the source is Baymard's research blog and my fetch returned some garbled wording, so treat the exact 75% as indicative.
findings.source: Baymard Institute research blog, 'Usability Testing Accordion-Style Checkouts: 2 UX Pitfalls that 75% of Sites Neglect'

findings.claim: TTFA is already a defined voice-industry metric meaning 'time to first audio' with a sub-300ms bar — the collision is on the exact acronym, not a near-miss.
findings.detail: TTFA appears as a standard glossary term across voice-AI vendors (Hamming AI, Gradium, Soniox, FutureAGI): the elapsed time between sending a TTS request and receiving the first playable audio sample, measured in milliseconds, distinct from total synthesis time and from time-to-first-byte. The stated bar is that human conversational turn-handoff is ~200–300ms, so a TTS TTFA over 300ms adds a perceptible pause to every turn. Hamming's readiness framework sets Time to First Audio under 800ms as a pre-launch gate. The repo's KPI doc anticipated this collision but names the runtime metric 'TTFAB'; the industry acronym is literally TTFA.
findings.soWhat: Rename the onboarding clock before the doc circulates. Every voice engineer at Agora will read 'TTFA' as milliseconds-to-audio, and the KPI table puts a minutes-scale number next to it. Either keep TTFA for the runtime metric and rename the onboarding clock (TTFT — Time To First Talk, or simply 'time to first answer' spelled out), or accept permanent confusion in every review. This is a five-minute fix now and an unfixable one after the metric ships to a dashboard.
findings.source: Hamming AI voice-AI glossary; Gradium; Soniox streaming-TTS wiki

findings.claim: The measured competitive baseline pass 1 said did not exist DOES exist — just for runtime latency, not setup time: Vapi 720ms p50 / 1,050ms p95, Retell 680/920, Bland 850/1,180, across 500 production calls each.
findings.detail: Tested Media measured voice-to-voice latency (end of caller speech to start of agent speech) across 500 production calls per platform in March 2026: Vapi 720ms median / 1,050ms p95; Retell 680/920; Bland 850/1,180. Separately, Cekura held the stack constant (GPT-4.1, Deepgram Nova-3, ElevenLabs Flash) and measured full-turn p50 of 1,730ms for ElevenLabs and 2,460ms for LiveKit. Vapi's own published target is p50 under 500ms and p95 under 800ms — i.e. the independent measurement is ~44% slower than the vendor claim. Telnyx and Twilio carrier-leg p95 (network only) were 118ms and 161ms over 120 calls.
findings.soWhat: Two uses. First, the gap between Vapi's claimed sub-500ms and its measured 720ms is the template for how Agora's own claims will be treated — publish measured p50/p95 from real calls, not component latency, or expect the same discount. The repo doc already says vendor component latency must never be quoted; this shows what happens when it is. Second, the latency-vs-cost slider can display a real, defensible number per stack instead of an abstract position, which turns the slider from a preference control into an informed choice.
findings.source: Tested Media (500 calls per platform, Mar 2026) and Cekura fixed-stack benchmark, compiled by Telnyx

findings.claim: Production fleet medians across 10+ live deployments: 680ms p50, 1,180ms p95, $0.07–$0.21 per connected minute, and 78% median containment — with ~1,200ms p50 named as the point where callers start interrupting.
findings.detail: DestiLabs published anonymised production telemetry from 10+ live voice deployments across healthcare, fintech, real estate, e-commerce and logistics. Fleet medians: 680ms p50, 1,180ms p95. By architecture, speech-to-speech ran 560ms p50 versus 700ms for cascaded STT→LLM→TTS. Cost: $0.07–0.13/min cascaded, $0.18–0.21/min speech-to-speech, with LLM tokens the largest variable component ($0.02–0.08). Volume tiers ran $0.16–0.21/min at ~1k min/month down to $0.07–0.11 at ~100k. Containment (calls resolved without human escalation) ranged 62–88% with a 78% median. They name ~1,200ms p50 as where the awkward pause starts and callers interrupt, and p95 under ~1,400ms as the production bar.
findings.soWhat: This gives the Voice & Models slider its two real axes with real numbers — the speech-to-speech versus cascaded split is 140ms of latency for roughly double the per-minute cost, which is exactly the trade the slider exists to express, and it should say so in those terms rather than 'faster/cheaper'. Containment median of 78% is also the honest benchmark to show on Go Live: it tells a first-time deployer what good looks like before they have data of their own.
findings.source: DestiLabs, '2026 AI Voice Agent Benchmark: Latency & Cost per Minute (10+ Projects)'

findings.claim: There is a published production-readiness checklist for voice agents with hard thresholds — task success >85%, first-call resolution >75%, barge-in accuracy >95%, hallucination <1%, containment >70% — which is the missing content for 'confidence in production'.
findings.detail: Hamming AI's evaluation framework sets pre-launch gates: P50 latency under 1.5s, P95 under 5s, P99 under 8s, time to first audio under 800ms; word error rate under 10% on clean audio and under 15% with office noise; task success rate above 85%; first-call resolution above 75%; reprompt rate under 10%; barge-in detection accuracy above 95% with response-to-interruption under 200ms; hallucination rate under 1% (2% in noise); zero compliance violations on security-critical flows. Production health: alert at >3% error rate, page on-call at >10%; alert at >10% escalation increase, critical at >25%; containment target above 70%.
findings.soWhat: Section 5 (Go Live) currently offers settings, region, structured outputs and review. This gives it a real readiness panel: a checklist of named thresholds the agent has or has not met, derived from the test runs in Section 4. That converts 'review & deploy' from a confirmation screen into the trust ladder the owner asked for — and it is the single highest-value addition to the builder that is not about speed. The barge-in numbers (>95% accuracy, <200ms) also give Advanced Speech Settings something to be measured against rather than tuned blind.
findings.source: Hamming AI, 'How to Evaluate Voice Agents: Complete Framework for Testing & Monitoring' (2026)

findings.claim: Published regression gates give Studio X a concrete deploy-blocking rule: block on >3% task-completion drop, >10% latency increase, >2% WER increase, or >5% escalation increase.
findings.detail: The same framework recommends converting every production failure into a permanent regression test case and blocking deployments when regressions exceed those four thresholds. Test-set composition is specified too: a minimum of 50 scenarios, 200+ for production readiness, 500+ for enterprise or multilingual, split roughly 40% happy-path, 30% edge cases (multi-intent, corrections, hesitations), 15% error handling, 10% adversarial (off-topic, prompt injection), 5% acoustic variation (noise, accents, speakerphone).
findings.soWhat: Section 4's 'generated test scenarios' currently has no stated target for how many or of what kind. The 40/30/15/10/5 mix is a ready-made generation spec, and the 50/200/500 ladder gives the UI an honest progress statement ('12 of 50 minimum scenarios') instead of an open-ended list. Pair it with the four regression gates on the Go Live review step and TCR (Trusted Change Rate) in the KPI doc becomes computable from the product rather than inferred from rollbacks.
findings.source: Hamming AI voice-agent evaluation and production-reliability guides (2026)

findings.claim: Voice A/B tests need 1,000+ calls per variant for 95% confidence — so builder experiments must be judged on builder events, not call outcomes.
findings.detail: Reported across the voice-eval tooling literature as the practical sizing rule for comparing two agent configurations on call outcomes. At a realistic early-account call volume this is weeks to months per experiment.
findings.soWhat: This settles an argument the measurement plan will otherwise have later. Every design experiment in the builder (preset naming, test-from-anywhere, voice picker) must be powered on builder-side events — section completion, time-to-convert, change-away-from-default — which accrue per session and reach significance in days. Call-outcome metrics (containment, task success) are monitoring metrics and guardrails, not experiment readouts. Wiring an A/B test to containment rate will produce no readable result inside a design cycle.
findings.source: Voice-agent testing platform guidance (Cekura, Hamming), 2026

findings.claim: LiveKit's quickstart now claims under 10 minutes with NO vendor API keys for the default pipeline — Agora's zero-key advantage is no longer unique and the differentiator has to move.
findings.detail: Read the LiveKit docs directly. The page claims 'build and deploy a simple voice assistant in less than 10 minutes', with four discrete steps after CLI init (select project, cd, install deps, run in dev mode). Only LiveKit Cloud API keys are needed, written automatically into .env.local by the CLI. The documentation states 'No additional setup is required' for the default STT-LLM-TTS pipeline because the starter templates use LiveKit Inference for model access; an OPENAI_API_KEY is needed only for the Realtime-model alternative. Alongside: Synthflow's vendor claim is a live call in under an hour from signup, and third-party reviews put Bland as the slowest to a first working call — roughly half a day of engineering for a basic outbound agent, and effectively a non-starter for a non-technical operator.
findings.soWhat: This is the most strategically uncomfortable finding here. The brief states the zero-vendor-key default is 'unusual versus competitors'; LiveKit has managed inference too. The surviving differentiators are that LiveKit's 10 minutes is a terminal/CLI flow requiring a local dev environment and a deployed agent process, while Studio X reaches a talking agent in a browser with no install — and that LiveKit's measured full-turn p50 in the fixed-stack benchmark was 2,460ms. Position on 'no install, no terminal, browser to talking agent', not on 'no API keys', and the competitor claim table now reads: Vapi under 5 min, LiveKit under 10 min, Retell 15 min, ElevenLabs ~7 steps, Synthflow under 1 hour, Bland slowest.
findings.source: LiveKit Agents documentation, voice AI quickstart (read directly); Synthflow vendor claim and third-party Bland/Synthflow reviews

findings.claim: Task times are lognormal, so the way you average TTFA changes the number you report — use the geometric mean below n=25 and the median above, never the arithmetic mean.
findings.detail: Sauro & Lewis (CHI 2010, and MeasuringU's practitioner summary) show task-time data is positively skewed and lognormal. For samples under 25 the geometric mean is the better estimator of the population median — on average 13% less error and 22% less bias than the sample median itself. Above 25, use the median. The arithmetic mean is heavily skewed by a few outliers. They also distinguish three different things people call 'average task time': completion time for successful users only, mean time to failure (time before quitting), and total time on task regardless of outcome — these give materially different numbers from identical data. On benchmarking, they offer expert/fastest time × 1.5 as one approach but flag it as needing validation, and warn that all lab task times are wrong in absolute terms; the value is in relative comparison under consistent method.
findings.soWhat: Write the averaging rule into the KPI doc before the first number is quoted, because moderated sessions with 5–8 participants will fall squarely in the geometric-mean regime while the PostHog funnel will be in the median regime — and the two will disagree unless the method is fixed in advance. Also pick one of the three definitions explicitly: TTFA should be successful-completions-only, with the abandoners reported separately as a mean-time-to-failure number, otherwise the people who give up at 40 seconds will flatter the median.
findings.source: Jeff Sauro & James R. Lewis, 'Average Task Times in Usability Tests: What to Report?' (CHI 2010); MeasuringU, '10 Things to Know About Task Times'

findings.claim: A measured time-to-hello-world number does exist: Postman timed an API at 17 minutes to first successful call, cut to 10 minutes with a ready-made collection — a 1.7× improvement, and up to 56× across the APIs tested.
findings.detail: Postman ran an experiment timing developers to a first successful API call. Company A's API took 17 minutes unaided and 10 minutes when developers used a publisher-provided collection — 1.7× faster. Across the set of APIs tested, forked collections made developers 1.7× to 56× faster to a first call. Postman defines TTFC as spanning browse (docs and site), sign-up (account and key), and the first call — i.e. it starts at discovery, not at the console. Lack of documentation was the top blocker for 52% of developers in their 2023 State of the API report.
findings.soWhat: This is the empirical backing for the definitional recommendation in gap 2, and it agrees with the Axway convention: the headline clock starts at first contact, not first builder paint. It also validates the repo's A7 assumption about importing from Vapi/Retell — a prefilled starting artefact is precisely the 'provided collection' intervention, and Postman measured it at 1.7× on a flow that was already only 17 minutes. Expect a similar order of effect from import and from templates, not an order of magnitude.
findings.source: Postman blog, 'Improve Your Time to First API Call by 20x' and 'The Most Important API Metric Is Time to First Call'

findings.claim: PostHog's 'time to convert' funnel graph type is the actual instrument for TTFA — and PostHog's own activation metric turned out to be a compound of two actions, found empirically against 3-month retention.
findings.detail: PostHog documents time-to-value as the average time to reach activation, measured by building a funnel from signup to the activation event and switching the graph type to 'Time to convert'. Their own method for finding the metric: build a large list of candidate hook events, group them into 5–10 combinations of 3–5 events each, test each group's correlation with retention via SQL, and keep the group whose retention is nominally higher than baseline. The answer for their session-replay product was a compound — watched 5+ replays AND set a replay filter at least once — on a 3-month retention window. They note users generally have to do something more than once to reach the moment, and that activation varies significantly by product type.
findings.soWhat: Two things for the plan. First, the TTFA/TTFD clocks are literally a funnel + time-to-convert insight, so they need the funnel steps instrumented as person-level events with the right properties — which the KPI doc's W0 milestone already sequences correctly. Second, do not assert the activation definition up front: 'one successful test call' may well prove weaker than a compound like 'tested AND deployed' or 'tested more than once'. Run PostHog's own 5–10 groups × 3–5 events procedure against AR7 once two weeks of baseline exist, and let the data name the activation event.
findings.source: PostHog docs, 'Users getting value: Measuring activation' and 'How we found our activation metric'

findings.claim: Published B2B session-duration benchmarks (77.6s median, 4:26 average) are website metrics and must NOT be used as the builder's time budget.
findings.detail: Databox's benchmark across nearly 500 B2B companies puts the median average-session-duration at 77.61 seconds; Hike SEO reports 4:26 for B2B SaaS; another study found ~2 minutes desktop and ~1 minute mobile across B2B tech sites. These are GA4-style web-session figures dominated by marketing-page visits, and several commonly circulated companion stats (a Mixpanel 2.5× retention claim, an Amplitude 3-minute/60%-conversion claim) surfaced only through secondary aggregators and I could not trace either to a primary source.
findings.soWhat: Explicitly rule these out in the KPI doc so nobody later anchors the builder budget to 77 seconds. The defensible budget proxy is the Parnin session table (15–30 minute working blocks), and the only number that should ever be treated as Studio X's real session length is Studio X's own, once PostHog is live. Flagging this matters because 'average session is 77 seconds' is the kind of stat that gets quoted into a design constraint by accident.
findings.source: Databox B2B benchmark (~500 companies); Hike SEO average session duration by industry

findings.claim: GAP 7 STAYS OPEN — the canonical Doherty mirror is dead, so the 25–30% productivity figure remains uncheckable and should not be quoted externally.
findings.detail: The URL every UX blog chains to for Doherty & Thadani (vm.ibm.com/devpages/jelliott/evrrt8.html) now fails certificate validation via WebFetch and, fetched directly, returns an IBM marketing shell containing none of the paper's text. The jlelliotton.blogspot.com mirror returns HTTP 404. Secondary sources repeat '25-30% more transactions per hour' and '3:1 to 5:1 ROI' with no page citation, and the one specific figure that does recur with detail — $150,000/month savings at 50 concurrent users rising to $908,000 at 300 — is a 1982 mainframe-economics number with no bearing on a modern web builder. The paper is IBM Systems Journal Vol 21 No 3, November 1982; a physical copy is catalogued at the Computer History Museum (102751398).
findings.soWhat: Keep the 400ms threshold — it is well attested and the repo already uses it correctly as the per-control budget — but strike the 25–30% productivity claim from any external deck. If the owner wants it, someone has to order the CHM copy or pull the IBM Systems Journal archive; a paid-access check is not enough because the usual mirror no longer exists at all. Cite the threshold, not the productivity delta.
findings.source: Attempted retrieval of vm.ibm.com and jlelliotton.blogspot.com mirrors (both now dead); Computer History Museum catalogue 102751398
