numbers.value: 15 minutes
numbers.caveat: Free browser test at step 3 with no payment method or number; payment + $2–$5/mo number needed only at step 4.

numbers.label: ElevenLabs dashboard path
numbers.value: 7 steps, 5 decisions, no API key
numbers.caveat: No time claim stated on the page; a 5-minute claim circulates in secondary sources.

numbers.label: Labour illusion — chose to wait over instant results
numbers.value: 62% at 30 s and 63% at 60 s with transparency; 42% and 23% without
numbers.caveat: Simulated flight search, lab study, n≈100+ per experiment.

numbers.label: Labour illusion — perceived value lift
numbers.value: M=5.36 (SD 0.79) transparent vs M=4.96 (SD 0.91) blind, 7-pt scale; F(1,212)=10.68, p<0.01
numbers.caveat: There is still a significant downward main effect of wait time, F(5,212)=4.47, p<0.01 — transparency lifts the curve, it does not flatten it.

numbers.label: Perceived-duration reduction from progress-bar augmentation
numbers.caveat: A 16.75 s augmented bar (SE 0.45) was rated equal to a 15 s standard one — an 11.7% actual-time increase absorbed.

numbers.label: Progress-bar shapes perceived fastest / slowest
numbers.value: accelerating (Power, Fast Power) fastest; any pause near the end slowest
numbers.caveat: Actual duration held constant at 5.5 s across nine functions; peak-and-end effect.

numbers.label: Endowed progress — time to complete the same 10 purchases
numbers.value: median 10 days (12-stamp card, 2 pre-stamped) vs 15 days (10-stamp card)
numbers.caveat: Coffee loyalty cards; inter-purchase interval also fell ~20% near the goal.

numbers.label: Default-effect magnitude
numbers.value: ~6× higher registration in opt-out vs opt-in countries
numbers.caveat: Country-level comparison; the often-quoted 42% vs 82% lab figures were not verified from a primary source in this sweep.

numbers.label: Choice-overload meta-analytic effect
numbers.value: mean effect size ≈ zero (63 conditions, 50 experiments, N=5,036)
numbers.caveat: Large between-study variance; no sufficient conditions identified. Do not cite the jam study as settled.

numbers.label: Mobile abandonment above 3 s page load
numbers.source: Google / Think with Google, Mobile Site Speed Playbook
numbers.caveat: Mobile web page loads; one in two mobile visitors expect under 2 s.

numbers.label: Conversion lift from 1 s faster mobile load
numbers.value: up to +27%
numbers.caveat: E-commerce mobile pages.

numbers.label: Skeleton-screen working range
numbers.value: 400 ms – 3 s actual load
numbers.caveat: Not verified against the NN/g article itself in this sweep; treat as a working hypothesis for the loading-state state machine.

numbers.label: Multi-step form conversion lifts
numbers.value: +35% (BrokerNotes), +59% (Vendio), 53% completion on a 30+ question four-step form
numbers.caveat: Vendor/agency case studies, not controlled research; directionally consistent across several.

numbers.label: Counter-evidence on field reduction
numbers.value: 11→15 fields = +109%; 11→10 = +87%; field cuts caused −14% in one Unbounce test; modern field-removal tests mostly <5% lift
numbers.source: MarketingExperiments / Unbounce via Venture Harbour; CXL
numbers.caveat: Directly contradicts the popular 11→4 = +120% claim, whose provenance (Experian vs Imagescape) is unclear. Use 'fewer required decisions', not 'fewer fields'.

numbers.label: Programming sessions where first edit happens within 1 minute of resuming
numbers.source: Parnin & Rugaber, ICPC 2009 (85 programmers, 9,899 sessions, 4.5M events)
numbers.caveat: IDE events only; some 'breaks' may be related work outside the IDE (code review, web search)

numbers.label: Programming sessions with edit lag over 30 minutes
numbers.caveat: Authors attribute many of these to debugging, not pure resumption cost

numbers.label: Resumed within 1 minute even when returning to the same method last edited
numbers.source: Parnin & Rugaber, ICPC 2009, Table 3 (Visual Studio dataset only)
numbers.caveat: Only the VS dataset had fine-grained navigation data; n=12 developers

numbers.label: A developer's typical day, by session length
numbers.caveat: 2005 data, Eclipse/VS desktop era; sessions segmented at a 15-minute activity gap

numbers.label: Interrupted tasks never resumed at all
numbers.source: O'Conaill & Frohlich, cited in Parnin & Rugaber §1
numbers.caveat: Office observational study, not developers specifically; cited secondhand

numbers.label: Tasks that get interrupted at all
numbers.source: Mark et al., cited in Parnin & Rugaber §1
numbers.caveat: Cited secondhand from the related-work section

numbers.label: Developers who consider recovering from interruptions a serious problem
numbers.source: Microsoft internal survey, cited in Parnin & Rugaber §1
numbers.caveat: Single-company survey, cited secondhand

numbers.label: Time to recover from an interruption (industrial software teams)
numbers.value: ~15 minutes, ~1 hour/day total
numbers.source: van Solingen, cited in Parnin & Rugaber §1
numbers.caveat: Cited secondhand; this is the true origin of the '15 minutes' figure often misattributed

numbers.label: Effect of interruption on completion time and quality
numbers.value: Faster completion, no quality difference, higher stress/frustration/time-pressure/effort
numbers.caveat: Simulated office email task, not a configuration task; lab setting

numbers.label: Wait at which labour-illusion benefit starts to decline
numbers.value: 30 s (travel search) / 15 s (dating search)
numbers.caveat: Decline point tracks user expectation for that service class — for a voice preview the expectation anchor is sub-second, so assume well under 15s

numbers.label: Labour illusion when the service outcome is unfavourable
numbers.value: Negative effect on perceived value
numbers.caveat: Online dating simulation; the mechanism (blame attribution on visible effort + bad result) should generalise to a narrated setup that ends in a failed test call

numbers.label: Johnson & Goldstein online experiment — effective consent by default
numbers.value: 42% opt-in / 79% neutral / 82% opt-out
numbers.caveat: n=161; opt-out and neutral did NOT differ significantly — only opt-in was significantly lower. Switching cost was one mouse click

numbers.label: Field gap between opt-in and opt-out countries
numbers.value: ~60 percentage points, distributions do not overlap
numbers.caveat: Larger than the lab effect because real-world switching requires forms, calls and mail — the field/lab gap IS the effort cost

numbers.label: Default effect on actual donation rate
numbers.caveat: Gimbel et al. estimate 10.8 → 16.9 (+56.5%) on a broader country set; estimates vary with country selection

numbers.label: NN/g loading-state thresholds
numbers.value: <1 s: nothing; 2–10 s: spinner (module) or skeleton (full page); >10 s: progress bar
numbers.caveat: Contradicts the '400ms–3s' range in pass 1; skeletons are scoped to full-page loads and are annoying on fast pages

numbers.label: Accordion checkout implementations with major usability problems
numbers.caveat: E-commerce checkout, not a config builder; my fetch of the blog returned partially garbled text — treat the figure as indicative

numbers.label: Accordion adoption among top 100 US e-commerce sites
numbers.caveat: Historical; Baymard's point is that adoption rose without evidence of superiority

numbers.label: Voice-to-voice latency, measured over 500 production calls each (Mar 2026)
numbers.caveat: Third-party benchmark published by a competing vendor (Telnyx); config-dependent

numbers.label: Vapi's own published target vs its measured p50
numbers.value: Claimed <500 ms p50 / <800 ms p95; measured 720 / 1,050
numbers.source: Vapi published standard vs Tested Media measurement
numbers.caveat: Different configurations; illustrates the discount independent testers apply to vendor claims

numbers.label: Full-turn p50 on a fixed stack (GPT-4.1, Deepgram Nova-3, ElevenLabs Flash)
numbers.value: ElevenLabs 1,730 ms; LiveKit 2,460 ms
numbers.caveat: Fixed third-party stack, not each platform's optimised path — flattering to neither

numbers.label: Production fleet latency across 10+ live deployments
numbers.caveat: Anonymised and rounded vendor telemetry; 10+ projects is a small fleet

numbers.label: Speech-to-speech vs cascaded architecture
numbers.value: 560 ms p50 vs 700 ms p50
numbers.caveat: 140ms bought at roughly double the per-minute cost

numbers.label: All-in cost per connected minute
numbers.value: $0.07–$0.13 cascaded; $0.18–$0.21 speech-to-speech
numbers.caveat: LLM tokens are the largest variable ($0.02–0.08); drops to $0.07–0.11 at ~100k min/month

numbers.label: Containment rate (resolved without human escalation)
numbers.caveat: Varies hugely by use case; not comparable across industries

numbers.label: Latency at which callers start interrupting the agent
numbers.value: ~1,200 ms p50; production bar p95 under ~1,400 ms
numbers.caveat: Practitioner judgement from fleet telemetry, not a controlled study

numbers.label: Human conversational turn-handoff baseline
numbers.caveat: Widely repeated conversation-analysis figure; varies by language and culture

numbers.label: Voice agent pre-launch gates
numbers.value: Task success >85%; FCR >75%; reprompt <10%; barge-in accuracy >95% with <200 ms response; WER <10% clean / <15% noisy; hallucination <1%; TTFA <800 ms
numbers.caveat: Vendor-authored framework; thresholds are practitioner consensus rather than measured distributions

numbers.label: Deploy-blocking regression thresholds
numbers.value: >3% task-completion drop, >10% latency increase, >2% WER increase, >5% escalation increase
numbers.caveat: Vendor-authored; needs calibration against Agora's own variance before it becomes a hard gate

numbers.label: Test-suite size and composition
numbers.value: 50+ minimum, 200+ production-ready, 500+ enterprise/multilingual; 40% happy path / 30% edge / 15% error / 10% adversarial / 5% acoustic
numbers.caveat: Vendor-authored recommendation

numbers.label: Calls per variant for a 95%-confidence voice A/B test
numbers.caveat: Depends entirely on effect size and baseline rate; treat as an order-of-magnitude warning, not a computed figure

numbers.label: LiveKit published setup claim
numbers.value: Under 10 minutes, 4 steps after CLI init, no vendor keys for the default pipeline
numbers.source: LiveKit Agents docs, voice AI quickstart (read directly)
numbers.caveat: Terminal/CLI flow needing a local dev environment — not browser-to-agent like Studio X

numbers.label: Synthflow and Bland setup claims
numbers.value: Synthflow: live call under 1 hour from signup (vendor). Bland: slowest to first call; ~half a day of engineering for a basic outbound agent
numbers.source: Synthflow vendor claim; third-party Bland/Synthflow reviews
numbers.caveat: Both from competitor-adjacent review content; Bland's figure is a reviewer's estimate, not a measurement

numbers.label: Postman measured time to first successful API call
numbers.value: 17 min unaided → 10 min with a provided collection (1.7×); 1.7×–56× across APIs tested
numbers.caveat: Single vendor's experiment, small sample; the 56× case is an outlier on a badly documented API

numbers.label: Top blocker to consuming an API
numbers.value: Lack of documentation, 52% of developers
numbers.caveat: Self-reported survey

numbers.label: Geometric mean vs sample median for task times (n<25)
numbers.value: 13% less error, 22% less bias
numbers.caveat: Applies to small-sample lab data; use the median above n=25

numbers.label: PostHog's own activation metric shape
numbers.value: Compound of 2 actions (5+ replays AND 1+ filter set), found by testing 5–10 groups of 3–5 events against 3-month retention
numbers.source: PostHog, 'How we found our activation metric'
numbers.caveat: Their product, their retention curve; the method transfers, the specific events do not

numbers.label: B2B average session duration benchmarks
numbers.value: 77.61 s median (Databox, ~500 companies); 4:26 average (Hike SEO)
numbers.caveat: Website analytics, NOT in-app configuration time — explicitly unsuitable as the builder's time budget

numbers.label: Doherty & Thadani productivity claim
numbers.value: '25–30% more transactions per hour' — UNVERIFIED
numbers.source: Repeated across UX blogs; primary is IBM Systems Journal Vol 21 No 3, Nov 1982
numbers.caveat: The canonical mirror (vm.ibm.com) now returns an IBM marketing shell and the blogspot mirror 404s. Do not quote externally until the CHM copy (catalogue 102751398) is pulled

gaps: Gap 7 remains open and got worse: the Doherty & Thadani primary is no longer reachable online at all — the vm.ibm.com mirror now serves an IBM marketing page and the blogspot mirror 404s. Verifying the 25–30% productivity figure now requires ordering the Computer History Museum copy (catalogue 102751398) or an IBM Systems Journal archive, not just a paywall payment. The 400ms threshold itself is safe to keep using.

Gap 1 is still open for SETUP time and I now think it is unclosable from desk research — but it is CLOSED for runtime latency, where independent 500-call benchmarks exist for Vapi, Retell and Bland. Someone still has to stopwatch the six competitor signup-to-first-test flows. Recommend timing each one three times (cold account, warm account, and a deliberately interrupted run) and counting required decisions rather than fields, since pass 1 established that required decisions are the variable that matters.

No evidence found either way on whether five accordion sections is better or worse than three for a configuration builder. The Baymard accordion work is the closest analogue and its conclusion is that the count is not the lever — but that is e-commerce checkout, where users want to leave, versus a builder where users want to stay. This genuinely needs a PostHog section-level dropoff read plus about five moderated sessions, and I would not spend design effort on restructuring until both exist.

Could not retrieve the Mejtoft et al. (2018) study that NN/g rests its skeleton-screen perceived-speed claim on. Since I am recommending the loading-state rule be rewritten off NN/g's guidance, the underlying evidence for skeletons feeling faster at all is one step further away than it should be. Worth one fetch before the rule is encoded.

Two widely circulated onboarding stats could not be traced to primary sources and should not be quoted: a Mixpanel claim that high-retention SaaS apps show 2.5× longer sessions, and an Amplitude claim that users spending 3+ minutes on first interaction are 60% more likely to convert. Both appear only in SEO aggregator content. If the owner wants first-session-length evidence, these are not it.

Nothing found on how a semi-technical builder (as opposed to a developer) behaves on a configuration task — every attention and session number here, including the Parnin work I am recommending as the budget anchor, comes from professional programmers in an IDE. Studio X explicitly targets both audiences and they may have very different tolerance for a 15-minute block. The PostHog plan should carry a persona dimension from day one so this can be answered rather than assumed.

I did not test the live builder at https://ai-studio-console-redesign.vercel.app/agents/agt_default/edit against any of the thresholds in this sweep — no measurement of actual control response times against the 400ms budget, no check of whether collapsed accordion sections preserve an ongoing review, and no check of whether browser-back or section collapse loses entered configuration. Those last two are the Baymard failure modes and are checkable in about twenty minutes.

corpus.headline: Agora's zero-key managed default is no longer a differentiator — Vapi, Retell, ElevenLabs and LiveKit all reach a talking agent with zero vendor API keys, and the real 2026 race is won on two things Agora has not yet locked: testing an unsaved draft with no publish gate (Retell's guarantee) and provisioning a phone number in-product with no second vendor and no card (Vapi's free number).

findings.claim: Vapi's dashboard quickstart reaches a talking agent in 6 steps with only 2 required text decisions and zero vendor API keys.
findings.detail: The documented path is: sign up → Assistants → Create Assistant → replace First Message → replace System Prompt → Publish + Quick Publish → click Talk (mic permission) → hear it. No credential step appears anywhere in the flow. New accounts get $10 free credits with no credit card. The transcriber, LLM and voice are all pre-set to the "Balanced" Model Intelligence preset, so the entire model stack is a zero-decision default.
findings.soWhat: 6 steps / 2 decisions is the number Agora's builder must beat, not 'faster than configuring your own keys'. Agora's §1 Voice & Models sits first in the rail; if it is expanded by default it adds decisions Vapi does not make the user take. Instrument a strict step counter on the first-answer path and hold it at ≤6.
findings.source: Vapi docs — Assistants quickstart

findings.claim: Vapi forces a Publish before you can press Talk; Retell explicitly does not, and tests an unpublished draft for free, unlimited times.
findings.detail: Vapi's quickstart sequence is Publish → Quick Publish → Talk. Retell's quickstart states the opposite guarantee in its own words: web call testing works on a draft, unpublished agent, and "This step is free and doesn't need a phone number or payment method. You can test a draft agent this way as many times as you want before publishing it." That is a deliberate removal of a commit gate from the TTFA path.
findings.soWhat: This is Agora's single cheapest TTFA win. The docked right-hand test panel should call the *unsaved draft*, never require a publish, and say so in the panel copy. Add an explicit telemetry property `tested_draft: true|false` on `agent_test_session_succeeded` so we can prove no publish gate crept in.
findings.source: Retell AI docs — Quick start; Vapi docs — Assistants quickstart

findings.claim: Retell publishes a 15-minute claim for the FULL journey to a live phone agent, not just to first sound — and its step list matches Agora's five sections almost exactly.
findings.detail: The headline is "Build your first Retell AI phone agent in 15 minutes" and the documented flow is: create agent (pick type + template) → test in browser → add payment method → buy a number → make a call. New accounts get $10 in trial credits with no payment method required. Critically, Retell scopes the 15 minutes end-to-end, which is a harder and more honest claim than Vapi's "under 5 minutes" (first sound only).
findings.soWhat: Agora should adopt Retell's framing for its own public claim and its internal target: quote TTFA and TTFD as one end-to-end number. The current KPI doc's TTFA ≤3 min median + TTFD ≤20 min median sums to ~23 min, which is *slower* than Retell's advertised 15. Either the TTFD target tightens or the claim cannot be made.
findings.source: Retell AI docs — Quick start

findings.claim: Vapi gives every free account one free US phone number with no payment method — the fastest signup-to-real-inbound-call path in the market at roughly 9 total steps.
findings.detail: Vapi's phone quickstart: Phone Numbers → Create a Free Vapi Number (US area codes only, one free) → configure inbound settings to assign the assistant → call it. The free plan line item is "1 included Vapi phone number"; Core at $29/mo includes 5, Pro at $999/mo minimum includes 10. No Twilio account, no Stripe card, no SIP trunk.
findings.soWhat: This is where Agora is most likely SLOWER. Agora's channel section adds a phone number via SIP (`AddPhoneNumberSheet`). If that means bring-your-own-SIP-trunk, Agora's TTFD loses to Vapi by an entire external vendor signup. Resolve this before publishing any speed claim: either resell numbers in-product or make the web widget the default deploy channel.
findings.source: Vapi docs — Phone calls quickstart; Vapi pricing

findings.claim: Retell gates phone deployment behind a Stripe payment method, adding a hard commercial stop between a working agent and a deployed one.
findings.detail: The deploy path is Phone Numbers → Buy New Number → add payment method via Stripe → optionally specify area code → purchase → assign agent. Numbers cost $2/mo standard, $5/mo toll-free, US/Canada only. Retell is careful to place this gate *after* the free browser test, explicitly noting "You only need a number once you want to make or receive real phone calls."
findings.soWhat: The sequencing is the lesson, not the price: Retell puts every commercial and credential gate strictly downstream of first sound. Agora's §2 Deployment currently sits BEFORE §3 Prompt and §4 Test in the rail order, which puts a channel decision upstream of the first test. Reorder or make §2 skippable-by-default.
findings.source: Retell AI docs — Quick start

findings.claim: Agora's section ORDER is the biggest structural TTFA risk in the current builder: two configuration sections and a deployment decision sit upstream of Test.
findings.detail: `components/wizard/types.ts` defines STEP_TITLES as Voice & Models → Deployment → Prompt & knowledge → Test → Go Live, grouped as Customize (1,2,3) → Ship. So the literal rail order asks a user to pick a model stack and a deployment channel (Inbound / Batch / Code-SDK, a radio, not multi-select) before ever hearing the agent. Every competitor that wins on TTFA — Vapi, Retell, ElevenLabs, LiveKit Agent Builder — puts prompt-then-test first and defers channel entirely.
findings.soWhat: Move Deployment after Test, or keep the rail order but make §1 and §2 fully collapsed with defaults applied so the happy path is Prompt → Test. The persistent docked test panel already allows testing from any section — lean on it and measure `section_index_at_first_test`; if the median is >1 the IA is still pushing people through configuration first.
findings.source: Agora studio_x_2 repo — /Users/shaktisoni/Documents/Agora Design & FE/ai-studio-console-redesign/studio_x_2/components/wizard/types.ts

findings.claim: Vapi's "Model Intelligence" presets are a direct feature-for-feature match to Agora's latency-vs-cost slider — and Vapi shows latency, cost and quality numbers per preset.
findings.detail: Vapi ships Balanced, High Intelligence, Ultra Fast and Cost Saver presets that set transcriber + LLM + voice in one click, with the docs noting you "can see the latency, cost, and quality metrics for your chosen models so you can compare options and optimize with data." Balanced is the default on every new assistant.
findings.soWhat: Agora's bundled-stack slider is table stakes, not a differentiator — do not build the pitch on it. The one thing Vapi has that the slider may not is per-preset latency/cost/quality figures shown at the point of decision. Add those numbers to the slider; it converts a vague trade-off into a 45-second decision, matching the §1 dwell budget already in the KPI doc.
findings.source: Vapi docs — Assistants quickstart, What's New

findings.claim: ElevenLabs Agents needs zero vendor keys to talk but CANNOT sell you a phone number — it hard-requires your own Twilio account SID and auth token, or a third-party SIP trunk.
findings.detail: To attach a number you go to Phone Numbers, give a label, and enter your Twilio phone number, Twilio SID and Auth Token. The docs recommend API keys over account-wide credentials. ElevenLabs supports SIP trunks from Twilio, Vonage, RingCentral, Sinch, Infobip, Telnyx, Exotel, Plivo and Bandwidth — but sells no numbers itself. The web-widget path is by contrast very fast: paste an HTML embed snippet carrying the agent ID.
findings.soWhat: This is the clearest competitive opening for Agora. ElevenLabs is fast to first sound and fast to a widget, but its phone TTFD carries an entire second vendor signup (+6–10 steps). If Agora provisions numbers in-product, lead the benchmark table with phone TTFD, not TTFA.
findings.source: ElevenLabs docs — Twilio native integration

findings.claim: ElevenLabs' own FAQ contradicts its marketing: the homepage says "Deploy AI Agents in Minutes, Not Months" while the FAQ says "Most teams can configure their first agent within hours."
findings.detail: The agents landing page carries both "Deploy AI Agents in Minutes, Not Months" and "Build your first agent in minutes — no engineering required", with a free tier of 15 included minutes. The FAQ on the same property concedes hours. Independent G2 developer reports land in between: a basic voice agent working in 15–30 minutes through the dashboard, with the voice production-ready from the first test.
findings.soWhat: Whatever claim Agora publishes must be reproducible by a cold user on a timed run, because reviewers now check. Before any marketing number ships, run the 10-person timed cold-start study the KPI doc's A0 assumption depends on and quote the p75, not the best case.
findings.source: ElevenLabs — Agents product page and FAQ; G2 developer reports

findings.claim: LiveKit removed the API-key burden entirely with LiveKit Inference, and its default pipeline needs no provider accounts at all.
findings.detail: LiveKit Inference is built into LiveKit Cloud and gives access to STT, LLM and TTS "without needing separate API keys or accounts with each provider", included on every plan including the free Build plan. The default starter pipeline is Deepgram Nova-3 + Gemma 4 31B + Inworld TTS-2, with the docs stating "No additional setup is required." Only the OpenAI Realtime variant requires OPENAI_API_KEY. Free Build plan includes $2.50/mo in inference credits; Scale includes 50,000 session minutes plus $50 in credits.
findings.soWhat: Confirms the strategic conclusion: managed keys are now the industry default across every tier of competitor, including the open-source-adjacent one. Agora's credential story must be reframed from 'no keys needed' (everyone) to something sharper — e.g. no keys AND no card AND a number in the same product.
findings.source: LiveKit docs — Voice AI quickstart; LiveKit Inference knowledge base

findings.claim: LiveKit's SDK path costs 9 terminal steps and a local dev environment, but its new browser Agent Builder erases that gap while keeping an export-to-code escape hatch.
findings.detail: The CLI quickstart claims "Build and deploy a simple voice assistant in less than 10 minutes" across 9 steps: install Python≥3.10/Node≥20, install uv/pnpm, install the LiveKit CLI, `lk cloud auth`, `lk agent init --template agent-starter-python`, `cd`, `uv sync`, `lk agent dev`, open the browser link and start a session. Separately, Agent Builder lets you "create, test, and deploy production-grade LiveKit voice agents in minutes, with zero local setup" in a panel-based browser UI (prompt, models, HTTP tools, phone numbers) with a "Download code" button producing a runnable Python project.
findings.soWhat: Directly relevant to Agora's §2 Code/SDK channel. LiveKit has proven the pattern Agora should copy: configure visually, test in-browser, then export real code — rather than making Code/SDK a separate channel choice that forks the user out of the fast path before they have tested anything.
findings.source: LiveKit docs — Voice AI quickstart; LiveKit — Announcing Agent Builder

findings.claim: Every serious competitor now has an in-dashboard browser voice test; requiring a phone number for first contact is extinct.
findings.detail: Vapi has a Talk button (post-publish). Retell has a free unlimited draft web call. ElevenLabs has a "Test AI agent" button. LiveKit opens the Agent Console in the browser from the CLI, and Agent Builder tests in-page. Bland's Conversational Pathways builder has web-based chat in text or voice plus per-node unit testing. Synthflow tests in-dashboard with transcript, recording, action summary and call analysis returned.
findings.soWhat: Agora's docked test panel is correct but is now parity, not advantage. The differentiation must come from what the panel returns after the call — Synthflow returns transcript + recording + actions + analysis. Agora's §4 already generates scenarios; pair generated scenarios with a post-call result card and that becomes the confidence story the owner asked for.
findings.source: Vapi, Retell, ElevenLabs, LiveKit, Bland and Synthflow product docs

findings.claim: Bland has effectively a zero-step TTFA: it lets a prospect have the AI call their phone before they sign up at all.
findings.detail: Reviewers note that before even signing up you can test the system by having an AI call your phone — a pre-account demo. Bland is fully self-hosted end to end, so no vendor keys are involved at any point, and its API quickstart is "ten lines of code" to place a call, with named patterns for voicemail handling, proper-noun transcription and human escalation.
findings.soWhat: The cheapest possible TTFA is one that happens before the account exists. Consider a pre-auth demo agent on the Agora marketing surface that hands the visitor a pre-populated draft on signup — it collapses the 'blank account' half of the funnel entirely, and gives PostHog an anonymous-to-identified join point for measuring true time-to-first-sound.
findings.source: Bland AI docs and product reviews

findings.claim: Pipecat and Deepgram define the slow end of the market — Pipecat needs three separate vendor accounts before a single word is spoken.
findings.detail: The Pipecat quickstart requires DEEPGRAM_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY and CARTESIA_API_KEY set locally, plus a virtualenv, dependency install, a server on :7860, and a ~20s first-run model download before you click Connect. Deepgram's Voice Agent API is a single unified voice-to-voice WebSocket needing one DEEPGRAM_API_KEY, with server-side SDKs in Python/JS/C#/Go, plus a Browser Agent SDK offering a drop-in widget with six layouts.
findings.soWhat: These are the only places Agora's zero-key story is a genuine step-count win, and they are frameworks, not console competitors. Do not build the competitive narrative against them. Deepgram's one-line widget with six layouts is however a good model for Agora's web-widget deploy channel.
findings.source: Pipecat docs — Quickstart; Deepgram docs — Voice Agent, Browser Agent SDK

findings.claim: Synthflow's real-world time-to-live-phone-agent is 30–60 minutes despite a 4-step marketing flow — the gap is telephony and integrations, not configuration.
findings.detail: Synthflow advertises four steps to go live (template → build conversation → voice + integrations → test & launch) and a reviewer built a working appointment-booking agent in 11 minutes. But the same reviews put the honest end-to-end figure at "pick a template, write your prompt, plug in a Twilio number or use a bring-your-own configuration, and have a working inbound agent on the phone in 30 to 60 minutes." Free trial is 14 days with 15 minutes of free testing.
findings.soWhat: Confirms where TTFD time actually goes across the whole category: the last mile is telephony wiring, not the builder. Agora's TTFD instrumentation should break the clock into configure / test / channel-connect / publish sub-spans, because the category evidence says channel-connect dominates and that is the span worth designing against.
findings.source: Synthflow product pages and independent 2026 reviews

findings.claim: No competitor publishes activation rates, onboarding funnel conversion, or real TTFA distributions — every public number is a marketing claim.
findings.detail: Searches across company blogs, comparisons and review sites surfaced operational stats (Vapi cited at 62M monthly calls, 99.99% SLA) and vendor-authored latency comparisons, but zero published activation or funnel data from Vapi, Retell, ElevenLabs or LiveKit. The only quasi-empirical onboarding figures are third-party and self-reported: a developer report of setup dropping from 8 hours to 47 minutes on Retell, G2 reports of 15–30 minutes on ElevenLabs, and a Synthflow reviewer's 11 minutes.
findings.soWhat: Agora cannot benchmark against competitor telemetry because none exists. The benchmark must therefore be reproducible step counts and timed cold-start runs we conduct ourselves. Budget a recurring timed competitive run (one cold account per platform per quarter) as the baseline source for the TTFA/TTFD targets, since the KPI doc currently lists the TTFA baseline as 'unknown — not instrumented'.
findings.source: Sweep across vendor blogs, docs and third-party reviews; no primary funnel data found

findings.claim: Vapi charges $0.05/min for its own layer and passes model costs through at cost, meaning BYOK saves the user nothing on Vapi's fee — the same economics Agora's managed default already encodes.
findings.detail: Vapi pricing shows $0.05/min hosting on the free plan with "Models pass-through at cost", and the provider-keys doc frames BYOK purely as a billing redirection: "Once your API key is validated, you won't be charged when using that provider through Vapi. Instead, you'll be charged directly by the provider." Retell publishes component rates instead — ~$0.055/min infra + $0.015/min standard TTS, LLM from $0.025 (Claude 4.5 Haiku) to $0.16/min, telephony $0.015/min via its Twilio integration or $0 with your own SIP trunk — giving an all-in $0.13–$0.31/min.
findings.soWhat: Agora's `campaign-data.ts` already models exactly this (managed absorbs the vendor bill, BYO does not save the platform rate). The design implication: the Configure sheets must state that BYO changes *who bills you*, not *what you pay Agora* — otherwise users will open those sheets speculatively and burn the §1 dwell budget on a decision with no upside for them.
findings.source: Vapi pricing and provider-keys docs; Retell pricing analyses

findings.claim: GAP 1 CLOSED: Agora does not sell or port phone numbers — confirmed independently in Agora's own production docs and in the redesign's own UI copy.
findings.detail: docs.agora.io/en/conversational-ai/studio/deploy/sip-trunk requires an active SIP trunk account and a SIP-capable number as prerequisites; its "Buy a number" affordance buys from your SIP trunk provider, not from Agora. The redesign says the same thing in the sheet header at /studio_x_2/components/add-phone-number-sheet.tsx: "Bring a number you already own. Agora routes it, and doesn't sell or port numbers." The manual form demands 6 required fields (number, vendor, display name, SIP domain, username, password) plus a transport choice. The Quick-connect branch (components/sip-quick-connect.tsx) reduces that to ≤4 inputs by pasting a Twilio/Telnyx credential and auto-enumerating, auto-picking and auto-attaching the number.
findings.soWhat: Kill any "fastest to a live phone agent" claim. Agora's honest TTFD claim is scoped to the web widget (where it is genuinely zero-credential) and to users who already own a number. For phone, the competitive story is Quick-connect's ≤4 inputs versus a 6-field manual SIP form — sell the import, never the provisioning.
findings.source: Agora docs (SIP trunk deploy page) + repo: components/add-phone-number-sheet.tsx, components/sip-quick-connect.tsx

findings.claim: Agora's no-numbers deficit is a US-only deficit: outside North America every competitor collapses onto the same bring-your-own-Twilio path Agora requires.
findings.detail: Vapi's free number is "only available for US national use and cannot make outbound calls"; anything else must be bought at Twilio and imported. Retell sells US/Canada numbers only and can dial just 15 countries. LiveKit Phone Numbers is US-only and inbound-only today. ElevenLabs never sold numbers at all — numbers must be "purchased through Twilio" and appear in your Twilio account. So for a developer in London, Bengaluru, São Paulo or Singapore, all five platforms require the identical Twilio detour.
findings.soWhat: This is the strongest unmeasured competitive opening in the sweep. Segment the TTFD benchmark by region: publish US and non-US columns. If Agora's developer base skews non-US, Quick-connect (paste one credential, we build the trunk) is a category-leading experience, not a consolation prize — and it should be the headline of Deployment, not a fallback.
findings.source: docs.vapi.ai/phone-calling; docs.retellai.com/deploy/purchase-number; docs.livekit.io/telephony; elevenlabs.io/docs Twilio native integration

findings.claim: Non-US TTFD is measured in days, not minutes, for every platform — Twilio regulatory bundles take up to 3 business days typically and up to 21 business days in KYC countries.
findings.detail: Twilio's own support documentation states the review "generally takes up to three business days, but in some regions it might take several weeks," and that many countries require KYC documents where "approval can take up to 21 business days." Evaluations get a 48-business-hour review. A trial Twilio project additionally cannot provision more than one number and can only call verified caller IDs, and Twilio's trial credit is $15.15.
findings.soWhat: TTFD as a single median is meaningless once telephony is in scope. Instrument TTFD with a `blocked_on` dimension (`external_carrier`, `regulatory_review`, `payment_method`, `none`) so a 3-day bundle wait does not contaminate the builder's own clock. Add a suspend/resume state to the Deployment section so a user parked on carrier approval is not counted as an abandoned session.
findings.source: Twilio Support — regulatory bundle submission; Twilio free trial limitations

findings.claim: GAP 6 CLOSED: Agora's docked test panel already tests the unsaved draft — there is no save or publish gate, and the wizard says so explicitly.
findings.detail: components/wizard/agent-wizard.tsx carries the header comment "Publish is a HINT, not a gate," and `toggleTest()` fires `agent_test_started` with no reference to publish state. The only thing that can disable Talk is `talkDisabled={warming}` — first-run model warm-up, and the panel is documented to be "Disabled WITH its reason, never dead." `publishBlocks()` in lib/wizard-draft.ts gates only deploy (voice, channel, number binding, prompt); firstIncompleteStep notes "Test (4) runs on defaults."
findings.soWhat: Assumption A2 in docs/design/agent-builder-kpis.md is mis-specified: the capability already exists, so the change cannot buy −60 s by "making it possible." Rewrite A2 as a discoverability assumption — the cost is that nobody knows the draft is testable — and measure it with `agent_test_session_started{agentState:"draft"|"saved"}` plus time-to-first-Talk-click from builder mount. Also add a first-run `warming` duration metric; it is now the only thing standing between mount and first audio.
findings.source: repo: components/wizard/agent-wizard.tsx, components/wizard/test-panel.tsx, lib/wizard-draft.ts

findings.claim: CONTRADICTS PASS 1: Vapi's own documented happy path to first sound is a phone call, not the browser — provisioning a free US number is steps 5–7 of a 9-step quickstart, and Vapi publishes "In under 5 minutes" for that whole path.
findings.detail: docs.vapi.ai/quickstart/dashboard walks: create account → Assistants → Create Assistant (Customer Support template) → edit First Message and System Prompt → Phone Numbers → Create Phone Number → Free Vapi Number → enter US area code → assign assistant under Inbound Settings → then "Talk" or call the number. The literal claim is "In under 5 minutes, you'll create a voice assistant and start talking to it over the phone." That is 9 steps, not 6, and the browser Talk button is presented as an alternative at the end rather than the primary path.
findings.soWhat: The benchmark table needs two rows per competitor: documented-happy-path steps and shortest-possible steps. Vapi is 9/≈5. Quote Vapi's "under 5 minutes" as the number to beat for TTFA — it is the most aggressive published first-sound claim from a direct competitor, and it includes telephony provisioning that Agora cannot match.
findings.source: docs.vapi.ai — Dashboard quickstart

findings.claim: GAP 3 PARTLY CLOSED: Vapi's provider-keys doc confirms by implication that Vapi runs on its own keys by default — but never states it, so the zero-key comparison is still not safe to publish.
findings.detail: docs.vapi.ai/customization/provider-keys says verbatim: "Once your API key is validated, you won't be charged when using that provider through Vapi. Instead, you'll be charged directly by the provider." That sentence only makes sense if Vapi otherwise bills you for provider usage on Vapi's own credentials. The pricing page adds "Models pass-through at cost" and "Provider costs with no markup." Nowhere does Vapi write "you do not need an API key."
findings.soWhat: Keep the claim internal. In any public comparison, say what Vapi documents ("models pass through at cost; BYOK moves the bill to your provider") rather than what we infer. Agora's differentiator survives either way and is stronger and citable: Agora charges the same $0.10/min with or without BYOK, so on Agora BYOK is strictly worse for the customer.
findings.source: docs.vapi.ai/customization/provider-keys; vapi.ai/pricing

findings.claim: CONTRADICTS PASS 1: Bland's pre-signup demo is a browser click-to-speak widget, not an AI that phones you — and Bland's headline claim is now "live in production in 30 days," not minutes.
findings.detail: bland.ai's homepage CTA is "Talk to an agent" / "Click to speak with an agent" across four verticals (general, Healthcare, Insurance, Financial services). The deployment story on the same page is an enterprise timeline: Day 1 Discovery, Day 7 Build begins, Day 14 first end-to-end run, Day 21 dry run, Day 30 live in production. The page makes no "build in minutes" claim at all.
findings.soWhat: Remove "Bland has effectively zero-step TTFA because it calls your phone" from the benchmark. The accurate read is that Bland has a pre-signup browser demo — which Agora lacks and which is cheap to build from the existing Test panel — and that Bland has vacated the self-serve speed position. A logged-out "hear an Agora agent" page is now a clear, costed competitive move.
findings.source: bland.ai homepage

findings.claim: CONTRADICTS PASS 1: Agora's bundled managed-key economics are not unique — Bland bundles LLM + STT + TTS into one per-minute rate with no pass-throughs, gives a free inbound number, and requires no card.
findings.detail: Bland's Start plan is $0.14/min with a $0 platform fee, and the pricing page states the rate "covers the LLM, STT, and TTS in one number, with no token charges and no model-provider pass-throughs." Start includes "2 credits + an inbound number ($15/mo value)" and is explicitly marked "No card required." Build is $0.12/min on a $299/mo platform fee.
findings.soWhat: Stop framing the zero-key managed default as unusual. The defensible framing is price plus symmetry: Agora is $0.10/min all-in (cheaper than Bland's $0.14 bundled) and is the only platform where BYOK costs the same as managed. Put that sentence — not "no API keys needed" — on the credential row in §1 and in any comparison asset.
findings.source: bland.ai/pricing

findings.claim: MAJOR NEW: LiveKit now sells phone numbers in-product and publishes the most aggressive TTFD claim in the market — "zero to ringing in 60 seconds", with one free US number on every plan.
findings.detail: LiveKit Phone Numbers lets you buy local or toll-free US numbers directly in LiveKit and assign them to agents via dispatch rules, "without requiring separate SIP trunk configuration." "All of our plans include one free US local phone number and a monthly allotment of free inbound calling minutes"; the Build plan includes 50 free inbound minutes. Currently US-only and inbound-only, with international numbers and outbound on the roadmap. Combined with the browser Agent Builder (Deploy new agent → configure → live preview → Deploy → Launch Console, 6 steps, no local setup) and LiveKit Inference removing provider keys, LiveKit has closed both of the gaps pass 1 attributed to it.
findings.soWhat: Re-rank the threat list: LiveKit, not Vapi, is now the closest structural analogue to Studio X — real-time infra company, bundled inference, browser builder, in-product numbers, code export. Their "60 seconds" is the number a sceptical exec will quote at us. Our counter has to be TTFA (hearing it answer), where a docked draft-testable panel beats a deploy-then-call loop — which means instrumenting TTFA is now urgent, not later.
findings.source: LiveKit blog + docs (Phone Numbers, Agent Builder)

findings.claim: CONTRADICTS PASS 1: Synthflow has closed its self-serve funnel — enterprise contracts from $30,000/year, no published per-minute rate, no confirmable trial.
findings.detail: synthflow.ai/pricing now shows an enterprise tier only, "Enterprise contracts start at $30,000 annually," with pricing scoped per contract and no per-minute number anywhere on the page. Third-party analysis notes the white-label add-on and Enterprise path both route to Contact Sales, and that the widely-repeated "14-day free trial" traces to a mid-2024 social post not confirmed by any current page. Independent estimates put realistic all-in cost at $0.11–$0.24/min.
findings.soWhat: Drop Synthflow from the TTFA/TTFD benchmark table — it no longer has a self-serve clock to measure. Keep it only as evidence for the strategic point that two of six named competitors (Synthflow, Bland) have left the self-serve speed race, which makes the position Agora is targeting less crowded than the brief assumes.
findings.source: synthflow.ai/pricing; third-party pricing analyses

findings.claim: GAP 5 CLOSED: ElevenLabs bills LLM and telephony separately on top of agent minutes — it is a three-bill platform, not a bundled one — and its docs name no default LLM.
findings.detail: elevenlabs.io/pricing/agents: Free plan 15 minutes; Starter $6/75 min; Creator $22/275 min; Pro $99/1,238 min; Scale $299/3,738 min; Business $990/12,375 min. Overage $0.08/min, burst $0.16/min over concurrency. The page states "The LLM model and any telephony are billed separately on top, based on usage." The supported-LLM page lists Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and — new — ElevenLabs' own hosted Qwen models, but designates no default. Silent periods are billed at 5% of the usual per-minute rate.
findings.soWhat: ElevenLabs is the cleanest foil for Agora's one-number pricing: three bills versus one, and 15 free minutes versus Agora's 300. Use it in the credential row's supporting copy. Also note ElevenLabs shipping first-party LLMs — the bundling trend is industry-wide, so Agora's managed default is table stakes within ~12 months and the durable differentiator must be the symmetric BYOK price, not the bundle itself.
findings.source: elevenlabs.io/pricing/agents; elevenlabs.io/docs agents LLM pages

findings.claim: Agora's designed free tier is the most generous test allowance in the set by roughly 5x — 300 minutes/month, 150 usable with no card at all.
findings.detail: Agora docs: $0.10/min, "first 300 minutes are free," "usage of ASR, LLM, and TTS providers is included in the unit price" with a managed key, and "you are charged the same price even if you bring your own key (BYOK)." The redesign splits that into 150 card-free minutes then a card-unlock for the remaining 150 (components/free-minutes-nudge.tsx). Competitors: Retell $10 credit ≈ 60 minutes; Vapi $10 credit ≈ 200 minutes of Vapi's own $0.05 fee only, with provider costs eating into it; ElevenLabs 15 minutes/month; LiveKit 50 free inbound minutes on Build; Bland "2 credits" plus a free inbound number.
findings.soWhat: Make the free-minutes number visible in the builder from section 1 — it is a bigger differentiator than the credential row and nobody else can match it. Instrument `free_minutes_remaining` as a property on `agent_test_started` so the KPI doc can test whether a visible allowance raises test-attempt rate, and add the 150-minute card-free ceiling as an explicit guardrail metric (nobody should hit the card nudge before their first successful deploy).
findings.source: docs.agora.io conversational-ai pricing; repo lib/campaign-data.ts, components/free-minutes-nudge.tsx; retellai.com/pricing; elevenlabs.io/pricing/agents

findings.claim: Retell publishes two mutually inconsistent build times — 15 minutes in docs, "the 30 minute build is the floor, not the ceiling" on its own blog.
findings.detail: Retell's documentation carries "Build your first phone agent in 15 minutes," while a Retell blog post frames the honest path as a 30-minute floor over six steps: sign up → pick a template → write the prompt → wire a function → simulate → connect a number. Retell's pricing page separately claims "Go live in minutes with $10 in free credits" and prices agents at $0.07–$0.31/min unbundled (example split: LLM $0.04, Retell voice infra $0.055, TTS $0.015), with Retell-managed numbers at $2.00/month.
findings.soWhat: Use 30 minutes, not 15, as Retell's comparator in the benchmark table — a sceptical reviewer will find the blog post. It also validates the KPI doc's 20-minute TTFD target as genuinely competitive rather than arbitrary: beating a self-published 30-minute floor is a defensible external claim once we have instrumented numbers.
findings.source: docs.retellai.com; retellai.com/blog; retellai.com/pricing

findings.claim: Vapi's publish gate is confirmed and has now been softened by Version Preview and Version History — the gate stands, but Vapi has shipped a rollback story Agora has not.
findings.detail: Vapi's dashboard requires clicking Publish to save changes (server SDKs apply immediately with no publish step); publishing creates a new assistant version, after which you can "Talk to start a web call." Version Preview shows "a diff view that highlights any unpublished changes compared to your live version"; Version History tracks every version for "comparing iterations or reverting to something that just worked." Vapi's own Canny board carries an open bug that the Publish button intermittently fails to save changes.
findings.soWhat: Agora keeps the TTFA win (test the draft, no publish) but is now behind on TCR: the KPI doc targets TCR ≥ 95% and 24h rollback as the tiebreaker, with no version-history surface to support it. Add a config-version diff to the Go Live preflight (A8) and a one-click revert in Monitor — otherwise we will win the speed comparison and lose the trust one.
findings.source: vapi.ai blog — Version Preview, Version History and RBAC; Vapi docs; vapi.canny.io bug report

findings.claim: RISK: Agora's shipped ConvoAI Playground still asks for an LLM API Key and sits behind a login — the zero-key managed default is a redesign promise, not a measurable baseline.
findings.detail: Fetching conversational-ai.agora.io returned an authenticated agent-settings surface exposing "LLM API Key" and "TTS Vendor" fields, not a public demo. Agora's own blog describes the playground as a place where "you provide API keys for ASR (Microsoft, Deepgram, or use Agora's built-in), TTS (Microsoft, ElevenLabs, OpenAI, etc), and your LLM endpoint." That is the opposite posture from the redesign's Agora Managed Key default (components/wizard/stack-config.tsx: "Agora Managed Key by default; a switch brings your own key").
findings.soWhat: Assumption A0's baseline must be measured on the live ng-console, not the prototype, and the migration brief should treat "managed key is the default, visibly" as a shipped-product change with its own rollout risk — not a design given. If the live console still asks for keys, the 8–12 minute baseline guess in A0 is probably optimistic.
findings.source: conversational-ai.agora.io (fetched); agora.io blog — A Playground for testing Voice AI Agents; repo components/wizard/stack-config.tsx

findings.claim: Agora has no logged-out "hear it talk" affordance, and it is now the cheapest TTFA win left — Bland and LiveKit both put a talkable agent in front of an anonymous visitor.
findings.detail: Bland's homepage offers "Click to speak with an agent" across four verticals with no account. LiveKit's Agent Builder preview runs in-browser with "zero local setup." Agora's nearest equivalent is gated. The redesign already contains every part needed — the TalkTab in components/wizard/test-panel.tsx, a default managed stack, and a default voice — so a logged-out variant is a routing and quota problem, not a build problem.
findings.soWhat: Propose a pre-signup demo as its own tracker row with its own assumption: a logged-out talk reduces signup-to-first-test to near zero and gives us a TTFA distribution on people who never signed up. Instrument it as `agent_test_started{authState:"anonymous"}` and read signup conversion from the anonymous cohort — this is the only TTFA measurement that can ever reach 0 minutes.
findings.source: bland.ai homepage; livekit.com Agent Builder; repo components/wizard/test-panel.tsx

findings.claim: The dwell budgets in the KPI doc are all far beyond the attention threshold the UX literature establishes, so every budgeted section needs an explicit progress or partial-result affordance.
findings.detail: Nielsen's response-time limits put 1 second as the boundary for uninterrupted flow and 10 seconds as "about the limit for keeping the user's attention focused on the dialogue," after which "users start thinking about other things" and need a percent-done indicator plus a way to interrupt. The KPI doc's p75 budgets are 45 s (preset), 90 s (voice), 60 s (speech), 2 min (manual models), 5 min (prompt), 90 s (test). Every one is 4x–30x the 10-second threshold. SipQuickConnect already solves this correctly with a timestamped fact-log instead of a spinner.
findings.soWhat: Make the fact-log pattern a rule, not a one-off: any section whose p75 budget exceeds 10 s must show incremental progress or partial output (voice auditions streaming in, prompt template filling live, test connecting with named stages). Add `section_progress_shown` to the tracking plan so we can test whether the fact-log pattern actually lowers dwell, and treat the 90-second test budget as the one that most needs it — the `warming` state is currently a disabled button.
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Response Time Limits; repo components/sip-quick-connect.tsx; docs/design/agent-builder-kpis.md §2.3

findings.claim: GAP 2 remains open and is now the single highest-value missing artifact: no timed cold-start runs exist, and no competitor publishes one either — whoever measures first owns the claim.
findings.detail: This second pass confirmed pass 1's conclusion that every public figure is a step count or a marketing claim. Cross-industry SaaS onboarding benchmarks exist but come from low-credibility SEO sources: median time-to-aha cited as 11 minutes for horizontal SaaS, best-in-class first value in 2–5 minutes, median onboarding completion 38.4% with top quartile 67%. None are voice-AI specific and none should be quoted externally.
findings.soWhat: Run the stopwatch study before the benchmark table ships: one cold account each on Vapi, Retell, ElevenLabs, LiveKit and Agora, identical task ("a receptionist that books appointments, talking in my browser"), same operator, screen-recorded, three trials each. That produces the only real TTFA distribution in the market and converts the owner's speed thesis from a claim into evidence. It also gives A0 its baseline, which currently reads "unknown — not instrumented."
findings.source: This sweep (absence of evidence); SaaS onboarding benchmark blogs (low credibility)
