corpus.headline: PostHog cannot alert on — or take a percentile of — a funnel's time-to-convert, so TTFA and every p75 dwell budget in the KPI doc must be captured as an explicit numeric `duration_ms` property on the completion event; the funnel becomes the cross-check, not the source of truth.

findings.claim: PostHog's own docs give two contradictory event-naming conventions, so the repo must pick one and freeze it rather than cite "PostHog says".
findings.detail: The product-analytics best-practices page says: only lowercase, snake_case, and **present-tense** verbs — "use present-tense verbs, e.g., 'submit' and 'create' instead of 'submitted' and 'created'" — with a `category:object_action` shape like `account_settings:forgot_password_button_click`. The JS SDK features page says the opposite: "Use a `[object] [verb]` format... For example, `project created`, `user signed up`, or `invite sent`" — past tense, space-separated. studio_x_2's `lib/analytics.ts` already declares `object_verb_past_tense` snake_case at the top of the file and has 88 `track()` call sites following it (`agent_published`, `deployment_went_live`, `test_run_completed`).
findings.soWhat: Do not churn 88 call sites to chase a doc page. Write `snake_case, object_verb, past tense` into the spec as an Agora decision with both PostHog pages cited as "PostHog is internally inconsistent here", and add the allowed-verb dictionary PostHog does recommend (click, submit, create, view, add, invite, update, delete, remove, start, end, cancel, fail, generate, send) — extended with `previewed, selected, configured, evaluated, imported, succeeded, failed`. Enforce it with a lint rule over the `Events` map, not by review.
findings.source: PostHog — Product analytics best practices; PostHog — JavaScript SDK features

findings.claim: The live property-naming split between ng-console (camelCase) and studio_x_2 (snake_case) will produce two parallel property namespaces in one PostHog project the day the builder ships.
findings.detail: `ng-console/src/lib/observability/sanitize.ts` hard-codes a camelCase allowlist: `durationMs`, `routePattern`, `productArea`, `schemaVersion`, `errorStage`, `isInternalUser`. studio_x_2's stub emits snake_case: `agent_id`, `time_to_first_agent_ms`, `from_project_id`, `pct_used`. PostHog's best-practices page recommends snake_case with an `object_adjective` pattern (`user_id`, `item_price`, `member_count`), `is_`/`has_` prefixes for booleans, and `_date`/`_timestamp` suffixes for temporal values. PostHog will happily store `durationMs` and `duration_ms` as two unrelated property definitions; no funnel can break down across both.
findings.soWhat: Decide now, before the builder's new events land. Cheapest correct move: keep ng-console's camelCase wire format (it is already sanitizer-enforced and schema-2.1.0-versioned) and change studio_x_2's stub to match, since studio_x_2 has no production data yet. Whichever way it goes, the spec needs one `properties` table with the casing stated once, and the sanitizer allowlist becomes the generated artifact rather than a hand-edited Set.
findings.source: PostHog — Product analytics best practices; repo files sanitize.ts and lib/analytics.ts

findings.claim: Funnel alerts explicitly exclude the time-to-convert view — so TTFA can never be alerted on if it is only a funnel statistic.
findings.detail: The alerts doc states alerts work on "trends, funnels (steps and trends views only), and SQL (HogQL) insights" and that funnel alerts "specifically exclude time-to-convert and flow/sankey views." Check frequencies are real-time (Scale/Enterprise, 10–20 slots), every 15 min (Boost+), hourly, daily, weekly, monthly. Free tier caps at 5 alerts total. Destinations include email, Slack, Discord, Teams and webhooks, plus threshold, relative-change and anomaly (Z-score, MAD, IQR, Isolation Forest, KNN, LOF) conditions.
findings.soWhat: This settles the duration-measurement question. The KPI doc's kill rule ("if a change does not move its metric by half the predicted effect within two reporting weeks") needs an alert on TTFA regression; therefore `agent_test_session_succeeded` must carry a numeric `ttfaMs` property, charted as a Trends insight, and that is what the alert hangs off. Budget 5 alerts if the project is on free tier — spend them on TTFA p75, first-publish failure rate, TCR, event-volume drop (data-quality canary) and publish error rate.
findings.source: PostHog — Alerts

findings.claim: Only Trends property aggregation gives p75 — and every dwell budget in the KPI doc is written as a p75, so the budgets are unmeasurable without an explicit duration property on each completion event.
findings.detail: PostHog Trends offers property-value aggregations for numeric properties: Average, Sum, Minimum, Maximum, Median, and 75th / 90th / 95th / 99th percentile, with the caveat that "property aggregation only works on properties with numerical values." The funnel's time-to-convert view shows a distribution and average, not a selectable percentile. §2.3 of the KPI doc sets seven p75 budgets (preset 45 s, voice 90 s, speech 60 s, model sheet 2 min, prompt 5 min, test 90 s, deploy 60 s).
findings.soWhat: Every section-completion event gets a `sectionDwellMs` and an `activeDwellMs` (idle >60 s removed, per §2.3). One Trends insight per section, aggregation = 75th percentile of `activeDwellMs`, broken down by `section` — that single tile is the dwell-budget dashboard. Without it the budgets are prose.
findings.source: PostHog — Trends aggregations

findings.claim: The funnel's default 14-day conversion window will silently inflate TTFA; the KPI doc needs two funnels with explicit windows, not one.
findings.detail: PostHog funnels apply a conversion window with a 14-day default. A person who creates an agent, leaves, and returns six days later to run a first test converts inside that window and contributes ~6 days to the average conversion time. PostHog offers three step orders: Sequential ("Step B must happen after Step A, but any number of events can happen between A and B"), Strict order ("without any events in between"), and Any order.
findings.soWhat: Build two named funnels, never one: **TTFA (same sitting)** with a 1-hour window — this is the number against the 3-min median / 10-min ceiling target — and **Activation (eventual)** with a 7-day window, which is what feeds Weekly Proven Agents. Report them side by side; the gap between them is the size of the "came back later" population, which is itself a finding about whether the builder is a one-sitting task.
findings.source: PostHog — Funnels; PostHog — User paths

findings.claim: Strict-order funnels are unusable while autocapture is on — use Sequential, and say so in the spec so nobody "tightens" it later.
findings.detail: Strict order requires that Step B happen "directly after Step A without any events in between." ng-console's `posthog-client.ts` initialises with `autocapture: true`, which emits an `$autocapture` event on essentially every click in the builder. A strict-order TTFA funnel would therefore report near-zero conversion. Separately, PostHog warns that dynamic names "end up with thousands of unique event definitions" — autocapture's element-derived definitions are the same category of noise, and autocapture structurally cannot see the events this funnel needs (a Configure-sheet save, a successful test call, a duration).
findings.soWhat: Pin `Sequential` in the spec for all four builder funnels and add a one-line comment explaining why. Keep autocapture on for exploratory work but mark every KPI event `Verified` in Data Management so the builder funnels are assembled from verified custom events only; consider `autocapture: { dom_event_allowlist: ['click'] }`-style narrowing if definition sprawl becomes a problem.
findings.source: PostHog — Funnels; PostHog — Product analytics best practices; ng-console posthog-client.ts

findings.claim: Funnel breakdowns default to an attribution mode that will mislabel the A1 preset-vs-manual comparison unless you pick "Specific step".
findings.detail: PostHog funnel breakdowns offer four attribution types: First touchpoint (initial property value across all funnel events), Last touchpoint (final value seen), All steps (user may appear multiple times), and Specific step (value from one designated step). Only one cohort can be used at a time for a funnel breakdown.
findings.soWhat: A1 asks whether preset users reach first answer faster than manual users. `modelConfigMode` can legitimately change mid-funnel (someone picks a preset, then opens manual config). Under Last touchpoint those people land in the manual bucket and the preset arm looks artificially clean. Set attribution to **Specific step = the model-selection step** and write that into the spec next to the insight definition, because it is not the default and is invisible once the insight is saved.
findings.source: PostHog — Funnels

findings.claim: `@posthog/next` (beta) solves App Router pageviews, flag flicker and ad-blocker loss in one install — a materially better starting point than the instrumentation-client.ts pattern in the main Next.js doc.
findings.detail: `npm install --save @posthog/next` gives a `postHogMiddleware({ proxy: true })` that "routes PostHog API calls through your domain at `/ingest`, which helps avoid ad blockers", plus `<PostHogProvider clientOptions={{ api_host: '/ingest' }} bootstrapFlags>` wrapping `<PostHogPageView captureRouteTemplate />` in `app/layout.tsx`. `bootstrapFlags` "evaluates flags server-side" and "enables automatic browser exception capture by default"; `captureRouteTemplate` "adds normalized route templates to pageview events". Server components use `createPostHog({ getDistinctId })` then `await getPostHog()`. The older `posthog-js` path uses `instrumentation-client.ts` with `posthog.init(..., { defaults: '2026-05-30' })` and no provider at all.
findings.soWhat: studio_x_2 is the Next.js App Router app and has zero PostHog wiring today. Start it on `@posthog/next`: `captureRouteTemplate` gives the normalized `routePattern` the existing 2.1.0 schema already expects; `bootstrapFlags` removes the 100–500 ms flag flicker that would otherwise contaminate every A-row experiment's first paint; the `/ingest` proxy prevents ad-blocker loss skewing TTFA downward (blocked users never emit a start event, so only the fast survivors are measured). Flag it as beta in the spec and pin the version.
findings.source: PostHog — @posthog/next beta integration

findings.claim: ng-console today captures no pageviews at all: `capture_pageview: false` with no manual replacement — and PostHog has a documented single-value fix.
findings.detail: `ng-console/src/lib/observability/posthog-client.ts` initialises with `capture_pageview: false`, `capture_pageleave` left at its default `true`, `autocapture: true`, `disable_session_recording: true`. The config reference lists `capture_pageview` as accepting `true | false | 'history_change'`, where `'history_change'` "captures path changes via browser history API for single-page apps". It also documents `defaults` as a date string enabling "new default behaviors introduced on that date", with options through `'2026-08-30'`.
findings.soWhat: Two one-line changes with real measurement consequence: set `capture_pageview: 'history_change'` (or keep the existing `page_viewed` custom event and delete the ambiguity by documenting which one is canonical), and pin `defaults` to an explicit date so a posthog-js upgrade cannot silently change ingestion behaviour mid-baseline. The KPI doc's W0 wave demands "two weeks of untouched baseline" — an unpinned `defaults` is exactly the thing that ruins a baseline.
findings.source: PostHog — JavaScript SDK configuration; ng-console posthog-client.ts

findings.claim: Client-computed durations have four specific traps, and PostHog's docs name two of them — the current localStorage helpers in studio_x_2 hit three.
findings.detail: studio_x_2's `markBuildStart`/`timeToLiveMs` persist `Date.now()` in localStorage and subtract on completion. Traps: (1) `Date.now()` is wall-clock and jumps on NTP correction or manual clock change — `performance.now()` is monotonic but resets per document so it cannot span a reload; the correct split is `performance.now()` deltas for within-page active time, persisted `Date.now()` stamps for across-page spans, never mixed. (2) Background tabs throttle `setInterval`/rAF to ≥1 s or freeze them, so active-dwell must be accumulated from `visibilitychange` + `Date.now()` deltas, never from a tick counter. (3) localStorage is per-browser — a user who starts on a laptop and tests on a phone gets no duration, while PostHog's person-level funnel still converts them. (4) PostHog warns that "person properties are set in ingestion order... not by event timestamps", so a late-arriving event can overwrite a duration written to a person property.
findings.soWhat: Write a single `useDurationClock(key)` hook in the shared kit that emits three numbers on every completion event — `wallMs` (persisted Date.now delta), `activeMs` (visibility-aware accumulation), and `resumedCount` (how many separate sittings) — and never write a duration to a person property with `$set`; use `$set_once` for first-time milestones only (`first_agent_created_at`, `first_test_succeeded_at`). `resumedCount > 0` is the signal that distinguishes "our builder is slow" from "this person had a meeting", which is exactly the `TTFA_active` distinction §2.1 asks for.
findings.source: PostHog — Person properties (ingestion order, 512KB limit); studio_x_2 lib/analytics.ts

findings.claim: The blanket "session replay is disabled" policy is stricter than PostHog's actual privacy model requires, and it is costing the design team the exact evidence §2.3 says it lacks.
findings.detail: PostHog masks all inputs by default — "as any input element is highly likely to contain sensitive text such as email or password, we mask these by default." Text is *not* masked by default, but `maskTextSelector: '*'` masks all text (inputs excluded, already masked). `ph-no-capture` replaces an element with a blank block and also suppresses autocapture on it; `ph-no-mask` opts a subtree back in. `maskCapturedNetworkRequestFn` redacts request names and query params in the browser before transmission. Recording can be narrowed by `disable_session_recording: true` at init plus programmatic `posthog.startSessionRecording()` / `stopSessionRecording()`, sampling, minimum duration, linked feature flag, and URL/event triggers.
findings.soWhat: Propose a scoped exception to `docs/observability/privacy.md` rather than accepting the blanket ban: recording off at init, started only inside the builder route, `maskTextSelector: '*'` plus `maskAllInputs: true` (so prompt text, greeting text and credentials are never in the pixels), `ph-no-capture` on every credential field and the Configure sheets, an event trigger on `agent_builder_section_viewed`, and a sample rate. That turns §2.3's "we cannot watch a struggling user" into "we watch the 20 sessions that blew the voice-picker budget" — which is what the owner actually needs to act on a dwell number.
findings.source: PostHog — Session replay privacy; PostHog — Limit session recordings tutorial

findings.claim: Replay-to-funnel wiring is a two-click path that needs no extra instrumentation — but only if replay is on.
findings.detail: On any funnel insight, clicking the persons number beside "completed step" or "dropped off" opens the list of those users with their sessions attached. Inside a replay, the "Only show matching events" toggle filters the session's event stream down to the funnel's events. Correlation-analysis rows carry the same conversion/drop-off person lists with linked replays. Any of these lists can be saved as a cohort.
findings.soWhat: The design review ritual writes itself: open the TTFA funnel → click the drop-off count at the Test step → watch five replays with "Only show matching events" on → save that list as a cohort named for the tracker row. Put that four-step recipe in the spec as the standing procedure for closing a Design Tracker row, so "did it work?" has a defined evidence path and not just a number.
findings.source: PostHog — Explore insights with session recordings tutorial

findings.claim: Funnel correlation analysis will name the drop-off cause automatically, but needs volume — and it is the cheapest way to test the A8 preflight hypothesis before building preflight.
findings.detail: Correlation analysis sits inside any funnel insight behind a "Load results" / "Select properties" button and surfaces both event correlations (users who did X during the funnel) and property correlations (device type, etc.) as multipliers — "1.3x more likely", "8.0x more likely to convert". Accuracy "depends heavily on sample size; small user counts produce unreliable results". Trivial signals can be removed permanently via "Exclude event from project".
findings.soWhat: A8 assumes first-publish failures are credential/number-binding/quota problems. Rather than asserting that, run correlation analysis on the Activation funnel at the publish step the moment W0 has data — it will rank the actual anti-correlated events. If `credential_sheet_opened` does not show up, A8's preflight checks are aimed at the wrong failures and the row should be re-derived from the `errorStage` distribution, exactly as the ledger's fallback says.
findings.source: PostHog — Correlation analysis

findings.claim: PostHog's sample-size formula makes the TCR guardrail roughly three times more expensive to power than the speed metric it guards — so guardrails must be declared "monitored, not powered".
findings.detail: PostHog publishes N = (16 × variance) / d² per variant, where 16 encodes "80% statistical power at 95% confidence", d is the absolute effect, and variance is p(1−p) for funnel metrics, 2 × baseline for counts, and 0.25 × baseline² for sum/average metrics. Default MDE is 30% relative, "a reasonable starting point". Working the KPI doc's own numbers: A2 (test-attempt rate 40% → 52%) needs ~267/variant; A1 (TTFA mean 480 s → 435 s) needs ~455/variant; A4 (backup attach 15% → 35%) needs ~51/variant; but detecting a TCR fall from 95% to 92% needs ~844/variant. Experiment metrics support Winsorization (clamping at configurable percentiles, with an option to ignore zero values) and a conversion window, beyond which metric events are excluded.
findings.soWhat: Write the N for each A-row into the assumptions ledger next to its predicted effect, and state explicitly that TCR is a **monitored** guardrail with a stopping rule ("halt if TCR point estimate drops below 92% at any read"), not a powered one — otherwise every experiment waits on the guardrail and nothing ships. Turn Winsorization on for TTFA (a single 4-hour session otherwise moves the mean); note that the 0.25 × baseline² variance proxy assumes a coefficient of variation of 0.5, which is optimistic for a long-tailed duration like TTFA, so treat the A1 figure as a floor.
findings.source: PostHog — Running time and sample size; PostHog — Experiment metrics

findings.claim: Dynamic behavioural cohorts cannot target feature flags — so "activated" must be a person property if it is ever to gate a rollout.
findings.detail: PostHog: "You cannot use dynamic cohorts that include behavioral or lifecycle criteria as a feature flag target." Only person-property-only dynamic cohorts work directly; otherwise you need a static cohort copy or the "Criteria · One-time snapshot" option. Dynamic cohorts recalculate "once every 24 hours". Behavioural filters available include completed-event-N-times-in-period, completed a sequence, did-not-complete, and lifecycle filters (first time, regularly, stopped, started again).
findings.soWhat: Define activation twice on purpose: as a **dynamic cohort** (`agent_test_session_succeeded` ≥ 1 AND `agent_publish` succeeded ≥ 1, last 30 days) for analysis, and as a **person property** `activationState: 'none' | 'tested' | 'deployed' | 'proven'` written with `$set` at each milestone, for flag targeting and for the A-row rollouts. The 24-hour recalculation also means a cohort-based dashboard read is up to a day stale — do not use cohorts for the daily design-agent report; use the person property.
findings.source: PostHog — Cohorts

findings.claim: AR7 needs retention's "first ever occurrence" mode, and retention's one-cohort-per-user rule quietly changes what AR7 means.
findings.detail: Retention insights take a start event (cohortizing) and a return event, which may differ. Three modes: "First time" (first occurrence of the start event falls in the cohort period), "First ever occurrence" (the very first instance across all time), and "Recurring" (any occurrence). Intervals are hourly/daily/weekly/monthly; the mean row can be weighted or simple; "users cannot appear in multiple cohorts simultaneously"; retention "only shows whether users returned, not frequency — use Stickiness for engagement depth".
findings.soWhat: AR7 as written ("share of first agents still holding real conversations a week later") is per-agent, but PostHog retention cohortizes persons. Either aggregate retention by the `agent` entity via a group type, or restate AR7 as a person-level metric and add a separate SQL insight for the per-agent version. Use start event = first `agent_publish` succeeded in **First ever occurrence** mode, return event = production session, weekly interval — and pair it with a Stickiness insight, because "answered one call in week 1" and "answered 400" are the same cell in a retention table.
findings.source: PostHog — Retention

findings.claim: PostHog Schema Management plus the PostHog CLI is literally the repo-committed, CI-validated event spec the owner asked for — it already exists as a product feature.
findings.detail: Data Management > Events lets you create event definitions **before** any event is captured (names immutable after creation; description, owner, tags). Data Management > Property Groups defines reusable typed property collections — String, Number, Boolean, Object, each property with name, type, required flag and description — attachable to multiple events. The CLI: `npm install -g @posthog/cli`, `posthog-cli login`, `posthog-cli exp schema pull` (generates typed definitions, writes a schema hash into `posthog.json`, only updates when the schema changed) and `posthog-cli exp schema status`. Generated languages: TypeScript, Go, Python. Both `posthog.json` and `posthog-typed.<ext>` "must be committed to version control". The typed client validates properties against the schema at the type level; `captureRaw()` bypasses it. Events can be marked Verified or Hidden.
findings.soWhat: This is the deliverable shape. Commit `docs/observability/tracking-plan.md` as the human spec (one row per event: name, trigger, owner, KPI it serves, flag key, schema version, properties with type/required/PII verdict) plus machine-checked `posthog.json` + `posthog-typed.ts`. Add `posthog-cli exp schema status` to CI so a drift between the PostHog project and the repo fails the build — that is the validation step the owner wants, and it replaces hand-maintaining the camelCase Set in `sanitize.ts`. Mark every KPI event Verified so nobody builds the TTFA funnel on an autocapture lookalike.
findings.source: PostHog — Schema management

findings.claim: Super properties and `before_send` are the two SDK hooks that make the existing 2.1.0 base-property contract enforceable instead of merely conventional.
findings.detail: `posthog.register({ key: value })` attaches a property to every subsequent event; `register_once()` "ensures that if a property is already set, it is not set again"; `unregister(key)` removes it. `before_send` is documented as "a function that allows you to amend or reject events before they are sent", and `property_denylist` as "a list of properties that should never be sent with capture calls". `posthog.capture(name, props, { transport: 'sendBeacon', send_instantly: true })` handles page-unload cases, though transport "does not skip PostHog's event queue".
findings.soWhat: Move `schemaVersion`, `release`, `environment`, `eventSource`, `productArea`, `isInternalUser` and `isFirstAgent` from per-call props into `register()` at init/identify time — that removes the single biggest source of missing-dimension data quality bugs (the §6.4 "events missing isFirstAgent" tile exists precisely because this is passed by hand today). Then move the `sanitizePostHogProperties` allowlist into `before_send` so it is enforced at the SDK edge and cannot be bypassed by a direct `posthog.capture` — the current sdk-import-guard test proves intent, `before_send` proves behaviour. Use `sendBeacon` for the section-exit dwell event, which fires on unload.
findings.source: PostHog — JavaScript SDK features; PostHog — JS config reference

findings.claim: Adding `project` as a second group type is cheap technically but changes the billing basis for the whole project.
findings.detail: PostHog allows "up to 5 group types" per project with unlimited groups inside each. `posthog.group('company', 'id', { ...props })` in the web SDK "associates all subsequent events in the session with the group"; at least one group property is required for a group to appear in the People and groups tab. Funnels and trends can aggregate by group type instead of user ("Aggregating by"). Limitations: one group per type per event, and group types "aren't supported for lifecycle insights or user paths". Billing: "Once you subscribe to group analytics, billing applies to all identified events in your project, not just events with group properties attached."
findings.soWhat: ng-console already sends `cid` as a group. Adding `project` (and possibly `agent`) as group types would let the Activation funnel aggregate by account rather than person — which is the right unit for a B2B console where two engineers share one agent. But flag the billing clause to the owner before enabling it, and note that group aggregation kills user-paths analysis, so keep at least one person-aggregated copy of the TTFA funnel. Also note groups only attach to events sent *after* `group()` is called — call it in the same tick as `identify()`, before any builder event fires, or the first event of every session lands ungrouped.
findings.source: PostHog — Group analytics

findings.claim: PostHog Error Tracking and LLM Analytics both exist today and both map onto surfaces this console already has — error tracking overlaps Sentry, LLM analytics does not overlap anything.
findings.detail: Error tracking "captures exceptions from across your stack and turns them into issues you can prioritize, assign, and resolve", with "the affected user's session replay, events, and properties attached", source-map/symbol-set upload, and automatic grouping. In Next.js it is wired via `posthog.captureException(error, additionalProperties)` in error boundaries plus an `onRequestError` hook in `instrumentation.ts` that reads distinct_id from the PostHog cookie; `capture_exceptions` in the JS config "falls back to remote configuration when undefined", and `@posthog/next`'s `bootstrapFlags` "enables automatic browser exception capture by default". LLM analytics defines four manual-capture events: `$ai_generation` (required `$ai_trace_id`, `$ai_model`, `$ai_provider`, `$ai_input_tokens`, `$ai_output_tokens`; optional `$ai_latency`, `$ai_time_to_first_token`, `$ai_is_error`, `$ai_stream`), `$ai_trace`, `$ai_span` (required `$ai_trace_id`; optional `$ai_span_id`, `$ai_span_name`, `$ai_latency`, `$ai_is_error`) and `$ai_embedding` — all sendable from any SDK's `capture()`, so no supported-provider list is required.
findings.soWhat: Do not rip out Sentry — but note that PostHog error tracking is the only way to get an exception sitting on the same timeline as the funnel drop-off and the replay. Recommend it as a W2 decision, not W0. The bigger unclaimed win is LLM analytics: the test-call turn payload already parsed in `src/lib/latency-metrics.ts` (`e2eLatencyMs`, `asr_ttlw`, `llm_ttft`, `tts_ttfb`, `transport`) maps cleanly onto one `$ai_trace` per test call plus one `$ai_span` per component with `$ai_latency` and `$ai_time_to_first_token`. That buys the trace UI for free, keeps raw ms out of the product-event stream (satisfying the privacy rule that product events carry only buckets), and gives §4's "our own measured p50/p95" a home that is not a spreadsheet.
findings.source: PostHog — Error tracking; PostHog — LLM analytics manual capture

findings.claim: `$feature_flag_called` is the exposure event and is free — but for experiment funnel metrics PostHog makes exposure the first step automatically, which changes how the A-row funnels must be written.
findings.detail: PostHog: feature flags "are charged based on requests made to our /flags endpoint... They are not billed based on `$feature_flag_called` events, which are optional events sent for metrics tracking." Properties are `$feature_flag` and `$feature_flag_response` (false = no condition matched; None/empty = flag disabled, failed to load, or not locally evaluatable; otherwise the variant key). For experiment funnel metrics, "the exposure event automatically serves as the first step; you specify only subsequent events." Flag evaluation latency is "typically 100–500 ms", mitigated by bootstrapping or hiding the element until flags load.
findings.soWhat: When an A-row funnel is used as an experiment metric, drop `agent_create` from the step list — exposure is already step 1, and including it double-counts and shrinks the denominator. Bootstrap flags server-side (`bootstrapFlags` in `@posthog/next`) so the builder never renders the control variant for 300 ms before swapping: in a product whose whole metric is time-to-first-answer, a 300 ms flicker is both a UX defect and a measurement artefact. Keep the flag key identical to the assumption id (`builder-a1-model-preset`) as the KPI doc already specifies, so `$feature_flag` breaks the funnel down by ledger row with no extra property.
findings.source: PostHog — Feature flags common questions; PostHog — Experiment metrics

findings.claim: Dashboard tile-level date ranges silently override dashboard filters — which will break the "two weeks of untouched baseline" read if the baseline tiles carry pinned dates.
findings.detail: Dashboard property filters apply to all insights "unless individual tiles override them", combining with AND except where a tile contradicts the dashboard on the same property, in which case the tile wins. For dates: "if a tile has its own `date_from` or `date_to` configured, its entire date range is used and the dashboard override is ignored." Dashboards support templates saved at team or organization scope, and public link sharing / embedding.
findings.soWhat: Build the Builder Activation dashboard with **no** tile-level date ranges so the dashboard date picker actually controls it — otherwise the W0 baseline tile and the W1 post-change tile will show different windows and the comparison is invalid without anyone noticing. Save it as an org-scope dashboard template so the same nine tiles (§6.4) can be cloned per environment. A public share link is also the cheapest way to put the funnel in front of the owner without provisioning PostHog seats.
findings.source: PostHog — Dashboards

findings.claim: The PostHog MCP server lets the existing daily design agent create annotations, flags and insights from Claude Code — which closes the loop between a shipped design change and the metric read.
findings.detail: Install with `npx @posthog/wizard mcp add`; auth "automatically routes you to the correct data region (US or EU)". Exposed capabilities include running HogQL queries, executing governed metrics from the semantic layer, shipping feature flags from prompts, managing experiments, retrieving top errors with stack traces, and CDP destinations. The annotations doc separately confirms agents can "create annotations to mark deployments, releases, or incidents" and list/retrieve/update/delete them, naming Claude Code explicitly; annotations are date-anchored notes that appear across Trends and dashboards, scoped to one chart or all charts.
findings.soWhat: Wire this into the daily-design-agent contract already in the repo: every time a Design Tracker row deploys behind a flag, the agent writes a PostHog annotation carrying the assumption id and the ClickUp task id. Two weeks later the same agent runs the HogQL read and posts the verdict. That makes §5's kill rule automatic rather than aspirational, and it means the annotation, the flag key and the ledger line are all the same string.
findings.source: PostHog — Model Context Protocol; PostHog — Annotations

findings.claim: PostHog's funnel time-to-convert view exposes median and mean only — never p75 or p90 — so the KPI doc's §6.4 line "TTFA | Funnel, time-to-convert | median + p75 + p90" cannot be built.
findings.detail: PostHog issue #24208 (opened 6 Aug 2024, still open) is a customer request for richer conversion-time statistics and states the current state plainly: PostHog "currently displays median and mean statistics for funnel conversion times", with a distribution histogram between steps. The funnels doc itself describes the view only as showing "steps with the highest friction" and names no statistic. So the funnel gives you a median TTFA cross-check for free — which closes the first pass's open question in the affirmative — but p75 and p90, which every dwell budget and both clock targets are written in, are simply not available from that view.
findings.soWhat: Rewrite §6.4: the TTFA/TTFD funnel rows claim median only. Every p75/p90 in §2.1, §2.2 and §2.3 must come from a numeric duration property on the completion event, read through a Trends percentile aggregation or a SQL insight. The funnel median becomes the independent cross-check on the client-computed value, not the source of truth.
findings.source: PostHog/posthog issue #24208 + PostHog funnels doc

findings.claim: PostHog Schema Management is compile-time only; PostHog has no ingestion-side schema enforcement today, and its own enforcement plugin was archived on 26 July 2024 with the note that a native replacement is still being built.
findings.detail: The schema-management doc sells only client-side guarantees — "Type safety: Properties are validated against your schema", IDE autocomplete, a generated posthog-typed.<ext> client, and `captureRaw()` "when you need to bypass type checking". It documents exactly two commands, `posthog-cli exp schema pull` and `posthog-cli exp schema status`, warns that "Schema management is currently an experimental feature. The exp prefix will be removed once the feature is stable", and documents no CI workflow. Independently, PostHog/posthog-schema-enforcer-plugin — which did reject non-conforming events at ingestion — was archived 2024-07-26: "This plugin has been deprecated. We are currently working on a native solution." The data-management doc confirms the live behaviour: malformed events are not rejected, "we do our best to still ingest the event and we log an ingestion warning", and the "verified" flag on an event definition is documentation, not a gate.
findings.soWhat: Closes gap 2 decisively. The event spec must say: the only real gate is CI. Add a job that runs `posthog-cli exp schema pull` and fails the build on a diff, plus `exp schema status`, and commit posthog.json and posthog-typed.ts. Ban `captureRaw()` in lint. And because the `exp` prefix means the command surface can change, pin the CLI version in CI.
findings.source: PostHog schema management, data management, and the archived schema-enforcer-plugin

findings.claim: The exact session-replay trigger config is now pinned, and it supports a surgical exception: record only the builder route, only when a test session starts, at a sample rate — no blanket replay needed.
findings.detail: Keys and semantics: `sample_rate` is a float 0–1 applied per trigger group AFTER conditions match; `minimum_duration_milliseconds` is enforced against actual buffered recording data in strict mode (the default once `defaults >= '2025-11-30'`) versus total session age in legacy mode; `linked_flag` records only sessions where a flag is on; `url_triggers` are regular expressions auto-anchored with ^ and $; `event_triggers` match on event NAME only — "properties not filtered"; `trigger_match_type` is "ANY" or "ALL" within a group, and "Groups themselves are always combined with ANY". Masking defaults: `maskAllInputs: true` and password inputs masked, but "General text is not masked by default" — so `maskTextSelector` plus `.ph-no-capture` on credential rows is mandatory for this console, and `.ph-no-mask` overrides masking where you want the text back.
findings.soWhat: Closes gap 3 and gives the privacy exception a concrete shape to put to the owner: `url_triggers` on the /agents/*/edit path, `event_triggers: ['agent_test_session_started']`, `sample_rate: 0.2`, `minimum_duration_milliseconds: 5000`, `maskAllInputs: true` plus `maskTextSelector: '[data-ph-mask]'` on every credential and API-key field. Because event_triggers ignore properties, the trigger event must be its own name — you cannot trigger on operation_started{operation:'agent_test'}.
findings.source: PostHog — How to control which sessions you record; Session replay privacy

findings.claim: The group-analytics add-on costs $0.000071/event and bills every identified event in the project — a higher unit price than the $0.00005 base analytics rate, so turning it on roughly 2.4x the identified-event bill.
findings.detail: PostHog's add-ons pricing lists group analytics from $0.000071/event, and the group-analytics doc states the billing basis: "Once you subscribe to group analytics, billing applies to all identified events in your project, not just events with group properties attached", and billing starts when you enable it on the billing page, not when you deploy code. Base product-analytics tiers for comparison: first 1M free, then $0.0000500 (1–2M), $0.0000343 (2–15M), $0.0000295 (15–50M), $0.0000218 (50–100M), $0.0000150 (100–250M), $0.0000090 (250M+).
findings.soWhat: Closes gap 4's real cost exposure. Price it before proposing: at 1M billable identified events/month the add-on is ~$71/month on top of ~$50 of base events, and it scales with total identified volume, not with agent count. Propose it as a Wave-3 decision tied to AR7, not a Wave-0 default — and keep `cid` as an event property for the launch dashboard.
findings.source: PostHog add-ons pricing + group analytics doc + product analytics pricing

findings.claim: An agent CAN be a PostHog group type (max 5 per project, unlimited instances) and retention DOES support group aggregation — but the retention doc says outright "This requires group analytics", so agent-level AR7 is a billing decision, not a modelling one.
findings.detail: Group analytics docs: "Maximum of 5 group types per project", "You can have unlimited individual groups within each type", and examples include non-company shapes (channel, project, segment_group) — nothing forces an organization shape. "Group types aren't supported for lifecycle insights or user paths"; funnels, trends, retention and stickiness do support them. Retention's own page: "Analyze retention for groups of users, such as all users in the same organization, company, or account… This requires group analytics." Retention settings include first-time / first-ever-occurrence / recurring, and hour/day/week/month granularity. A group is only visible in the UI once it has at least one group property.
findings.soWhat: Closes gap 6, which the KPI doc lists as open decision §8. Answer: AR7 can be agent-level, at the add-on's price. Design the events so the switch is cheap later — send `posthog.group('agent', agentId, {...})` behind one env-gated helper, and keep `agentId` as an event property regardless so the person-level version works on day one. Budget the second group type ('project') against the 5-type cap now.
findings.source: PostHog group analytics + retention docs

findings.claim: @posthog/next is explicitly pre-release with an API-stability warning, and the route property it captures is `$route` — not the repo's `routePattern`, so schema 2.1.0 needs an explicit mapping.
findings.detail: The doc states: "@posthog/next is currently in pre-release. The API may change before the stable release." Recent changelog churn confirms it — getPostHog and getServerSidePostHog were replaced by a createPostHog() factory. Exports: PostHogProvider (a React Server Component), PostHogPageView, usePostHog, useFeatureFlag, PostHogFeature, createPostHog, postHogMiddleware, onRequestError. Pageview properties are `$current_url`, `$pathname`, and `$route` "when captureRouteTemplate enabled; normalized route template like /posts/[id]". `postHogMiddleware({ proxy: true })` routes ingestion through `/ingest` — the same path ng-console's own reverse-proxy research already chose. bootstrapFlags "opts the route into dynamic rendering (incompatible with static generation / ISR)".
findings.soWhat: Closes gap 5. Two concrete spec lines: (1) map `$route` → `routePattern` in a `before_send` hook, or change schema 2.1.0 to adopt `$route` and retire routePattern — do not let both exist; (2) note that ng-console reads VITE_POSTHOG_KEY while the Next.js builder needs NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_* — §8.4's "VITE_POSTHOG_KEY must be set" is wrong for the builder. Pin an exact @posthog/next version and treat minor bumps as breaking.
findings.source: PostHog — Next.js: @posthog/next

findings.claim: posthog-js behaviour is now gated on a dated `defaults` string, and which date you pin silently changes pageview capture, replay duration semantics, rageclick filtering and internal-user detection.
findings.detail: From posthog-js source (packages/browser/src/posthog-core.ts): `defaults` accepts 'unset' or a date, and the gates are exact — >= '2025-05-24' sets `capture_pageview: 'history_change'`; >= '2025-11-30' sets `session_recording.strictMinimumDuration = true` and rageclick `content_ignorelist`; >= '2026-01-30' sets `external_scripts_inject_target: 'head'` AND `internal_or_test_user_hostname: /^(localhost|127\.0\.0\.1)$/`; >= '2026-05-30' adds `persistence_save_debounce_ms: 250`, `split_storage: true`, `detect_google_search_app: true`, canvasCapture at resolutionScale 0.6; >= '2026-06-25' adds `streamNetworkBody` and `disable_capture_url_hashes`; >= '2026-08-29' `cookieWinsOnConflict`; >= '2026-08-30' `captureJsonLd`. Separately, the project-level "Filter out internal and test users" is a list of property filters applied across product analytics, web analytics, revenue analytics, session replay and CDP destinations, with a project setting that decides whether it is on for all NEW insights.
findings.soWhat: The event spec must pin one `defaults` date verbatim and record why, because an unpinned bump changes what a baseline means mid-read. And §6.4's rule "do not globally exclude internal traffic — keep it visible as its own series" requires actively turning OFF "enable this filter on all new insights" — the default is not neutral, and once you pin >= 2026-01-30 localhost traffic is auto-flagged as internal.
findings.source: posthog-js source, packages/browser/src/posthog-core.ts (getSessionRecordingDefaults / defaultsThatVaryByConfig) + PostHog internal-user filter docs

findings.claim: `capture_pageleave` defaults to `'if_capture_pageview'`, so ng-console's `capture_pageview: false` has also silently disabled $pageleave — there is no server-side time-on-page anywhere in the product today.
findings.detail: posthog-js defaultConfig sets `capture_pageleave: 'if_capture_pageview'` with the comment "We'll only capture pageleave events if capture_pageview is also true". ng-console's init sets `capture_pageview: false` with no manual replacement (per the existing reverse-proxy research doc's own snippet), which means both halves of the dwell pair are missing. PostHog's cost doc lists exactly this pattern as a cost-cutting move — disable both, then capture manually — so the fix is to capture pageview manually AND set capture_pageleave explicitly rather than relying on the pair.
findings.soWhat: Adds a second line to the first pass's pageview fix: setting capture_pageview alone does not restore pageleave. For the builder this matters less (one route), which is itself the point — section dwell can never come from pageview/pageleave and must be an explicit active-dwell property on each completion event.
findings.source: posthog-js defaultConfig + PostHog cutting-costs doc

findings.claim: A PostHog session ends after 30 minutes idle or 24 hours total — so the KPI doc's TTFD p75 target of 45 minutes routinely crosses a session boundary, putting it in direct tension with the same-document "same-session conversion ≥ 45%" target.
findings.detail: PostHog defines a new session on "no activity for 30 minutes" or at "the maximum session duration of 24 hours"; activity includes autocapture and replay mouse movement; `session_idle_timeout_seconds` is configurable. `$session_id` is stable across tabs and windows of the same browser but not across browsers. Session properties available: $session_id, $start_timestamp, $end_timestamp, $session_duration, $entry_pathname, $exit_current_url, $is_bounce. TTFA's 10-minute ceiling sits inside one session; TTFD's 20-min median is inside; its 45-min p75 is not.
findings.soWhat: Either define "same-session" as your own idea of a session (a person-level 'same calendar day' or 'same builder visit' property you stamp) or raise session_idle_timeout_seconds for the project — and say which in §2.2. Also: never scope a TTFA/TTFD funnel by $session_id; scope it by person plus an explicit conversion window.
findings.source: PostHog — Sessions doc

findings.claim: PostHog rewrites event timestamps to correct client clock skew using `timestamp = now + timestamp - sent_at` — so a server-derived funnel duration and a client-computed ms property will legitimately disagree, and the spec must name one as canonical.
findings.detail: The timestamp doc gives the priority order: with `timestamp` and `sent_at`, PostHog applies skew correction `timestamp = now + timestamp - sent_at`; with `timestamp` only, it is used as-is; `$ignore_sent_at` disables correction for historical imports; `offset` (ms) is subtracted from server capture time; otherwise server `now`. Events more than 23 hours in the future trigger a warning and fall back to server time. Related hard limits: events over 1MB are discarded ("Discarded event exceeding 1MB limit"), distinct IDs are truncated to 200 characters, and replay events dated 7+ days ahead are dropped.
findings.soWhat: A genuine qualification of the first pass's duration traps: the funnel-derived TTFA is skew-corrected and the client-computed ttfaMs is not. Spec line: ttfaMs (client, uncorrected, monotonic-clock-based) is the reported number; the funnel median is the sanity check; a gap of more than ~10% between them is a data-quality alarm, not a metric change. Use performance.now() deltas rather than Date.now() deltas so a mid-task system clock change cannot produce a negative duration.
findings.source: PostHog — Timestamps and ingestion warnings docs

findings.claim: studio_x_2's existing duration helpers destroy their own measurement: `timeToLiveMs()` reads-and-clears the localStorage stamp in one call, and `markSignup()` writes once forever — plus `time_to_live_ms` is an event name, not a metric, and the repo carries two units for one clock.
findings.detail: In /Users/shaktisoni/Documents/Agora Design & FE/ai-studio-console-redesign/studio_x_2/lib/analytics.ts: `timeToLiveMs()` calls `localStorage.removeItem(BUILD_START_KEY)` before returning the value, so a failed dispatch, a thrown capture, or a React StrictMode double-invoke in dev yields undefined on the second read and the measurement is gone with no retry. `markSignup()` only writes "if (!localStorage.getItem(SIGNUP_KEY))", so a returning user's second, third and fourth agents all measure from the original signup — an unbounded value that will dominate any p75. Taxonomy: `time_to_live_ms: { ms: number }` is a measurement used as an event name, against the file's own stated rule "object_verb_past_tense"; and `agent_test_ended` carries `duration_sec` while ng-console operations carry `durationMs`.
findings.soWhat: Three concrete spec edits before any of this is wired to PostHog: (1) read the stamp, capture, and only clear on the capture callback; (2) scope the signup/build stamps per agent id and per attempt, not per browser; (3) delete `time_to_live_ms` as an event — put `ms` on `deployment_went_live` as `durationMs` and standardise on milliseconds everywhere, so one Trends percentile query serves both apps.
findings.source: Repo: studio_x_2/lib/analytics.ts (lines ~283–320)

findings.claim: Trends offers percentiles in two distinct places — property-value aggregation AND "count per user" — and the percentile set is exactly 75th, 90th, 95th and 99th.
findings.detail: The Trends aggregations doc lists property-value aggregations (average, sum, minimum, maximum, median, and 75th/90th/95th/99th percentile) and separately a "Count per user" aggregation offering average, minimum, maximum, median or 75th/90th/95th/99th percentile per individual user. It also lists "Unique sessions" and "Unique groups". There is no p50-by-another-name problem: median and 75th are both first-class.
findings.soWhat: The struggle index in §6.4 (doc links + failed saves + sheet re-entries + config churn) does not need a computed property at all — "count per user, 75th percentile" over each contributing event, broken down by `section`, gives a p75 struggle count directly. Reserve the numeric-duration-property mechanism for the dwell clocks, where it is unavoidable.
findings.source: PostHog — Trends aggregations

findings.claim: HogQL does support quantile() — contradicting PostHog's own ClickHouse-functions page, which omits it — so a SQL insight is a real independent p75 path, not a hope.
findings.detail: The supported-aggregations page lists `quantile`, `quantileIf`, `quantiles` and `quantilesIf` among the enabled aggregate functions (quantileExact is not listed), alongside count/min/max/sum/avg/stddev/variance and PostgreSQL-style array_agg/json_agg/string_agg. The /docs/sql/clickhouse-functions and /docs/sql/expressions pages list dateDiff, median, avg and uniq but no quantile at all — the two pages disagree, and the aggregations page is the specific one. `dateDiff('unit', start, end)` is confirmed for duration maths.
findings.soWhat: Write the TTFA verification insight as SQL now, in the spec, so it ships with the instrumentation: quantile(0.75)(properties.ttfaMs) filtered to first agents. It is the only read that does not depend on the Trends UI picking the right property, and it is the arbiter when the funnel median and the client ms disagree.
findings.source: PostHog — Supported aggregations (vs the ClickHouse functions page)

findings.claim: Alert capability is plan-gated in ways that change the monitoring design: free organisations get 5 alerts total, 15-minute checks need Boost, and real-time needs Scale (10) or Enterprise (20).
findings.detail: The alerts doc: "Alerts are supported on trends, funnels (steps and trends views only), and SQL (HogQL) insights" — time-to-convert and the flow/sankey view are excluded. Conditions are "has value" and "increases by / decreases by", absolute or percentage. Frequencies are hourly, daily, weekly, monthly; the 15-minute interval "requires a Boost plan or higher" and real-time checking needs "Scale or Enterprise plan". "Free tier organizations can create up to 5 alerts total. Paid plans have no limit."
findings.soWhat: Closes the alerts half of gap 4. On the free tier you get five alerts — spend them on the guardrails, not the speed metrics: publish failure rate, 24h rollback rate, TCR, data-quality (events on the wrong schemaVersion), and one TTFA-proxy alert on a SQL insight (which IS alertable, unlike the funnel time-to-convert view). Hourly is the fastest free cadence; do not write "we'll be alerted within 15 minutes" into the plan.
findings.source: PostHog — Alerts doc

findings.claim: PostHog experiments are Bayesian by default, show nothing until 50 exposures per variant, default to a 30% minimum detectable effect, and winsorize mean/funnel/ratio metrics — which will quietly clip TTFA's long tail.
findings.detail: Statistics doc: Bayesian engine by default, reporting "the probability that one variant is better than another"; significance when "chance to win is above 95% or below 5%" at the default 95% confidence (90% and 99% selectable). Sample size: "N = (16 × variance) / d²", where 16 "comes from achieving 80% statistical power at 95% confidence". MDE default is "30%, which is a reasonable starting point for most experiments". Common-questions doc: "a minimum of 50 exposures per variant before showing experiment results", and "with fewer than ~1,000 exposures, a 55/45 split on a 50/50 experiment is statistically normal". Metric types are funnel (exposure is always step one), mean, ratio and retention, with Winsorization clamping values at percentile bounds on mean, funnel and ratio metrics.
findings.soWhat: Two spec consequences. (1) If TTFA is run as an experiment mean metric, declare the winsorization bounds explicitly — otherwise the tail that the 10-minute ceiling exists to catch is clipped before the read, and a change that fixes only slow users will look like no change. (2) The A-row plan's "2 reporting weeks or the pre-declared sample" needs a floor of 50 exposures/variant just to render, and sample-ratio noise below ~1,000 exposures is expected — write both into the ledger so nobody calls a broken flag.
findings.source: PostHog — Experiment statistics, sample size, metrics, common questions

findings.claim: Dynamic cohorts recalculate only once every 24 hours and cannot be nested — so an "activated" cohort is a day-stale object, unusable for any same-day read.
findings.detail: Cohorts doc: "Dynamic cohorts are updated once every 24 hours." They cannot reference other dynamic cohorts. Behavioural or lifecycle criteria disqualify a cohort from feature-flag targeting ("You cannot use dynamic cohorts that include behavioral or lifecycle criteria as a feature flag target") and from CDP destinations, which error. Static cohorts don't change unless updated and can be created from an insight export, CSV upload of distinct IDs / person IDs / emails, manual selection, or a one-time snapshot of a dynamic cohort's criteria.
findings.soWhat: Extends the first pass's flag-targeting point with a timing one: the weekly design read cannot use a behavioural "activated" cohort for anything dated to today. Define activation as a person property set at the moment of the qualifying event (so it is instant and flag-targetable), and keep the dynamic cohort purely as a reporting convenience.
findings.source: PostHog — Cohorts doc

findings.claim: Feature flags bill per /flags request, and server-side local evaluation is charged as TEN requests each — roughly 864,000 charges a month for a single always-on server at the default 30-second polling.
findings.detail: Flag pricing tiers: first 1M requests/month free, then $0.0001 (1–2M), $0.000045 (2–10M), $0.000025 (10–50M), $0.00001 (50M+). Requests occur when SDKs initialise, users are identified, properties update, or flags are explicitly evaluated. "Each local evaluation request is equivalent to, and charged as, 10 feature flag requests", and with 30-second polling one constantly-running server is about 864,000 monthly charges. Mitigations documented: raise the polling interval (e.g. 5 minutes), or bootstrap flags once and set `advanced_disable_feature_flags`. Separately, `$feature_flag_called` events are excluded from product-analytics billing.
findings.soWhat: The A-row experiment plan gates every builder change behind a flag; budget it. On the client, bootstrap flags through @posthog/next's bootstrapFlags (which also kills flicker) rather than letting each page load hit /flags. If any Agora backend evaluates the same flags, set the polling interval to 300s in the spec — the default will burn most of the free million on one box.
findings.source: PostHog — Cutting feature flag costs; pricing principles

findings.claim: PostHog publishes an event-volume benchmark of 87 events per MAU for B2B web products with autocapture, which puts the whole console at roughly 11,500 monthly active users before it leaves the 1M-event free tier.
findings.detail: The estimating-usage-costs doc gives the formula "Events per month = MAUs × Average events per MAU" and a benchmark table: PostHog itself (B2B, web, autocapture) 87 events/MAU; a speech-to-text API company (B2B, no autocapture) 583; a B2C meditation app 118; a B2C React Native booking app 8. Free allowances renew monthly and cover 1M analytics events, 5K session recordings, 1M flag requests, 100K error-tracking exceptions, 1,500 survey responses, 100K AI-observability events, 10GB logs.
findings.soWhat: Gives the owner a cost answer without a PostHog account: at 87 events/MAU the builder plan is free until ~11.5k MAU, and the 5,000 free recordings/month is what makes the sampled, trigger-scoped replay exception cheap (20% sampling of test sessions, not blanket capture). It also reframes the group-analytics decision — the add-on, not the events, is the first real bill.
findings.source: PostHog — Estimating usage & costs; pricing page

findings.claim: PostHog Surveys can be triggered by a custom event and rendered through your own UI — which is the missing instrument for the owner's "confidence in production" question, and it is free up to 1,500 responses a month.
findings.detail: Display conditions include: linked feature flag; URL contains / exactly matches / regex; device type; CSS selector match; a wait period ("Hide surveys from users who have seen any survey in the last X days"); person and group properties with percentage rollout; and "User sends events" — "Display a survey to users who have sent a specific event during their session", configurable as "Every time the event is sent" or "Just once". Question types: freeform text, link/notification, rating emoji, rating number, single choice, multiple choice. The API presentation type lets you "implement your own survey UI and use PostHog to handle display logic, capturing results, and analytics". Surveys are on by default in the SDK (`disable_surveys: false`).
findings.soWhat: Instrument a one-question confidence rating triggered by `agent_publish` succeeded ("How confident are you putting this in front of callers?", 1–5, once per person), rendered through the API type so it uses Studio X components rather than PostHog's. That is a direct measure of the trust ladder that no funnel can produce, it costs nothing at this volume, and it can be cross-cut against TCR to test whether stated confidence predicts 24h survival.
findings.source: PostHog — Creating surveys; pricing free tier

findings.claim: Competitors publish their own onboarding clocks, and the 3-minute TTFA target is aggressive but not absurd against them: Vapi claims under 5 minutes to a phone call, Retell claims 15 minutes with a no-keys browser test first, LiveKit claims under 10 minutes but only after a CLI install.
findings.detail: Vapi's dashboard quickstart: "In under 5 minutes, you'll create a voice assistant and start talking to it over the phone" — the dashboard path needs no vendor keys (its managed services), while the SDK path pulls in OpenAI/ElevenLabs credentials. Retell's quickstart is titled "Build your first Retell AI phone agent in 15 minutes", and its web-call test "works on a draft, unpublished agent with no payment method or phone number required" — the same zero-key posture Agora treats as its differentiator, already shipped. LiveKit: "Build and deploy a simple voice assistant in less than 10 minutes", but requires the LiveKit CLI, uv or pnpm, and Python 3.10+/Node 20+ before anything speaks; its STT-LLM-TTS pipeline needs no extra vendor keys because LiveKit Inference supplies the models. ElevenLabs' agents quickstart publishes no time estimate at all.
findings.soWhat: Closes gap 7 with external anchors. Two things follow: (1) the marketing claim "fastest" has to beat a published 5-minute number, so a 3-minute median TTFA is the right target and a 10-minute ceiling is already slower than Vapi's headline — say so in §3; (2) Retell has neutralised the zero-key advantage for TESTING, so the defensible claim is zero keys through to a DEPLOYED agent, which is a TTFD story, not a TTFA one.
findings.source: Vapi, Retell, LiveKit and ElevenLabs quickstart docs

numbers.label: Funnel conversion window default
numbers.value: 14 days
numbers.caveat: Must be overridden explicitly; a 3-minute TTFA target read through a 14-day window counts people who returned the following week.

numbers.label: Experiment sample size formula (per variant)
numbers.value: N = (16 × variance) / d²
numbers.source: PostHog — Running time and sample size
numbers.caveat: The 16 encodes 80% power at 95% confidence; d is the ABSOLUTE effect, not relative.

numbers.label: Variance term — funnel/conversion metric
numbers.source: PostHog — Running time and sample size

numbers.label: Variance term — count metric
numbers.value: 2 × baseline
numbers.source: PostHog — Running time and sample size

numbers.label: Variance term — sum/average metric
numbers.value: 0.25 × baseline²
numbers.source: PostHog — Running time and sample size
numbers.caveat: Implies a coefficient of variation of 0.5; optimistic for a long-tailed duration like TTFA, so treat derived Ns as floors.

numbers.label: Default minimum detectable effect
numbers.value: 30% relative
numbers.source: PostHog — Running time and sample size
numbers.caveat: 30% of a 480 s baseline TTFA is 144 s — three times the 45 s effect A1 predicts, so A1 cannot run at the default MDE.

numbers.label: A2 (test-attempt rate 40% → 52%) sample size
numbers.value: ~267 per variant (534 total)
numbers.source: Derived from PostHog formula with p=0.40, d=0.12

numbers.label: A1 (TTFA mean 480 s → 435 s) sample size
numbers.value: ~455 per variant (910 total)
numbers.source: Derived from PostHog formula with baseline=480 s, d=45 s

numbers.label: A4 (backup attach 15% → 35%) sample size
numbers.value: ~51 per variant
numbers.source: Derived from PostHog formula with p=0.15, d=0.20

numbers.label: A5 (voice previews 6 → 3) sample size
numbers.value: ~16 per variant
numbers.source: Derived from PostHog formula with baseline=6, d=3
numbers.caveat: Implausibly cheap — the 0.25 × baseline² proxy understates variance for small counts; power it as a count metric (2 × baseline) instead, giving ~22 per variant.

numbers.label: TCR guardrail (95% → detect a fall to 92%) sample size
numbers.value: ~844 per variant (1,689 total)
numbers.source: Derived from PostHog formula with p=0.95, d=0.03
numbers.caveat: ~3x the cost of the speed metric it guards — declare TCR monitored-with-a-stopping-rule, not powered.

numbers.label: Trends property-value percentiles available
numbers.value: 75th, 90th, 95th, 99th (plus avg, sum, min, max, median)
numbers.caveat: Numeric properties only; the funnel time-to-convert view offers no selectable percentile, so p75 dwell budgets require an explicit duration property.

numbers.label: Group types per project
numbers.value: Maximum 5 (unlimited groups within each)
numbers.caveat: cid is already one; project and agent would take it to three.

numbers.label: Dynamic cohort recalculation interval
numbers.value: Once every 24 hours
numbers.caveat: Behavioural/lifecycle cohorts also cannot target feature flags at all.

numbers.label: Person property size limit
numbers.value: 512 KB per person record
numbers.caveat: Updates exceeding it are rejected outright, not truncated.

numbers.label: Feature flag evaluation latency
numbers.caveat: Bootstrap flags server-side or the control variant flashes — a measurement artefact in a time-to-first-answer product.

numbers.label: Alert limits
numbers.value: 5 alerts on free tier; unlimited on paid; real-time slots 10 (Scale) / 20 (Enterprise)

numbers.label: Alert check frequencies
numbers.value: Real time (Scale/Enterprise), 15 min (Boost+), hourly, daily, weekly, monthly

numbers.label: Insight types that support alerts
numbers.value: Trends, funnels (steps and trends views only), SQL/HogQL
numbers.caveat: Explicitly excludes funnel time-to-convert and flow/sankey — the decisive constraint for how TTFA must be instrumented.

numbers.label: Anonymous vs identified event cost
numbers.value: Anonymous events up to 4x cheaper
numbers.caveat: Set $process_person_profile: false for anonymous backend events; the console itself is authenticated so this mainly affects the marketing→signup edge.

numbers.label: posthog-js person_profiles default
numbers.value: identified_only
numbers.caveat: Under identified_only, $set/$set_once on an event will NOT create a person profile for an anonymous user.

numbers.value: LIMIT 100
numbers.caveat: Raise it explicitly on dashboard tiles or long date ranges, or the tile silently truncates.

numbers.label: posthog-js defaults date options
numbers.caveat: Pin one explicitly; leaving it unset means an SDK upgrade can change ingestion behaviour mid-baseline.

numbers.value: 88 track() call sites, dispatch() is a console.debug TODO
numbers.caveat: The stub the front-end engineer implements against today already exists — the work is swapping dispatch(), not designing a taxonomy from zero.

numbers.caveat: Hand-maintained; PostHog schema management + CLI can generate this instead.

numbers.value: median and mean only (no p75/p90)
numbers.caveat: Stated in the issue body describing current behaviour; the funnels doc itself names no statistic

numbers.value: 2024-07-26, "working on a native solution"

numbers.label: Group analytics add-on price
numbers.value: $0.000071/event, billed on ALL identified events

numbers.label: Anonymous vs identified event cost
numbers.value: anonymous up to 4x cheaper
numbers.caveat: No absolute figure published for the anonymous rate

numbers.label: Max group types per project
numbers.value: 5 (unlimited instances per type)

numbers.value: 1M analytics events · 5K replays · 1M flag requests · 100K exceptions · 1,500 survey responses · 100K AI-observability events · 10GB logs
