corpus.headline: Confidence is not one test — every credible source describes a layered ladder (turn-level check → chat sim → voice sim → canary → post-call scoring), and Agora's differentiator is that it can run the SAME rubric offline and online, but it is currently missing the two things competitors shipped in 2026 that make confidence real: immutable published versions with percentage rollout, and production scorers attached to live calls.

findings.claim: Anthropic's own eval guidance says start with 20–50 tasks drawn from real failures, not a big curated benchmark — and warns that an eval at 100% pass gives no signal.
findings.detail: "Demystifying evals for AI agents" (Anthropic Engineering, Jan 2026) defines the vocabulary the whole industry now borrows: task, trial, agent harness, eval harness, transcript/trace, outcome, grader, suite. It advises sourcing tasks from bug trackers, support queues and existing manual testing; building balanced sets that test presence AND absence of a behaviour; and creating a reference solution per task to prove the task is solvable and the grader correct. It distinguishes pass@k (probability of ≥1 success in k attempts) from pass^k (probability ALL k succeed) and says customer-facing reliability needs pass^k. It also gives a diagnostic: 0% on pass@100 means a broken task or grader, not an incapable agent.
findings.soWhat: The Agora Test section should never present an empty 'create your first test' state. Generate ~20 starter scenarios from the agent's own prompt, tools and Opening config, and label each run pass^k (e.g. '5/5 runs passed' not 'passed'). Surface a 'this suite is saturated' nudge when a suite hits 100% — that is exactly the moment the console should offer harder variants rather than let the user feel safe.
findings.source: Anthropic Engineering — Demystifying evals for AI agents

findings.claim: Anthropic frames confidence as a Swiss-cheese stack of six methods, each catching different failure modes — automated evals, production monitoring, A/B tests, user feedback, transcript review, systematic human studies.
findings.detail: No single layer is treated as sufficient. Automated evals are the pre-launch/CI first defence (fast, reproducible, run on every commit). Production monitoring is called the ground truth but is reactive. A/B testing validates with real users but takes days-to-weeks. Manual transcript review builds intuition and does not scale; human studies are the reference standard but expensive. The mapping is explicitly temporal: automated evals pre-launch, monitoring post-launch, periodic human review to recalibrate the LLM graders.
findings.soWhat: Go Live's review screen should print which layers this agent has actually passed, as a ladder with holes visible: 'Tested by you: 1 voice call · Simulated: 12/12 scenarios · Real callers: 0 · Human-reviewed transcripts: 0'. That single component converts an abstract feeling into an inspectable claim, and it is the honest answer to 'how do I build confidence in production'.
findings.source: Anthropic Engineering — Demystifying evals for AI agents

findings.claim: Hamel Husain's field guidance: binary pass/fail beats Likert scales, an LLM judge needs 100–200 labelled examples per failure mode before you trust it, and a ~70% pass rate is where an eval is actually informative.
findings.detail: His evals FAQ recommends manually annotating at least 30 traces to start error analysis and continuing to 'theoretical saturation' (~100 diverse traces as a guardrail), then reviewing 100+ fresh traces per 2–4 week cycle with 10–20 outlier traces reviewed weekly in between. For judge validation: 100–200 labelled examples per failure mode, split roughly 10–20% few-shot / 40–45% dev / 40–45% held-out test, with 30–50 Pass and 30–50 Fail in both dev and test, validated on TPR and TNR. He is blunt that Likert adjacent points are subjective and inconsistent across annotators. He reports 60–80% of development time going to error analysis and evaluation.
findings.soWhat: Agora's eval-tests.tsx already uses a binary verdict with named assertion kinds (rubric, tool-call, data-point, exact) — that is the right call and should be defended against any request for a 0–100 'agent quality score'. Add a lightweight thumbs-up/down on each simulated verdict; those labels are the only cheap path to a calibrated judge, and 'judge agreement with the builder' becomes a shippable product metric.
findings.source: Hamel Husain — AI Evals FAQ

findings.claim: LLM-as-judge is systematically biased and agrees with humans only ~70% of the time — so a judge verdict must never be the sole gate on a deploy.
findings.detail: Known failure modes are position bias (favouring the response shown second), verbosity bias (preferring longer outputs), and self-preference bias (a judge rating its own family's outputs higher). A 2026 RAND study found no judge uniformly reliable across benchmarks, with frontier models exceeding 50% error rates on hard bias benchmarks. Human–model agreement clusters around 70%. Vapi's own test-suite docs concede the limit: 'Simulation scores also depend on the evidence available to the judge' and 'synthetic callers do not fully represent real callers and their environments.'
findings.soWhat: Every failing verdict in the Test section must show its evidence anchored to the offending turn (eval-tests.tsx already does this via flaggedTurnIndex — keep it) and offer a one-click 'I disagree' that flips the verdict and logs it. Copy rule: the Go Live gate should say 'no test disagreed' not 'the agent is safe'. Product metric: judge-override rate per suite — if it exceeds ~30% the rubric, not the agent, is broken.
findings.source: RAND / arXiv survey work on LLM-judge reliability; Vapi test-suite docs

findings.claim: Vapi ships a three-rung test ladder with explicit cost/fidelity trade-offs — turn-level Evals, then Chat Simulations, then Voice Simulations — and the rungs exist because each catches something the one below cannot.
findings.detail: Evals feed the conversation up to a decision point and validate the next response by exact match, pattern, or AI judge. Chat simulations run a full adaptive conversation faster and cheaper. Voice simulations are the only rung that exercises transcription, pronunciation and turn-taking, because they place a real synthetic call. The simulation object model is concrete: a Scenario (instructions + evaluations as structured outputs with name/type/comparator/expected value), a Personality (built-in, e.g. 'Skeptical Sam'), and a Suite pairing one scenario with one personality, run N iterations. API surface: POST /eval/simulation/scenario, /eval/simulation, /eval/simulation/suite, /eval/simulation/run, GET /eval/simulation/run/<id> with queued/running/ended status.
findings.soWhat: Make the ladder legible as three buttons with honest prices: 'Check one answer (instant, free)', 'Simulate the conversation (~20s)', 'Simulate the call (~90s, exercises voice + turn-taking)'. Default a first-time user to chat sim so TTFA is not paid twice, but require at least one VOICE simulation before the first publish — it is the only rung that tests what the Advanced Speech Settings in §1 actually configure.
findings.source: Vapi docs — Test Suites, Simulations quickstart

findings.claim: Retell's simulation test case is four fields — user prompt persona, success criteria, dynamic variables, and custom function mocks — and mocking tools is what makes offline testing possible at all.
findings.detail: The user prompt describes identity, the caller's goal and a personality that shapes responses. Success criteria are judged together in a single pass: the run passes only if EVERY criterion is met, with one combined explanation, not a verdict per criterion. Hard limits are published: tests time out at 10 minutes, conversations terminate at 400 utterances or when the simulated user repeats itself or the agent stops responding. The API supports CI gates — create/update cases, launch batch, poll status, read pass/fail counts to decide deployability. Retell also ships deterministic rule tests (required strings, forbidden strings, regex) that are fast and free, recommended for compliance checks like PII leakage.
findings.soWhat: Agora's eval case sheet has persona + plain-language assertions but no tool mocking or dynamic variables. Without mocks, any agent with an MCP server or connector cannot be tested safely — you would fire real bookings. Add 'What should this tool return?' inside the case sheet, reusing the existing ResourceField/Sheet idiom. And add free deterministic rule assertions (must-say the AI disclosure, must-never-say a competitor name, never read back a full card number) — they cost nothing, run instantly, and are the compliance story enterprises ask for.
findings.source: Retell AI docs — LLM simulation testing

findings.claim: ElevenLabs closes the loop competitors leave open: its simulation API evaluates results using the SAME criteria applied in production — one rubric, run offline and online.
findings.detail: Its Agent Testing offers two shapes: full multi-turn simulation against a simulated AI user, and 'Next Reply (Scenario)' tests that supply conversation history and score only the agent's next message. Tool mocking is configurable per test as mock-none / mock-all / mock-selected. Extra evaluation criteria can be defined beyond those in the agent config. Endpoints are /v1/convai/agent-testing/create and /v1/convai/agents/:agent_id/run-tests. Vapi does the production half separately via Scorecards (attached through artifactPlan.scorecardIds, metrics with comparators and points totalling 100, returning score / scoreNormalized / metricPoints in call.artifact.scorecards within seconds of call end).
findings.soWhat: This is Agora's cleanest strategic move and it is nearly free given the existing components: the assertions authored in §4 Test should be offered, at Go Live, as the production success criteria. One checkbox — 'Keep scoring live calls against these 12 checks'. It turns a pre-launch artefact into the first 24-hour dashboard with zero new authoring, and it makes 'proportion of agents with an eval suite' and 'proportion of live agents with production scorers' the same number.
findings.source: ElevenLabs docs — Agent Testing / Simulate Conversations; Vapi Scorecard quickstart

findings.claim: The caller-perceived latency cliff is well characterised: ~200–300ms is the human turn gap, 500ms feels slow, at ~800ms callers say 'hello?' into the gap, and by 1.2s they assume the line dropped.
findings.detail: Human conversational turn handoff runs ~200ms, faster than the ~600ms needed to produce even a one-word reply. The classic Roberts & Francis (2013) gap-tolerance work shows perceived willingness dropping noticeably at 600ms with the effect becoming statistically significant between 700–800ms. A stitched pipeline spends roughly 100–300ms on STT, 350–1,000ms on LLM, 90–200ms on TTS and 50–200ms on inter-vendor network hops. Hamming's post-call guidance puts time-to-first-word targets at <300ms natural, 300–500ms acceptable, >800ms breakdown — while noting the production industry median is actually 1.4–1.7 seconds.
findings.soWhat: The Advanced Speech Settings presets in §1 must resolve to a printed caller-perceived number, not raw ms fields — 'callers will hear about a 700ms pause before your agent replies' with the 800ms line drawn. And the right-hand Test panel should show measured per-turn e2e against that line, using the e2eLatencyMs / asr_ttlw / llm_ttft / tts_ttfb fields already parsed in latency-metrics.ts. Hearing it AND seeing the number is what converts a test call into confidence.
findings.source: Roberts & Francis 2013 via Picovoice/Hamming; Telnyx and Hamming latency guides

findings.claim: An independent 2026 benchmark measuring real phone calls puts every major platform between 1,296ms and 1,740ms median TTFAB — which contradicts the competitor table currently in docs/design/agent-builder-kpis.md.
findings.detail: Openbenchmarks dialled each platform's agent over a real phone call with a caller robot reading a fixed script, dual-channel recorded, with speech boundaries detected by Silero VAD plus energy refinement and an independent cross-check — no platform-reported timestamps. 108 calls per platform, last run 1 Aug 2026. Results (median / p95): Telnyx 1,296 / 1,856 ms; ElevenLabs 1,424 / 1,768 ms; Bland 1,520 / 2,248 ms; Vapi 1,558 / 2,008 ms; Retell 1,740 / 2,259 ms. The site is explicit that TTFAB measured caller-to-caller is necessarily higher than vendor server-side numbers.
findings.soWhat: The KPI doc at /Users/shaktisoni/Documents/Agora Design & FE/ng-console/docs/design/agent-builder-kpis.md §4 lists Retell at 680ms median / 920ms p95 alongside ElevenLabs 1,424 and Vapi 1,558 — that row mixes a server-side figure with two caller-perceived ones and reads as Retell being 2x faster than it measures. Fix it before the doc goes to the owner, or the whole latency target (p50 ≤900ms) looks either unreachable or dishonest. Measured caller-perceived p50 ≤900ms would in fact be best-in-class by a wide margin — that is the claim worth making, stated with the measurement method attached.
findings.source: Openbenchmarks — voice agent latency TTFAB benchmark

findings.claim: Call abandonment is the most usable quality proxy because its leading indicators are all loggable: 73% of abandonments follow a latency spike above 1200ms, 45% follow ASR confidence below 80%, 31% follow a tool-call failure, 28% follow a clarification loop.
findings.detail: Hamming's drop-off framework, drawn from 10M+ minutes across 10K+ voice agents on LiveKit, Pipecat, ElevenLabs, Retell and Vapi, benchmarks abandonment at 2–3% for high performers, 5–6% average, 7–10% below average, critical above 10%, with sub-3% expected in healthcare and financial services. It quantifies the slope: each 100ms beyond 800ms reduces completion by 4–6%; 800–1200ms adds 6–10% abandonment; above 1200ms adds 15–25%. Silence gaps over 2 seconds read as system failure and trigger disconnection. It proposes a six-stage funnel (connection → intent capture → information gathering → task execution → confirmation → close) with under 3% per-stage drop-off as good and above 8% as poor. Contact-centre convention independently puts acceptable human-queue abandonment at 3–8%.
findings.soWhat: This is the specification for Agora's first-24-hours screen. Show abandonment against the 2–3%/5–6%/>10% bands, then the four leading indicators as a ranked 'why' list, each linking to the calls that caused it. It is far more actionable than a sentiment score and every input is already in the runtime payload. Make the six-stage funnel the shape of the post-deploy view, not a generic call list.
findings.source: Hamming AI — voice agent drop-off analysis (10M+ minutes)

findings.claim: Barge-in quality decomposes into six measurable signals — false interruption, missed interruption, resume success, repeated user speech, silence-after-interruption, and post-interruption task completion — and no platform surfaces them as a set.
findings.detail: Hamming's interruption runbook separates three distinct causes of false interruption: background noise/echo stopping the agent, backchannels ('yeah', 'uh-huh') cancelling speech, and long entity pauses (reading an account number) triggering premature endpointing. Amazon Nova Sonic's sensitivity levels are cited as waiting roughly 1.5 / 1.75 / 2.0 seconds before responding. The runbook's strongest operational advice is not aggregate at all: 'Review the top 20 production interrupted calls after release.' Endpointing is named as frequently the largest single contributor to dead air because it sits directly between user speech and system response.
findings.soWhat: Tie the turn-taking preset in §1/row 02 to its own post-deploy report card. If a user picks 'more interruptible', the Monitor view should show false-interruption rate for that choice — that closes the loop between a config knob and a consequence, which is the only way a non-engineer learns to trust the knob. Also ship the 'top 20 interrupted calls' list as a literal named view; it is cheap and it is what practitioners actually do.
findings.source: Hamming AI — voice agent interruption handling runbook

findings.claim: Published ASR word error rates are not achievable on phone calls — real-world degradation runs 2.8–5.7x, and a model at 5% on a benchmark hits 15–20% on a noisy 8kHz call.
findings.detail: Documented degradation spans controlled medical dictation at ~8.7% WER to multi-speaker clinical conversation above 50% WER. A 2026 evaluation of five STT models across 40 hours of real 8kHz call audio — accented names, spelled-out policy numbers, speakerphone from moving cars, overlapping speakers — found WER rising monotonically with audio quality: ElevenLabs Scribe from 15.31% to 25.20% and Gemini-3-Pro from 13.42% to 23.44% between the best and worst quality quartiles. AssemblyAI has published directly on why WER as a single number is broken. Hamming's production bands put enterprise at <5%, production 5–8%, acceptable 8–12%.
findings.soWhat: Hard rule for the Voice & Models section: never print a vendor's benchmark WER or 'sub-100ms' component latency in the preset recap. Print Agora's own measured number for that stack on telephony audio, or print nothing. When the deployment channel is a phone number rather than a web widget, the preset recap should warn that accuracy is measured on 8kHz audio — that single line is a credibility differentiator no competitor offers.
findings.source: AssemblyAI, Deepgram and 2026 8kHz STT evaluations

findings.claim: Both leading platforms have converged on a large end-reason taxonomy as the primary post-call diagnostic — Vapi publishes 50+ values across ~10 categories, Retell ~30 across three status buckets — and this is the backbone of production confidence.
findings.detail: Vapi groups by call-start errors, assistant actions (assistant-ended-call, assistant-forwarded-call, explicitly flagged as intentional not errors), customer actions (customer-ended-call, customer-did-not-answer), LLM pipeline errors (401-unauthorized, 429-exceeded-quota), voice/transcriber errors (voice-not-found, transcriber-failed), transport (phone-call-provider-closed-websocket, twilio-failed-to-connect-call), SIP (outbound-sip-403-forbidden), timeouts (silence-timed-out, exceeded-max-duration), transfer failures, and other (manually-canceled, voicemail). Retell splits by call status: ended (user_hangup, agent_hangup, call_transfer, transfer_bridged, transfer_cancelled, voicemail_reached, ivr_reached, inactivity, max_duration_reached), not_connected (dial_busy, dial_no_answer, invalid_destination, telephony_provider_permission_denied, sip_routing_error, marked_as_spam, user_declined), and error (concurrency_limit_reached, no_valid_payment, error_llm_websocket_*, error_no_audio_received, error_asr, error_user_not_joined). Crucially both carry a per-reason fix instruction, not just a label.
findings.soWhat: Agora must design its own taxonomy now, and the design decision that matters is the top-level grouping. Group by WHO CAN FIX IT — caller behaviour (normal, no action), your configuration (fix in section N, deep-link it), Agora infrastructure (we are on it, status link), vendor/credential (rotate key, or switch to Agora Managed Key). That grouping is directly enabled by the Agora-Managed-Key advantage: a whole class of 401/429/quota reasons simply does not exist for default agents, and the console should say so out loud on the Monitor screen.
findings.source: Vapi call-ended reasons; Retell debug call disconnect

findings.claim: Versioned, immutable agent releases with percentage traffic splitting shipped at Retell in 2026 and are now table stakes — Agora's Go Live has no equivalent.
findings.detail: Retell added A/B testing in March 2026 splitting live call traffic by percentage across multiple agent versions to compare prompts and voices before full rollout, and Agent Versioning 2.0 in May 2026 with staging and production environment tags plus one-click promotion. Published versions cannot be edited — only drafts can — and specific versions attach to specific phone numbers or environment tags. Generic progressive-delivery practice sets the pattern: 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% with a monitoring hold at each stage, feature flags decoupling deploy from activation, shadow mode duplicating production requests to a candidate with zero user impact, and pre-declared automatic rollback triggers.
findings.soWhat: Three concrete additions to §5 Go Live. (1) Immutable published versions with a visible version number on the deploy bar, so 'what changed' is always answerable. (2) 'Send 10% of calls to the new version' as a first-class control on the Deploy button, not a setting buried elsewhere. (3) An auto-rollback rule set AT deploy time, in the user's words: 'Put it back if more than 1 in 10 calls ends badly in the first hour.' Choosing the rollback condition before you deploy is the specific act that lets a builder flip the switch.
findings.source: Retell AI docs — agent versioning; Retell changelog; progressive-delivery practice

findings.claim: The single best-evidenced confidence device in the entire builder is the preflight checklist — WHO's surgical checklist cut complications by more than a third and halved failures to meet basic standards across eight hospitals in rich and poor countries.
findings.detail: Gawande's checklist work, itself derived from the preflight checklist Boeing engineers introduced after the 1935 B-17 prototype crash and from Pronovost's line-infection checklist, is a two-minute run-through before, during and after each procedure. The measured effect across 1,000 patients in eight hospitals: surgical complications down by more than a third on average, failures to provide six basic surgical standards halved. The mechanism is not new knowledge — it is forcing already-known steps to be verified out loud at the moment of commitment.
findings.soWhat: deploy-preflight.tsx is already this and should be protected as the builder's highest-value screen. Two upgrades from the evidence: the checklist must be run and shown for EVERY deploy including re-deploys (the component comment already says this — hold that line against any 'skip for repeat publishes' request), and it should print what was NOT checked as plainly as what passed. A screen of all-greens that silently omits 'no one has tested the refund path' manufactures exactly the false confidence the checklist exists to prevent.
findings.source: Gawande / WHO Surgical Safety Checklist; Harvard T.H. Chan

findings.claim: Trust-in-automation research says the design goal is calibrated trust, not maximum trust — and an interface that hides when the system struggles produces over-trust, which is a failure mode in its own right.
findings.detail: Lee & See's 2004 'Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance' gives the canonical model relating calibration, resolution and automation capability. Miscalibration runs in two directions: over-trust (relying more than capability merits, causing inappropriate use) and distrust/under-trust (refusing a capable system). Their prescription for calibration is transparency delivered through the interface itself — information about the underlying principles, about intended functionality, and specifically about when the tool might struggle — turning a black box into an inspectable machine.
findings.soWhat: This is the design argument for a 'Known weak spots' block on the Go Live review, generated not written: 'You have not tested what happens when a caller asks for a human', 'Your knowledge base has no answer for pricing', 'No backup provider configured for TTS (row 07)'. Pair it with the honest framing of the test panel — one successful test call proves the agent can talk, not that it is correct. Copy that oversells the green ticks is not kindness; it is the mechanism that produces a 3am rollback.
findings.source: Lee & See 2004, Human Factors — Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance

findings.claim: Assume the median Agora user has no evaluation practice at all: survey data puts automated-eval adoption at roughly a third of teams, with quality the top barrier to shipping agents.
findings.detail: Reported figures: only ~34% of surveyed developer teams use automated evals, ~70% evaluate outputs by manual testing, and ~15% run no formal evaluation. LangChain's 2026 State of AI Agents reports 57% of organisations with agents in production and quality named the top barrier to deployment by 32% of respondents. Gartner is quoted projecting 60% of software engineering teams adopting AI evaluation and observability platforms by 2028, up from 18% in 2025. These come via secondary aggregation and should be treated as directional.
findings.soWhat: The design consequence is decisive: an eval suite must be GENERATED, never authored from blank. When the user finishes the Prompt section, the Test section should already contain scenarios derived from that prompt, the configured tools, and the Opening settings — with 'Save a real call as a test' (already in eval-tests.tsx) as the growth path. An empty authoring UI will be used by roughly a third of builders and skipped by the rest, and those are the agents that produce the bad first 24 hours.
findings.source: 2026 State of AI Engineering / LangChain State of AI Agents, via secondary aggregation

findings.claim: Replaying real production calls as regression tests is the practice that catches what synthetic suites miss — but only audio replay tests the voice stack; text replay silently skips ASR, endpointing, noise and TTS queueing.
findings.detail: The pattern is to import real call transcripts as runs and replay them against the agent's current graph to check whether outcomes still hold — capture a production failure once, replay it forever. Practitioners describe the specific hole it fills: you ship a prompt change, LLM judges score everything green, and a week later tickets pile up because the agent confirms the wrong appointment type on a path nobody wrote a test for. Two stated limits: replay only covers behaviour you have already seen and cannot produce a novel input; and replaying text instead of audio misses ASR, endpointing, jitter, background noise and TTS queueing. Braintrust productises the same loop by converting production traces that fail an online scorer into eval cases, and gates merges via a GitHub Action that blocks below a score threshold.
findings.soWhat: On any failed or abandoned production call, the primary action should be 'Add this to my tests' — one click, pre-filled, which eval-tests.tsx already supports as a sheet. Show fidelity honestly on each saved case: a badge distinguishing a transcript replay from an audio replay, because the difference is exactly the difference between testing the prompt and testing the agent. Product metric: suite growth from production failures per agent per week — that is the cleanest possible measure of a maturing builder.
findings.source: Braintrust continuous-evaluation guidance; production-replay practice write-ups

findings.claim: Borrow DORA's change-failure-rate and time-to-restore as the agent-level confidence SLOs — elite is under 5% change failure and under one hour to restore — and add time-to-DETECT, which is the number a console can uniquely improve.
findings.detail: 2026 DORA benchmarks put elite change failure rate below 5%, mean time to restore under an hour, deployment frequency at multiple per day, and lead time in hours. Applied to LLM agents, published SLO practice recommends starting at 5% of traffic with a 24-hour watch before scaling to 25%, 50%, 100%; pre-declared rollback triggers (error rate, p95 latency, guardrail-trigger rate); and error budgets computed against a quality SLO — e.g. a 0.85 quality SLO with 1,000 daily judged samples yields a budget of ~150 wrong answers per week, with a rule that consuming >50% of the budget in the first three days blocks anything but reverts.
findings.soWhat: The existing KPI doc's TCR ≥95% target maps cleanly onto DORA change failure rate ≤5% — cite it, it makes the target defensible rather than invented. Then add the missing metric: MTTD, time from a bad publish to the builder knowing. A console can drive this to minutes with a single proactive signal ('your agent's first 20 live calls are ending worse than your tests predicted') whereas users currently discover it via tickets. Time-to-detect is measurable, ownable by design, and no voice competitor advertises it.
findings.source: DORA 2026 benchmarks; LLM SLO/error-budget practice

findings.claim: PostHog's flag-and-experiment model means the confidence instrumentation and the rollout mechanism can be the same object — but only if flag exposure is emitted from the front end as the builder is built.
findings.detail: PostHog experiments run on top of feature flags, so every experiment is a controlled rollout by default; flag evaluations tie directly into product analytics so any insight, funnel or session replay can be filtered by flag value without extra setup, and any existing event or funnel can become an experiment metric. Flags support phased percentage rollouts, kill switches, multivariate variants and JSON payloads. The practical constraint is that exposure events must be emitted at the point of evaluation, which is a front-end decision made now, not later.
findings.soWhat: Every builder change on the tracker should be shipped behind a named flag with an exposure event, so the KPI doc's kill rule (revert if a change misses half its predicted effect in two reporting weeks) is executable rather than aspirational. Note the existing constraint in this repo: Session Replay is disabled by policy, so struggle must be inferred from allowlisted scalar signals — which makes exposure events and the dwell budgets in §2.3 of the KPI doc the only instrument available. Emit them from the first commit of each section.
findings.source: PostHog — Feature Flags, Experiments, Product Analytics docs

findings.claim: Agora's runtime already emits three of the six barge-in signals the first pass said nobody surfaces — and src/lib/latency-metrics.ts discards all three.
findings.detail: Notification event 112 (Turns Finished) carries, per turn, a `start` object with `type` ∈ {voice_input, greeting, silence_timeout, api_speak, api_think} and `metadata.speech_duration_ms` / `interrupt_duration_ms`, and an `end` object with `type` ∈ {ok, error, ignored, interrupted}. The console's parseTurnFinishedMessage() reads only agent_id, turn_id, start.start_at and metrics.*, so end.type, start.type and interrupt_duration_ms never reach the UI. Missed-interruption rate, silence-timeout rate and interrupt duration are therefore available today with a parser change, not a backend project.
findings.soWhat: The barge-in panel and the end-reason taxonomy can ship in the first instrumentation pass. Extend LatencyTurn with startType, endType and interruptDurationMs before designing the first-24-hours screen — the design can assume these fields exist.
findings.source: Agora Conversational AI notification event types + repo file /Users/shaktisoni/Documents/Agora Design & FE/ng-console/src/lib/latency-metrics.ts

findings.claim: Agora emits no per-turn ASR confidence anywhere, so the first pass's 'ASR confidence below 80%' abandonment predictor is not instrumentable on this platform.
findings.detail: Across events 103 (history), 110 (errors), 111 (metrics: asr_ttlw, llm_ttfb, llm_ttfs, tts_ttfb) and 112 (turns), the only ASR-adjacent fields are asr_ttlw (a latency number), speech_start_ms/speech_end_ms and speech_algorithmic_delay — and the last three are documented as custom-vendor only. There is no confidence score, no alternatives list, no per-word timing. Any UI that promises 'low recognition confidence' as a diagnosis would be fabricating it.
findings.soWhat: Drop ASR confidence from the day-one panel spec, or raise it with the runtime team as a feature request with a named consumer. Substitute the signals that do exist: end.type='ignored', silence_timeout turns, and repeated near-identical user turns in event 103's contents array.
findings.source: Agora Conversational AI notification event types

findings.claim: Agora already ships a full telephony call state machine (events 201/202), so answer rate and post-dial delay — the two numbers that decide whether an outbound agent works at all — are computable today with no new backend work.
findings.detail: Event 201 (inbound) reports state ∈ {START, ANSWERED, TRANSFERED, HANGUP}; event 202 (outbound) reports {START, CALLING, RINGING, ANSWERED, HANGUP}; both carry report_ms. Differencing START→RINGING gives post-dial delay, RINGING→ANSWERED gives ring time, and the ANSWERED/START ratio is answer-seizure ratio. None of this appears in the builder today.
findings.soWhat: Put a four-step call funnel (dialled → ringing → answered → completed) at the top of the first-24-hours review, and show TRANSFERED as a first-class outcome rather than a hangup. It is the cheapest credible production panel Agora can build.
findings.source: Agora Conversational AI notification event types

findings.claim: Agora has no end-reason taxonomy — where Vapi publishes 50+ values, Agora gives status STOPPED|FAILED plus a free-text message — so the console has to synthesise the taxonomy client-side.
findings.detail: Event 102 carries status ('STOPPED' or 'FAILED') and a human-readable `message` whose documented causes are manual stop, idle timeout, connection errors and task lifetime exceeded. Event 110 carries an errors array with `module` (documented values: 'llm', 'sip'), an integer `code`, a message and a turn_id. That is three loosely-coupled sources, not one enum, and free text cannot be counted or charted.
findings.soWhat: Specify a console-owned end-reason enum derived from (event 102 status/message) × (event 110 module+code) × (event 201/202 terminal state), pin it in the design doc, and treat it as the join key for the whole post-call view. Do not design UI that assumes a server-side reason string.
findings.source: Agora Conversational AI notification event types + webhooks reference

findings.claim: Agora publishes concrete turn-detection defaults, which gives Advanced Speech Settings a factual baseline instead of unlabelled sliders.
findings.detail: Documented defaults: interrupt_duration_ms 160, speaking_interrupt_duration_ms 320, prefix_padding_ms 800, speech_threshold 0.5 for start-of-speech (VAD); silence_duration_ms 320 and max_wait_ms 3000 for end-of-speech, with mode 'semantic' for AI-powered endpointing. These map one-to-one onto the turn-taking and listening controls in section 1.
findings.soWhat: Label every Advanced Speech Setting with its shipped default and the measured signal it moves (e.g. silence_duration_ms → silence_timeout turn rate; interrupt_duration_ms → false-interruption rate). That turns an expert panel into a closed feedback loop and is the strongest 'reuse, don't redesign' move available in that section.
findings.source: Agora docs — Interrupt the agent mid-response

findings.claim: The eval-adoption figure the first pass carried is wrong: the primary survey says 52.4% of teams run offline evals, not 34%.
findings.detail: LangChain's State of Agent Engineering — 1,340 responses collected 18 Nov–2 Dec 2025 — reports 57.3% with agents in production, 89% with some observability (94% among teams with production agents), 62% with detailed step/tool-call tracing (71.5% in production), 52.4% running offline evaluations and 37.3% running online evaluations. Evaluation methodology splits 59.8% human review and 53.3% LLM-as-judge. The top barrier to production is quality at 33%, then latency at 20%.
findings.soWhat: Correct the number before it reaches a deck. It also changes the design premise: the median Agora user is not eval-naive — they are observability-rich and eval-poor. Build the post-call observability view first and let eval suites grow out of real transcripts, which is the order the market is already in.
findings.source: LangChain, State of AI Agents / Agent Engineering (n=1,340)

findings.claim: Only about a quarter of eval-running teams do both offline and online evaluation — which makes ElevenLabs' one-rubric-both-places design rarer and more differentiating than the first pass implied.
findings.detail: 52.4% run offline evals and 37.3% run online, but roughly 25% of those running evals do both. The offline/online split is where confidence leaks: a suite that passes in simulation and a production dashboard measuring something else cannot corroborate each other.
findings.soWhat: Make Agora's test scenarios and its post-call success evaluation share one rubric object in the data model from day one. It is close to free at this stage and structurally hard to retrofit.
findings.source: LangChain, State of AI Agents / Agent Engineering

findings.claim: EU AI Act Article 50 has been binding since 2 August 2026, which makes the Opening section's AI-disclosure toggle a legal control rather than a courtesy.
findings.detail: Providers of AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons must design them so people are informed they are interacting with AI, 'at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure', in a clear and distinguishable manner conforming to accessibility requirements. Exemptions are narrow: where it is obvious to a reasonably well-informed observer, or for authorised law-enforcement detection. Non-compliance can reach €15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover. A limited grace period to 2 December 2026 applies only to the content-marking obligation for systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026.
findings.soWhat: The disclosure toggle should not be silently defaultable to off for EU hosting regions. Wire hosting region (Go Live) to the Opening section: if the region is EU and disclosure is off, the preflight shows a blocking item quoting the first-interaction rule. That is a defensible reason for Agora to ship a preflight at all.
findings.source: EU AI Act Article 50; Cooley; European Commission FAQ

findings.claim: US exposure is per-call and uncapped: the FCC treats AI-generated voices as 'artificial' under the TCPA, at $500–$1,500 per call, and a pending NPRM would require in-call AI disclosure at the opening.
findings.detail: The FCC's declaratory ruling made AI-generated voices in robocalls 'artificial' under the TCPA — the legal status follows how the voice is produced, not how human it sounds — so outbound needs prior express consent, or prior express written consent for marketing, with consent language that covers AI-delivered voice. The August 2024 NPRM proposes mandatory in-call AI disclosure at the start of the call; finalisation timing is uncertain. Colorado's AI Act (2026) may classify most voice AI as high-risk.
findings.soWhat: The preflight branches on direction, not just region: an outbound/batch deployment gets consent-source and disclosure items that an inbound web-widget agent does not. Batch calls in section 2 is the riskiest surface in the whole builder and currently has no gate.
findings.source: FCC Declaratory Ruling; TCPA practitioner guidance

findings.claim: For outbound agents the dominant production failure has nothing to do with the prompt: 86% of consumers do not answer calls from unknown numbers.
findings.detail: Hiya's State of the Call 2026 — Censuswide, 12,000+ consumers across US, Canada, UK, France, Germany and Spain (~2,000 each), fielded 17 Dec 2025–2 Jan 2026 — reports 86% not answering unknown numbers, 34% saying their trust in phone calls fell in the past 12 months against 16% saying it rose, 39% saying spam increased, an average of 7 unwanted calls per week, 31% reporting a deepfake voice call and 15% losing money to a phone scam. Caller-ID presentation and attestation, not agent quality, decide whether the agent ever speaks.
findings.soWhat: Answer rate belongs on the first-24-hours panel above every latency number, and the phone-number channel in section 2 should surface caller-ID/attestation status at configuration time. An agent showing a 95% success rate on 6 answered calls out of 100 dialled is not a working deployment.
findings.source: Hiya, State of the Call 2026 (Censuswide, n>12,000)

findings.claim: The rule of three gives the exact maths for a count-based canary and the exact copy for the Go Live screen — 20 clean calls only bounds the failure rate at 15%.
findings.detail: If zero failures are observed in n independent trials, the 95% confidence upper bound on the true failure rate is 3/n (Hanley & Lippman-Hand, JAMA 1983; derived from (1−p)^n = 0.05, giving n·ln(1−p) ≈ −3). So 20 clean calls bound failure at 15%, 60 at 5%, 100 at 3% and 300 at 1%. Hanley and Lippman-Hand's own point was that observing nothing go wrong does not mean nothing is wrong.
findings.soWhat: This closes the first pass's open question. Ship a count-based canary — 'watch the first N calls' — with the bound written into the UI: 'No failures in 20 calls. That still allows a failure rate as high as 15%. Keep watching to 60 for 5%.' Nobody in the category shows this, and it is honest rather than reassuring, which is what calibrated trust requires.
findings.source: Hanley & Lippman-Hand 1983, JAMA 249(13):1743–5; Jovanovic & Levy, The American Statistician 1997

findings.claim: Percentage-based canaries are statistically meaningless at first-agent volumes, and the general guidance confirms it: you need at least ~50 data points per metric for a canary comparison to mean anything.
findings.detail: Google Cloud canary guidance puts the floor at roughly 50 data points per metric for statistical tests to be meaningful, and canary release plans in the literature are specified as a triplet of (steps, requests per step, time per step) — i.e. count-based, not percentage-based, precisely so each step carries enough power. A 10% canary on an agent taking 30 calls a day yields 3 calls, which reads noise as signal or stretches the bake window into days.
findings.soWhat: Do not copy ElevenLabs' and Retell's percentage sliders into Go Live. Design the canary as 'route the next N calls to the new version' with N defaulting to something the rule of three can justify, and show the percentage only as a derived readout for high-volume accounts.
findings.source: Google Cloud canary best practices; canary deployment literature (arc42, MANATEE arXiv 2601.14009)

findings.claim: ElevenLabs has now shipped branch-based versioning with percentage traffic splitting and deterministic routing — so two of the three leading competitors split live traffic, and Agora is further behind on Go Live than the first pass concluded.
findings.detail: A version is an immutable snapshot with id agtvrsn_xxxx containing conversation_config (system prompt, LLM settings, voice, tools, knowledge base), platform_settings (evaluation, widget, data collection, safety) and workflow (nodes and edges). Branches (agtbrch_xxxx, name up to 140 chars) can be cut from any version on any branch and merged into any non-archived branch; traffic percentages must total exactly 100% and routing is deterministic on conversation ID so a caller stays on one branch. Notably there is no explicit rollback procedure — recovery means merging or branching from an earlier version — and name, tags, auth, call_limits, privacy and ban status are NOT versioned.
findings.soWhat: Go Live needs a version object before it needs a canary. Copy the snapshot contents (prompt + models + voice + tools + knowledge base) and improve on the competitor in one specific way: ship an actual one-click rollback, which ElevenLabs does not document.
findings.source: ElevenLabs Agents documentation — Agent versioning

findings.claim: Synthflow's version history excludes actions and knowledge bases — a rollback that silently fails to restore your tools is a false confidence signal, and Agora should say out loud what a rollback does and does not restore.
findings.detail: Synthflow creates a version automatically on every publish or update through the UI (API modifications do not trigger versioning), stores who changed what, and offers single-click revert with a version diff. But actions and knowledge bases fall outside version tracking, and only one published version serves traffic — drafts publish straight to 100%, with no staging environment, no traffic splitting and no approval step.
findings.soWhat: On Agora's rollback confirmation, list the restored objects and the excluded ones by name (MCP servers, connectors, knowledge base). This is a two-line UI decision that converts a trust trap into a trust builder, and it is the kind of thing only a console that has read the competitor's fine print will get right.
findings.source: Synthflow documentation — Version Control

findings.claim: ElevenLabs' Experiments feature hands Agora a ready-made agent KPI set — and exposes the exact weakness Agora can beat: no sample-size or significance handling at all.
findings.detail: The documented comparison metrics are CSAT, containment rate, conversion, average handling time, median agent response latency and cost per agent resolution. Best practice is to start with 5–10% of traffic on the variant, all splits summing to 100%. The documentation offers no significance testing, no minimum sample size and no duration threshold — only 'allow enough conversations to accumulate' and 'small sample sizes lead to unreliable results'.
findings.soWhat: Adopt the six metrics verbatim for the post-deploy panel (containment rate and cost per resolution are both missing from Agora's current KPI doc), then differentiate on the statistics: show the confidence bound next to every comparison rather than a bare percentage difference.
findings.source: ElevenLabs Agents documentation — Experiments

findings.claim: Bland runs a three-tier draft/staging/production model with per-call version targeting and a 'Use Candidate Model' pre-promotion toggle — the most complete promotion ladder in the competitive set.
findings.detail: Editing happens in draft without affecting live calls; publishing promotes a draft to a new production version; calls default to production but an individual call can target a specific version number. Testing covers web chat (text or voice), real phone calls and per-node unit tests replayed from historical call data, with a 'simulated variations' toggle generating multiple phrasings (default 5) and LLM pass/fail grading against a custom grading goal. Test configurations (start node, version, request variables) can be saved and shared, and a conversation branch can be forked by editing any user message.
findings.soWhat: Two portable ideas for Agora's Test section: replay a real call's turn against a changed prompt (Agora has event 103 transcripts to do it with), and let a test target a specific version. The 'edit any user turn and re-branch' interaction is the cheapest high-value thing in the whole competitive set and fits Agora's test panel directly.
findings.source: Bland documentation — Conversational Pathways

findings.claim: No competitor gates publishing on test results — Synthflow's suites explicitly do not block deploy — which leaves 'you cannot go live with a failing suite' as an unclaimed position.
findings.detail: Synthflow allows up to 25 test cases per suite, auto-generates 4 base cases plus one per selected scenario by analysing the specific agent rather than a template, runs all simulations in a session in parallel, and lets you configure pass as 'all criteria' or 'any criterion'. Results are Completed / Failed / In Progress with per-criterion LLM reasoning. The documentation describes testing 'before going live' but nothing that makes results a precondition of publishing.
findings.soWhat: Agora can be first to make the Go Live review show the test suite's last-run verdict and staleness ('last run 3 config changes ago'), without hard-blocking. Staleness is the more honest gate than pass/fail and matches the first pass's finding that a 100% pass rate carries no signal.
findings.source: Synthflow documentation — Simulations

findings.claim: Vapi has retired Test Suites in favour of Simulations, so a like-for-like import spec should target the Simulations objects — the test-suite API endpoints now 404.
findings.detail: The docs page now presents four layers: Evals (decision checkpoints, exact match / pattern / AI judgment), Chat Simulations (full conversations, no audio), Voice Simulations (audio, transcription and timing) and manual review of production recordings, with the caveat that 'synthetic callers do not fully represent real callers and their environments'. The legacy test-suite object was script + rubric questions + attempts (up to 5). The current create-simulation body is scenarioId, personalityId, optional name and an optional path supporting up to 3 levels.
findings.soWhat: Closes the first pass's gap 6. The importable unit is a (scenario, personality) pair, not a script+rubric — which is closer to Retell's four-field test case and to what Agora's generated test scenarios already look like. Agora's scenarios should carry a separable persona field.
findings.source: Vapi documentation — Testing voice agents; API reference

findings.claim: LiveKit ships agent tests as ordinary pytest/Vitest with an LLM judge helper — and explicitly makes no room connection, which means the whole voice stack is untested in CI.
findings.detail: Tests instantiate AgentSession, run a user turn and assert with chains like result.expect.next_event().is_message(role='assistant'), result.expect.no_more_events(), and .judge(llm, intent='...') for fuzzy intent checks. CI needs only LIVEKIT_API_KEY / LIVEKIT_API_SECRET, with LIVEKIT_EVALS_VERBOSE=1 for detail. 'Testing does not make a LiveKit room connection', which keeps runs cheap but skips ASR, endpointing, barge-in and TTS entirely.
findings.soWhat: Sharpens the first pass's audio-vs-text replay point into a UI rule: label every test row in section 4 with what it actually exercised (text path vs voice path). A green suite that never made a sound is the most dangerous confidence signal the builder could show.
findings.source: LiveKit Agents documentation — Testing and evaluation

findings.claim: Google's SRE launch checklist gives the governance rules a Go Live preflight needs — every item must be earned by a past disaster, and 30% of launches got a shortened checklist.
findings.detail: Google ran up to 70 launches per week; one Launch Coordination Engineer handled 350 launches and a team of five over 1,500 in 3.5 years. Governance was deliberately severe: at one point adding a question required VP approval; 'every question's importance must be substantiated, ideally by a previous launch disaster'; 'every instruction must be concrete, practical, and reasonable for developers to accomplish'; and the checklist was reviewed once or twice a year for obsolescence. By 2008 low-risk launches — no new server executables and a traffic increase under 10% — got an abbreviated checklist, and 30% of reviews qualified.
findings.soWhat: Two-tier the Go Live preflight the same way: a first deployment of an inbound web widget on managed keys gets three items; an outbound batch campaign on a new BYO credential gets the full list. And adopt the rule for the design doc — no preflight item ships without a named failure it would have caught.
findings.source: Google SRE book, ch. 27 'Reliable Product Launches at Scale' + Appendix E

findings.claim: SRE multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting is the concrete recipe for what 'watch the first 24 hours' should actually compute.
findings.detail: The standard configuration pairs a long and short window at three tiers: 14.4x burn over a 1-hour long window (5-minute short window), which fires when 2% of a 30-day error budget is consumed in an hour; 6x over 6 hours (30-minute short window), 5% of budget; and 1x over 3 days (6-hour short window), 10% of budget. Both windows must be true simultaneously, which is what suppresses noise while keeping detection fast.
findings.soWhat: Define the agent's SLO at deploy time (e.g. 95% of calls end with end.type='ok') and render the first-24-hours review as budget consumed against the 14.4x and 6x lines rather than as a raw failure count. This is also the mechanism behind time-to-detect, which the first pass identified as the number a console can uniquely improve.
findings.source: Google SRE Workbook — Alerting on SLOs

findings.claim: Design the Go Live screen for a sceptic: DORA 2025 finds 90% AI adoption but only 24% of practitioners trust AI 'a great deal' or 'a lot', while 30% trust it 'a little' or 'not at all'.
findings.detail: DORA's 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development draws on ~5,000 respondents and 100+ hours of qualitative work. Its headline finding for this sweep is that increased AI adoption correlates with increased software delivery instability even as individual effectiveness improves, and its cost model puts a change-failure-rate move from 5% to 6% at roughly $344,000 in downtime. This is the closest published proxy to the missing voice-AI pre-launch hesitation data: the population is adopting fast and trusting little.
findings.soWhat: Confidence copy that asserts readiness ('Your agent is ready to go live') will read as marketing to this audience. Show evidence instead — what was tested, on how many calls, what the bound is, what is not covered — and let the user conclude. It also argues for making rollback visible before deploy, not after.
findings.source: DORA / Google Cloud, 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development (n≈5,000)

findings.claim: The non-medical checklist literature is a better design source than the WHO surgical study, and it is specifically about the length/compliance trade-off a Go Live screen faces.
findings.detail: Degani & Wiener's NASA Contractor Report 177549, 'Human Factors of Flight-Deck Checklists: The Normal Checklist', treats function, format, design, length and use, plus the sociotechnical factors — crew culture, production pressure — that cause checklists to be skipped, and ships design guidelines in Appendix A. Their central tension is exactly Agora's: more items reduce memory load but lengthen completion time and depress compliance, so only items critical enough to earn a line belong on it.
findings.soWhat: Cite this rather than the surgical-checklist study when arguing the preflight's length in the design doc, and adopt the read-and-do vs challenge-response distinction: items the console can verify itself should be auto-checked and shown as already done, leaving only the items requiring human judgement as user actions.
findings.source: Degani & Wiener, NASA CR-177549 (NASA Ames)

findings.claim: 'Proportion of deploys preceded by a test' — one of the metrics the owner asked for and the first pass could not benchmark — is already derivable from studio_x_2's existing event taxonomy with zero new events.
findings.detail: lib/analytics.ts already defines test_authored, test_run_started, test_run_completed{verdict}, test_outcome_selected{outcome: 'tweak'|'deploy'}, agent_test_started/ended, test_call_placed/test_call_connected, deployment_went_live, time_to_live_ms and config_drift_detected{level, id, ran_version, current_version}. The test→deploy ratio is a funnel over events that exist. What is genuinely missing for production confidence is narrow: no rollback event, no version_promoted, no canary_started/canary_completed, no preflight_item_checked/preflight_blocked, no day-one review opened, and no post-deploy self-reported confidence.
findings.soWhat: Add six events rather than a taxonomy. config_drift_detected already carries ran_version and current_version, which means a version concept is half-present in the front end — name it, and make Go Live emit version_promoted with the same ids so PostHog can join deploys to outcomes when it arrives.
findings.source: Repo: /Users/shaktisoni/Documents/Agora Design & FE/ai-studio-console-redesign/studio_x_2/lib/analytics.ts

findings.claim: Transcript-only evaluation and safety guardrails each carry a measurable, designable price that the builder should state.
findings.detail: Practitioner estimates put the share of caller-impacting failures invisible in a transcript at roughly 25% — clipping, low TTS volume, robotic prosody, dropouts, mispronounced proper nouns, and response timing — because the transcript reads correct while the audio is wrong. On the safety side, NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails is reported to add on the order of 500ms of baseline latency per interaction, compounding across turns, which sits directly on top of a 1,296–1,740ms real-world TTFAB. Both figures come from vendor and practitioner sources rather than peer review.
findings.soWhat: If Agora ever adds an output guardrail, the control must show its latency cost inline next to the latency-vs-cost slider — a safety feature that silently breaks the turn gap will be blamed on the model. And section 4's test rows need an audio-quality dimension, not just a transcript verdict.
findings.source: FutureAGI voice-eval writing; NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails technical blog
