insights.name: First 24 hours (post-deploy)
insights.spec: (1) Call funnel dialled → ringing → answered → completed from Agora events 201/202 — answer rate sits ABOVE every latency number, because 86% of consumers do not answer unknown numbers; (2) abandonment against the 2–3% / 5–6% / >10% bands; (3) end-reason distribution grouped by WHO CAN FIX IT (caller behaviour / your config, deep-linked to section N / Agora infra / vendor credential — a group of reasons that simply does not exist for managed-key agents, and the console should say so); (4) measured caller-perceived p50/p95 turn latency against the 800ms and 1,200ms lines; (5) rule-of-three bound printed in words: 'No failures in 20 calls. That still allows a failure rate as high as 15%. Keep watching to 60 for 5%'; (6) barge-in signals from event 112 start.type / end.type / interrupt_duration_ms — all three are emitted today and discarded by latency-metrics.ts.
insights.answers: Is my agent actually working, and how sure can I be? The owner's 'confidence in production' question, answered with evidence rather than a green tick.

insights.name: Weekly Proven Agents
insights.type: Trends + Retention, split by account type
insights.spec: first_live_call_received-backed agent count, split into new-account and existing-account series (revenue is expansion-led: +18% revenue vs +0.4% customers). Retention start event = first deployment_went_live in 'First ever occurrence' mode, return event = production session, weekly interval, paired with a Stickiness insight — retention shows only whether they returned, not how much, and 'one call in week 1' vs '400' are the same cell. Add a PERSON-level D7 return metric beside it with 7% as the initial target (Amplitude's 2025 benchmark: 7% D7 = top quartile; 69% of top D7 performers were also top 3-month performers).
insights.answers: The north star, and whether activation actually predicts retention rather than being assumed to.

insights.name: Data quality
insights.spec: (a) client agent_audio_heard count vs server turn-finished count; (b) events on an unexpected schemaVersion; (c) telemetry_heartbeat eventsEmitted distribution; (d) share of events missing isFirstAgent / trafficType. Plus an SRM check on flag exposure and an isFirstAgent-share check — adopt Spotify's fourth ship clause: a quality test that significantly invalidates the experiment blocks the read, it is not a caveat.
insights.answers: Can we believe any of the above? Pre-register Twyman's law here: after the two-week baseline, record the week-to-week SD of median TTFT, and investigate any claimed improvement beyond 3 SD for telemetry loss or a changed stop condition before reading it as a win — A2 is the row most likely to produce a fake win.

insights.name: Alerts — spend the free tier's five
insights.spec: Free orgs get 5 alerts total and hourly is the fastest free cadence (15-min needs Boost, real-time needs Scale/Enterprise); funnel time-to-convert and flow views are NOT alertable. Spend them on: (1) TTFT p75 via the SQL insight; (2) first-publish failure rate; (3) 24h rollback rate; (4) data quality — events on the wrong schemaVersion; (5) publish error rate. Do not write '15 minutes' into any runbook.
insights.answers: What wakes someone up. Each alert needs a named human owner and an action threshold that triggers investigation, not a target — a metric with no owner and no action threshold is a vanity metric by definition.

traps: BACKGROUNDED TABS — browsers throttle setInterval/rAF to >=1 s or freeze them entirely, so any tick-counted duration silently under-reports. Accumulate activeMs from `visibilitychange` transitions plus Date.now deltas, never from a ticker. Emit both activeMs and wallMs on every completion event so the difference is itself a readable signal.

RELOADS AND CRASHES — performance.now() resets per document and cannot span a reload; Date.now() jumps on NTP correction or a manual clock change and can produce a NEGATIVE duration. Use performance.now() deltas within a page and a persisted Date.now() stamp only for cross-reload spans. Never mix the two in one number, and clamp negatives to null with a data-quality flag rather than shipping them.

READ-AND-CLEAR DESTROYS MEASUREMENTS — studio_x_2's timeToLiveMs() removes the localStorage stamp BEFORE returning, so a failed dispatch, a thrown capture, or a React StrictMode double-invoke in dev loses the number with no retry. Clear the stamp only inside the capture callback.

PER-BROWSER STAMPS MEASURE THE WRONG THING — markBuildStart() writes only if the key is absent and markSignup() writes once forever, so a returning user's second, third and fourth agents are all measured from their first-ever builder mount. Key every stamp by agentId + builderSessionId, expire after 2 h idle, and scope per attempt.

AUTO-STARTED TESTS FAKE A ZERO — the autoTalk path fires agent_test_started 150 ms after mount with no user action on agt_default. Every test event MUST carry `trigger`, and TTFT must exclude trigger='auto'. `trigger` is already on ng-console's property allowlist, so it survives sanitisation.

THE CANNED DEMO IS NOT A TEST — the Talk surface is not gated by configuration at all; an empty draft with no voice, prompt or channel plays the same hard-coded RAIL_TALK script. Without `configured` and `heardOwnGreeting` on the event, TTFT counts demo playbacks as agent tests and the headline metric is unfalsifiable.

MULTI-SESSION TASKS — 40% of interrupted tasks are never resumed in the same sitting, and only 10% of developers make their first edit within a minute of returning (~30% take over 30 minutes). Measure per person over an explicit window (60 min for 'same sitting', 7 days for 'eventual'), never per PostHog session — a session ends after 30 min idle or 24 h total, and TTFD's p75 target routinely crosses that boundary. Emit resumeCount on every duration event so 'our builder is slow' can be separated from 'this person had a meeting'.

DAYS-LATER RETURNS — PostHog funnels default to a 14-DAY conversion window, so a person who returns the following week is counted as an in-session conversion and drags the average. Pin the window explicitly on every funnel; a 3-minute target read through a 14-day window is a retention metric wearing a speed metric's name.

LONG-TAIL SKEW — task times are lognormal with a floor at zero and a handful of users taking 10–20× the rest. Winsorize TTFT at 600 s and TTFD at 24 h, count the truncated sessions as their own failure rate rather than as slow successes, report median/p75 at n>=25 and the GEOMETRIC MEAN with log-transformed CIs below n=25 (every moderated study and every early flag cell lives below 25), and never report the arithmetic mean. Note PostHog experiments winsorize mean/funnel/ratio metrics by default — declare the bounds explicitly or the slow tail the 10-minute ceiling exists to catch is clipped before you read it, and a change that fixes only slow users will look like no change.

AD BLOCKERS BIAS TTFT DOWNWARD — a blocked client never emits the start event, so only the unblocked population is measured. Route ingestion through the same-origin /ingest proxy (ng-console already has the vercel.json rewrites; @posthog/next's postHogMiddleware({proxy:true}) gives studio_x_2 the same).

CLIENT-ONLY STOP EVENTS ARE THE CLASSIC TELEMETRY-LOSS FAILURE — a live voice session is exactly where a client drops its last beacon, and biased loss invalidates every metric built on the affected event. Anchor agent_audio_heard on the runtime's first turn-finished, keep the client event secondary, and ship the client-vs-server count comparison as a first-class insight from day one.

ORPHANED TEST SESSIONS — closing the rail (setRailOpen(false)) does not touch `testing`, and there is no unmount handler or beforeunload, so a user who folds the panel or navigates leaves the session open forever. Fire agent_test_ended from a useEffect cleanup with a `reason` property, and use transport:'sendBeacon' for unload-time events.

CLOCK SKEW MAKES THE FUNNEL AND THE PROPERTY DISAGREE — PostHog rewrites timestamps as `now + timestamp - sent_at`, so a funnel-derived duration is skew-corrected while a client-computed wallMs is not. Declare the client number canonical, the funnel median the sanity check, and a persistent gap >10% a data-quality alarm rather than a metric move.

LOCALSTORAGE IS PER-BROWSER AND CAN THROW — a user who starts on a laptop and tests on a phone gets no duration at all, while PostHog's person-level funnel still converts them; private windows and blocked site data make every read throw. Wrap every access in try/catch, emit storageAvailable on the heartbeat, and treat a missing duration as null, never as zero.

PERSON PROPERTIES ARE SET IN INGESTION ORDER, NOT TIMESTAMP ORDER — a late-arriving event can overwrite a duration written with $set. Never store a duration on a person property; use $set_once only for first-time milestones (first_agent_created_at, first_test_succeeded_at).

THE RAIL STATE SILENTLY CHANGES THE CLICK PATH FOREVER — one click on the rail's close button writes a localStorage flag that permanently alters the shortest path to Talk for that browser, on every agent. Any TTFT expressed in clicks is wrong for returning users; carry railOpen and `trigger` as properties so the populations can be separated.

DESKTOP AND MOBILE ARE DIFFERENT FUNNELS — the two-click TTFT does not exist below 1024px: the builder header does not wrap or scroll, the mobile sticky strip has step chips and Deploy but NO test door, and the test panel falls back to a Sheet that never auto-opens. Never quote one TTFT across both; break down by viewport or the mobile p75 will be attributed to a design that mobile users cannot reach.

DWELL IS A DESIGN CONTRACT, NOT A SUCCESS METRIC — 'time on page' is on Amplitude's own list of vanity metrics, and in a builder more engagement is worse, not better. Declare Engagement explicitly OUT of scope in the HEART grid so nobody adds an engagement metric later, and always read a dwell number next to a completion rate.

GUARDRAILS ARE UNFALSIFIABLE AT THIS VOLUME — 'must not rise' cannot be tested when the rollback guardrail needs ~1,216 users/arm. Rewrite each as a non-inferiority statement with a declared margin and an honest MDE, split the block into two tiers (deterioration: publish failure and rollback, no acceptable margin; guardrail: support contacts and latency, bounded margin), and CUT the count — four guardrails inflate the required sample by ~75% per arm via Spotify's β* = β/(G+1) before a single extra user exists.

RATES WHOSE DENOMINATOR THE CHANGE ITSELF MOVES — A2 deliberately changes who tests, so 'tested-before-live' and 'simulation coverage' both have moving denominators and their delta can change in an arbitrary direction. Put numerator and denominator on the dashboard as their own series for every rate, and prefer the average of per-user ratios over the ratio of totals where a per-user ratio makes sense.

assumptions.change: Latency-vs-cost slider that picks a complete bundled ASR+LLM+TTS stack, replacing three separate vendor dropdowns, with a working default (Balanced: 750ms, $0.10/min, all Agora-managed) already selected on arrival. Manual per-vendor config collapsed behind an 'Or configure models manually' expander.
assumptions.belief: The decision a first-time builder actually has is a trade-off (fast vs cheap), not three independent vendor picks. Johnson & Goldstein's own numbers (Science 2003, n=161) are 42% opt-in / 79% neutral forced choice / 82% opt-out — the opt-out and neutral conditions did not differ significantly. So the risk is never 'we pre-selected'; it is 'we pre-selected the wrong thing and they had to undo it'. A pre-set stack removes three decisions from the first-answer path at the cost of one reversible one.
assumptions.prediction: Cuts §1 Voice & Models p75 active dwell from an assumed ~150s (three dropdowns, each requiring a vendor comparison) to the 45s budget in §2.3 — a −60s to −105s move, under the assumption that ≥70% of first agents never open the manual expander. Change-away-from-default rate ≤30% of first agents; manual-config expander open rate <30%. Discounted at Kohavi's π≈1/3 base rate the expected-value contribution to median first-answer time is −20s to −35s, which is the number that should go in the sum, not −105s.
assumptions.metric: p75 of a numeric `activeDwellMs` property on `agent_model_stack_selected{mode:'preset'|'manual', preset, costPerMinBucket, ttftBucket}`, read as a Trends 75th-percentile property aggregation. Secondary: rate of `agent_model_stack_selected{mode:'manual'}` over first agents, and `stack_preset_changed` count per session (change-away-from-default).
assumptions.test: PostHog Trends, 75th percentile of activeDwellMs broken down by `preset` — NOT a funnel time-to-convert view, which exposes median and mean only (PostHog issue #24208, open since Aug 2024). Flag `builder-b1-stack-slider` used for staged rollout and rollback, with a pre-declared before/after against a frozen two-week baseline. At ~1,880 international Agora accounts and +0.4% YoY customer growth, this is not a powered A/B.
assumptions.risk: Vapi already ships Balanced / High Intelligence / Ultra Fast / Cost Saver presets AND shows latency, cost and quality metrics per preset at the point of decision. An abstract slider that does not print $/min and a measured p50 is worse than the dropdowns it replaced, because the user opens manual config to find out what they are getting — which converts a −105s win into a +2min loss. Second risk: the Cheapest preset resolves to Whisper large-v3 (480ms, non-streaming); if the default lands on a stack most first agents must change, this is Johnson & Goldstein's bad-default failure, and the change-away rate will show it before the dwell metric does.
assumptions.sample: Dwell p75 is readable off ~100 first-agent sessions (roughly 3–4 weeks at current volume). The change-away rate at p=0.30, d=0.10 needs 16×0.21/0.01 = 336/arm by PostHog's own formula — unreachable; report it as a monitored before/after series with the numerator and denominator charted separately.

assumptions.change: Agora Managed Key by default for ASR, LLM and TTS, so the default agent needs no vendor API keys at all. Bring-your-own-key is an optional switch inside each Configure sheet.
assumptions.belief: Credential fields are the single worst field type known: Zuko's 93,022,997 tracked form sessions put password mean drop-off at 10.5% against 6.4% for email and 6.3% for phone, and Baymard attributes 18% of checkout abandonment to a required account creation. Removing every credential from the route to first answer removes the worst field in the flow. This is an internal speed win against ng-console (whose shipped ConvoAI Playground still asks for an LLM API Key), NOT a competitive differentiator — LiveKit Inference, Vapi, Retell and Bland all reach a talking agent with zero vendor keys.
assumptions.prediction: Zero credential fields on the default path lifts first-answer completion among builder-openers to ≥60%, against the 37.5% cross-SaaS activation average and the 50.6% software-vertical form-completion benchmark. BYOK switch opened by <10% of first agents. Hard exits to /project/vendor-credentials stay under 2% of builder sessions.
assumptions.metric: `agent_credential_mode_selected{component:'asr'|'llm'|'tts', mode:'managed'|'byo'}`; `builder_exit{target:'vendor-credentials', section, agentId}` fired immediately before the `window.location.assign` at stack-config.tsx:526; funnel `builder_opened → agent_test_session_succeeded{turnCount≥1}` filtered `isFirstAgent:true`.
assumptions.test: Before/after against the ng-console baseline, where a key is required. The credential exit is a full document navigation, not a router.push, so React state is destroyed and only the 600ms-debounced localStorage draft survives — the exit event must fire synchronously before the assign, via `sendBeacon`.
assumptions.risk: The premise as positioning is wrong and should not be built on: zero keys is table stakes across the whole competitive set. The defensible line is price symmetry — Agora charges $0.10/min with or without BYOK, so on Agora BYOK is strictly worse for the customer — plus 300 free minutes against Retell's $10 (~60 min), ElevenLabs' 15 min and LiveKit's 50 free inbound minutes. Second risk: if BYOK-open rate exceeds 10%, the Configure sheets are advertising a choice that costs the user both money and dwell with no upside, and the sheet copy must say so.
assumptions.sample: A rate at p=0.10 with d=0.05 needs 16×0.09/0.0025 = 576/arm — unreachable at Agora's volume. Monitored trend with a stopping rule, not an experiment.

assumptions.change: A right-hand test panel always present in the builder, testing the unsaved draft with no publish gate, no saved agent and no phone number. Proposed delta: default the rail to the Voice call tab (it currently opens on Simulations) and add a test control to the mobile sticky strip, which has step chips and Deploy but no test door at all.
assumptions.belief: The old A2 is mis-specified. The capability already exists — agent-wizard.tsx carries the header comment 'Publish is a HINT, not a gate', publishBlocks() gates only deploy, and the only thing that disables Talk is first-run `warming`. So the change cannot buy time by 'making it possible'. What it can buy is discoverability: Retell's quickstart guarantees the same thing in words ('free and doesn't need a phone number or payment method... as many times as you want before publishing') while Vapi forces Publish → Quick Publish before Talk. Agora has the better capability and worse signposting.
assumptions.prediction: Defaulting the rail to Voice call and adding the mobile test control moves the shortest path from 2 clicks to 1 and lifts tested-before-first-publish from an assumed ~60% to ≥85% (the §2.4 target), i.e. +25pp. Median time from builder mount to first Talk click falls 20–40s. Below 1024px, where the panel is a Sheet that is never auto-opened, the effect should be larger because today there is no header test door at all.
assumptions.metric: `agent_test_session_started{trigger:'auto'|'header'|'opening'|'rail'|'mobile_strip', agentState:'draft'|'saved', surface, msSinceBuilderMount}`. Tested-before-live rate = share of agents whose first `operation_succeeded{operation:'agent_publish'}` is preceded by ≥1 `agent_test_session_succeeded{turnCount≥1}`.
assumptions.test: Trends 75th percentile of `msSinceBuilderMount` broken down by `trigger`; flag `builder-b3-rail-default-tab` on the rail's initial tab. Funnel for tested-before-live with a 24h conversion window (never the 14-day default) and Sequential, not Strict, order — autocapture is on in ng-console and would break a strict funnel.
assumptions.risk: `trigger:'auto'` already fires `agent_test_started` 150ms after mount on agt_default via the autoTalk path, with no user action. If it is not excluded, the headline speed metric is generated by a setTimeout and reads ~0. Second: the rail's close button writes a localStorage flag that permanently changes the shortest path for that browser on every agent forever, so any click-count metric drifts upward for returning users with no product cause. Third: the panel plays a hard-coded RAIL_TALK script when the greeting is empty, so an unconfigured draft produces the same 'successful test' as a real one — the event needs `configured:boolean` and `heardOwnGreeting:boolean` or the metric is unfalsifiable.
assumptions.sample: 60% → 85% needs 16×0.24/0.0625 ≈ 62 per arm — one of the very few rows here that is genuinely powerable; roughly 6 weeks at current first-agent volume.

assumptions.change: Backup vendor configured inside each model's own Configure sheet, with its own credential, instead of a separate Backup providers section.
assumptions.belief: Backup was skipped because it lived in a section nobody opened, not because users reject failover. Things that belong together should live together.
assumptions.prediction: Attach rate among users who open a Configure sheet rises 15% → 30–40%. But apply Kohavi's dilution rule explicitly: B1 predicts <30% of first agents ever open manual config, so a +20pp lift on a 30% segment is only +4 to +7pp across all new agents. The honest headline is the diluted number, and sheet dwell rises by ≤10s.
assumptions.metric: `agent_backup_configured{component, vendor, credentialMode}` reported twice — conditional (over `agent_model_sheet_opened{component}`) and unconditional (over all first agents). Dmitriev §5.11's instruction is to publish both; the conditional rate alone is the Xbox pitfall, a large local win with no global movement.
assumptions.test: Before/after with numerator and denominator as separate dashboard series. The row may not close on attach rate alone — attach rate is a pure feature metric. It closes only when printed on the same scorecard line as TCR or a failover-survival number (agents where a backup actually took traffic).
assumptions.risk: On Agora Managed Key the whole 401 / 429 / exceeded-quota failure class largely does not exist for default agents, so this may be attaching backups against a failure mode the managed path already handles — a backup that is never exercised buys no trust and costs dwell. If attach rises and sheet dwell rises more than 20s, the recap line should be split out of the sheet.
assumptions.sample: 15% → 35% needs ~51 per arm (16×0.1275/0.04). Powerable within the sheet-opener population, but that population is small by design — expect a quarter to read it.

assumptions.change: One Select voice dialog with recommended voices badged at the top of the same table, ranked from the agent's own prompt, frozen header, no separate recommended pane.
assumptions.belief: The cost of picking a voice is scanning time, not decision paralysis. Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd pooled 63 conditions from 50 experiments (N=5,036) and found a mean choice-overload effect of virtually zero, and Hick's Law does not apply to finding a named item in a list. So do not prune the catalogue — rank it, badge it, and make the preview instant.
assumptions.prediction: Previews before a pick fall from 6 to 3–4; voice-row p75 active dwell falls from 90s to 50–60s (−30 to −40s). Conditional on the preview itself returning audio inside the 400ms Doherty budget — a 2s preview will make users audition fewer voices and pick worse, which would show as dwell falling while `recommended:true` selection share stays flat.
assumptions.metric: Count of `agent_voice_previewed{source:'table'|'compare'|'greeting'}` per `agent_voice_selected{recommended:boolean, previewCount, rankAtSelection}`; `interaction_latency_ms` on preview start, alarmed above 400ms p90.
assumptions.test: PostHog Trends 'count per user, 75th percentile' of `agent_voice_previewed` between dialog open and selection, broken down by `recommended`. This is why the count-per-user aggregation matters — the struggle signals here do not need a computed property.
assumptions.risk: If `recommended:true` selections sit below ~40%, the ranking is not trusted and the badge is decoration — the fix is to badge the reason ('matches your prompt's tone: warm, US English'), not the rank. Second risk: previews-per-pick is a count metric, and PostHog's 0.25×baseline² variance proxy (which assumes CV=0.5) badly understates it — power it as a count with variance 2×baseline (~22/arm), not as an average (~16/arm), or the row will be called on noise.
assumptions.sample: ~22–35 voice-pickers per arm. Readable in 3–5 weeks.

assumptions.change: Generated test scenarios derived from the agent's own prompt and channel (12 contextual cases from SCENARIO_SEEDS), run from a header button, with a printed per-case verdict anchored to the offending turn.
assumptions.belief: LangChain's State of Agent Engineering (n=1,340, fielded Nov–Dec 2025) puts offline-eval adoption at 52.4% and online at 37.3%, with only ~25% of eval-running teams doing both. An empty 'create your first test' state will be skipped by roughly half of builders. A generated suite converts evaluation from an authoring task into a reading task. Anthropic's own guidance is 20–50 tasks drawn from real failures, and it warns that a suite at 100% pass gives no signal at all.
assumptions.prediction: ≥60% of first agents run the generated suite at least once before first publish, against a ~0% baseline (no scenario surface exists in ng-console). Simulation coverage — agents with ≥5 scenario runs before first publish — goes 0% → ≥40%, the §2.4 target. Suite first-run pass rate should land in the 70–85% band; a suite reading ≥98% for two consecutive weeks is saturated and must generate harder variants.
assumptions.metric: `agent_simulation_run{scenarioCount, passCount, judge:'llm'|'rule', generated:boolean}`; `judge_override{caseId, fromVerdict, toVerdict}` from a one-click 'I disagree' control. Coverage funnel: `builder_opened → agent_simulation_run → agent_publish`, filtered `isFirstAgent`.
assumptions.test: Funnel with a 24h window; a PostHog alert on suite pass rate ≥98% (saturation) and on judge-override rate >30% (the rubric, not the agent, is broken). Alerts must hang off a Trends or SQL insight — funnel time-to-convert views are explicitly excluded from alerting.
assumptions.risk: The suite contains a guaranteed failure for structural reasons: DEFAULT_CALL_BEHAVIOR.transfer is false, so the 'Asks for a human' scenario's failsBecause() fires for every inbound and batch agent. A naive pass-rate chart is therefore floored below 100% for a config reason, not a quality one, and the metric must exclude or label it. Second: LLM judges agree with humans only ~70% of the time and carry documented position, verbosity and self-preference bias — a red row a builder disagrees with costs more trust than the suite buys, which is why the override control is part of the change and not a nice-to-have.
assumptions.sample: Coverage 0% → 40% needs ~38 per arm (16×0.12/0.16 rounded up for the zero-baseline case); readable in ~4 weeks. A 1,000-calls-per-variant bar applies only to agent-behaviour claims, never to this builder-side rate.

assumptions.change: An Opening section that composes the AI disclosure and greeting and shows the exact line callers hear, with 'Hear the opening' playing it in one click.
assumptions.belief: Reading and hearing the exact first line replaces a full test call for the greeting decision, and disclosure is a legal control rather than a courtesy: EU AI Act Article 50 has been binding since 2 August 2026, requiring that people be informed they are interacting with AI 'at the latest at the time of the first interaction', with a ceiling of €15,000,000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover.
assumptions.prediction: +8 to +15pp of first agents hear audio before their first publish (the one-click path collapses two clicks to one). Greeting edits within 24h of first publish fall 20–30%. Disclosure-on rate for EU-hosted agents ≥95%.
assumptions.metric: `greeting_previewed{agentId, seconds}` — already firing in ng-console at agent-opening-section.tsx:186, but `agentId` and `seconds` are both absent from the 48-key camelCase sanitizer allowlist and are silently dropped, so the event currently lands as a bare count with no agent and no duration. Fixing the allowlist is a one-line prerequisite. Plus post-publish `agent_update` touching the greeting field group within 24h, and `ai_disclosure_enabled{agentId}` crossed with hosting region.
assumptions.test: Before/after on greeting-edits-after-publish over ~100 publishes, not an experiment. Add a blocking preflight item when hosting region is EU and disclose is false.
assumptions.risk: There is a live compliance asymmetry that contradicts this row: EMPTY_DRAFT sets opening.disclose = true, but agentToDraft() never writes an `opening` object, so every existing agent — including the flagship agt_default — falls back to DEFAULT_OPENING with disclose = false. The demo agent ships non-compliant while a blank draft ships compliant. Second risk: if the preview is the scripted 500ms transcript rather than the real configured voice, post-publish greeting edits will not fall and the conclusion will wrongly be 'placement is fine' when the defect is fidelity.
assumptions.sample: Greeting-edit-after-publish is a low-frequency per-agent rate; read as a before/after across ≥100 first publishes, roughly one quarter.

assumptions.change: Five-section accordion on one page with an 'n of 5 done' left rail, replacing a linear multi-page wizard. Proposed delta: render a blank draft's genuine starting state as '3 of 5 ready' rather than '1 of 5 done', because the managed key, the bundled stack, the language, the advanced-speech defaults and the call-behaviour defaults really are pre-filled.
assumptions.belief: Endowed progress. Kivetz, Urminsky & Zheng: the same ten purchases were completed in a median of 10 days on a 12-stamp card with two stamps pre-filled, against 15 days on a plain 10-stamp card — a 33% cut in time-to-goal from an illusion of progress. Here the progress is not an illusion; the defaults are working values, so stating them is honest as well as fast.
assumptions.prediction: Showing the true starting state cuts median builder-mount → first-deploy for self-built agents by 15–30%. Against the §2.2 TTFD median target of 20 minutes that is a −3 to −6 minute move, and it is the cheapest intervention in the entire sweep because it changes a string and a predicate, not a flow.
assumptions.metric: Rail counter value at mount (`builder_opened{sectionsReady, sectionsTotal}`), `section_completed{section}`, and TTFD measured builder-mount → `operation_succeeded{operation:'agent_publish'}`.
assumptions.test: Flag the counter's semantics, before/after on TTFD. Report TTFD as a geometric mean with log-transformed CIs for any cell under n=25 (Sauro & Lewis: ~13% less error and ~22% less bias than the sample median at small n) and as median/p75 above 25.
assumptions.risk: The counter is currently wrong in both directions and must be fixed before it can be measured: isDone(4) is the literal `true`, and isDone(5) is computed once from existing.status and never recomputed after an in-session deploy — so a blank draft reads '1 of 5' and a just-deployed new agent never reaches '5 of 5'. Second risk: Baymard tested accordion checkouts directly and found no support for accordions outperforming multi-step or single-page formats, with 75% of implementations carrying major usability problems from exactly two causes — destroying the ongoing review (a collapsed section must still summarise what is set inside it) and breaking back-button expectations with data loss. The section count is not the lever; those two checks are.
assumptions.sample: Before/after over ≥60 self-built deploys — the rule-of-three floor for bounding a 5% failure rate — which is roughly a quarter at current volume.

assumptions.change: Deploy preflight that names what is blocking a deploy, listing every blocker at once with a Fix link per row, instead of surfacing them one at a time.
assumptions.belief: The WHO surgical safety checklist cut complications by more than a third and halved failures to meet six basic standards across 1,000 patients in eight hospitals; the mechanism is not new knowledge but forcing known steps to be verified at the moment of commitment. The concrete baseline here is worse than 'no checklist': ng-console's validateAgentDetailDraft is a chain of early returns that can only ever return issues[0], and handleDetailPublishConfirm re-runs the same check inside the dialog and closes the dialog on failure. N blockers therefore cost N publish attempts, each ending in a dismissed dialog.
assumptions.prediction: Publish attempts per successful first publish fall from an assumed 1.8 to ≤1.1 (−40%). First-publish failure rate falls 50%, from an assumed 10–15% to 5–7%, meeting the ≤5% §2.4 target at the optimistic end. Cost: +10 to +20s of dwell on the Deploy step, inside the 60s §2.3 budget.
assumptions.metric: `agent_preflight_evaluated{rows, blockingCount, warningCount, allGo, simsRun}`, `preflight_fix_clicked{rowId}`, `preflight_talk_first`, `preflight_abandoned`, `preflight_confirmed`; and `operation_failed{operation:'agent_publish', errorStage}`. Attempts-per-success is a ratio — chart numerator and denominator as separate series, per Dmitriev §5.1 on metric sample-ratio mismatch.
assumptions.test: Before/after against ng-console's one-at-a-time flow. Adopt Spotify's four-clause ship rule as the header: superior on at least one success metric, non-inferior on all guardrails with a stated margin, no deterioration, and no quality test (SRM, isFirstAgent share) invalidating the read.
assumptions.risk: The preflight currently emits no telemetry at all, and its 1,090ms staged verdict (rows × 140ms + 250ms) is cosmetic — the confirm button is armed immediately when allGo — so today it costs dwell before it buys anything. Google's SRE launch-checklist governance is the counterweight: every item must be earned by a named past failure, and by 2008 about 30% of low-risk launches got an abbreviated checklist. A six-row checklist on a managed-key inbound web widget is theatre; two-tier it by risk. Also: if failures do not drop, the checks are aimed at the wrong failure modes and must be re-derived from the observed `errorStage` distribution rather than defended.
assumptions.sample: Detecting a first-publish failure rate moving 10% → 5% needs 16×0.0975/0.0025 = 624 per arm. Not powerable. This is a monitored deterioration metric with a stopping rule ('halt and investigate if first-publish failure exceeds baseline at any weekly read'), plus attempts-per-success as the readable primary.

assumptions.change: Undo to live, and a visible 'Live. No changes' state on the deploy CTA.
assumptions.belief: A visible live state prevents redundant publishes and makes reverting a first-class act rather than a support ticket. DORA's 2026 elite bands — change failure rate below 5%, time to restore under an hour — are the external frame that makes the §2.4 TCR ≥95% target defensible rather than invented.
assumptions.prediction: Redundant publish attempts on an unchanged live agent fall below 2% of deploy-CTA clicks. 24h rollback rate stays within +1.5pp of baseline — stated as a non-inferiority margin, not as 'must not rise', because 'must not rise' is unfalsifiable at this volume.
assumptions.metric: `deploy_noop{agentId}` fired distinctly when deployCta === 'Live. No changes' (today that click only toasts 'Already live' and would otherwise be counted as deploy intent); `agent_rolled_back{fromVersion, toVersion, reason, restoredObjects[]}` — which does not exist yet because there is no version object.
assumptions.test: Monitored guardrail with a pre-declared stopping rule, never a powered test. Detecting a 24h rollback rate rising 5% → 7.5% needs 16×0.0475/0.000625 = 1,216 users per arm by PostHog's own formula — roughly two-thirds of Agora's entire international active-customer base (1,880 at last disclosure). Also note Spotify's β* = β/(G+1) correction: four guardrails inflate the required sample per arm by ~75% before a single extra user exists, which argues for cutting to two (rollback, publish failure) as deterioration metrics.
assumptions.risk: The repo's own audit already flags 'Live — no changes' as unreadable as button-versus-state, and clicking it is a no-op that the funnel will record as intent to deploy. Bigger risk: there is no version object, so 'undo to live' cannot say what it restores. Synthflow's version history silently excludes actions and knowledge bases; a rollback that quietly fails to restore an agent's tools or KB is a trust trap worse than no rollback at all. The confirmation must name the restored objects and the excluded ones.
assumptions.sample: n/a — monitored, with the stopping rule written down before the flag goes on.

assumptions.change: Reorder the rail so Deployment comes after Test, or make §2 fully skippable with defaults applied — today STEP_TITLES is Voice & Models → Deployment → Prompt & knowledge → Test → Go Live, so a channel decision (Inbound / Batch / Code-SDK, a radio not a multi-select) sits upstream of ever hearing the agent.
assumptions.belief: Every competitor that wins on first-answer time puts prompt-then-test first and defers the channel. Retell places its free browser test at step 3 and the payment method plus number purchase at step 4, explicitly noting 'You only need a number once you want to make or receive real phone calls.' Vapi's documented happy path is the opposite — it provisions a free US number at steps 5–7 of 9 — and it still claims under 5 minutes, because the number is free and in-product. Agora cannot copy that: Agora does not sell or port numbers, which its own docs and the redesign's own sheet copy state ('Bring a number you already own. Agora routes it, and doesn't sell or port numbers'). So deferring the channel is not a preference, it is the only version of this flow Agora can win.
assumptions.prediction: Moving the channel decision downstream of the first test lifts the first-test rate among builder-openers by 8–15pp and cuts median time to first answer by 30–60s. Median `sectionIndexAtFirstTest` should read 1, not 2 or 3.
assumptions.metric: `agent_builder_section_viewed{section, order, agentState, isFirstAgent}`; `sectionIndexAtFirstTest` as a property on `agent_test_session_started`; first-test rate = distinct persons firing `agent_test_session_succeeded` over persons firing `builder_opened`, `isFirstAgent:true`.
assumptions.test: Flag `builder-b11-section-order` on the rail order; before/after on first-test rate with a 24h window. If the median sectionIndexAtFirstTest stays above 1 after the reorder, the IA is not what is pushing people through configuration — the rail's default tab (B3) is.
assumptions.risk: publishBlocks() puts two of its four non-batch blockers inside §2 (no channel; inbound with a phone surface and zero numberIds), so deferring the section defers the blockers rather than removing them — they resurface at the Deploy click, where they cost a failed publish instead of a skipped step. That trade is only worth it if B9's preflight names them clearly. Second risk: for batch agents the caller-ID number genuinely is upstream of a meaningful test, so the reorder must be channel-aware rather than global.
assumptions.sample: An 8pp lift on an assumed 55% first-test rate needs 16×0.2475/0.0064 ≈ 619 per arm — not powerable. Staged rollout plus a 20-participant moderated benchmark is the readable instrument here.

assumptions.change: Anchor the first-answer stop event server-side and winsorize the clock: stop on the runtime's first `turn-finished` for that agent (already parsed in src/lib/latency-metrics.ts) with the client event kept as a secondary, truncate at 600s, and rename the onboarding clock off 'TTFA'.
assumptions.belief: Two separate hazards. First, telemetry-loss bias: the stop event fires from a panel holding a live voice session, which is exactly where a client drops its last beacon, and Microsoft's pitfall 5.3 records that this invalidated every client-event metric in a mobile experiment while server-side metrics stayed valid. Second, metric shape: Bing's own TimeToSuccess has skewness² = 4.4, requiring 1,550 users per arm untruncated and ~50 truncated. Separately, TTFA is already the voice industry's term for time to first audio with a sub-300ms bar and an <800ms pre-launch gate — putting a minutes-scale number beside it guarantees a misread in every review.
assumptions.prediction: Server anchoring plus truncation at 600s cuts the sample needed to read the clock by roughly 30× — from ~1,550 to ~50 per arm — and should bring client and server session counts within 10% of each other. A divergence above 10% is a data-quality alarm, not a metric movement.
assumptions.metric: Data-quality Trends tile comparing client `agent_test_session_succeeded` count to server turn-finished count for the same agent; the clock itself read as a SQL insight, `quantile(0.5)(properties.ttfaMs)` and `quantile(0.75)(...)`, because PostHog's funnel time-to-convert view exposes median and mean only (issue #24208) and every p75 target in §2 is therefore unreadable from a funnel.
assumptions.test: Ship in W0 with the schema-2.2.0 change, before any builder flag goes on. Pre-register Twyman's law: after two weeks of baseline, record the observed week-to-week standard deviation of the median, and treat any variant claiming more than 3σ of improvement as an instrumentation investigation rather than a win.
assumptions.risk: If the runtime turn event cannot be joined to the builder's person and agent ids, the server anchor is unavailable and the client number stands — in which case it must be published with a stated loss rate. Second: truncation discards exactly the slow sessions the dwell budgets exist to find, so the >600s population must be reported separately as a failure rate, never folded in as a long success. For any cell under n=25 (every moderated study, every early flag cell, every per-cid cut) use the geometric mean with log-transformed CIs, not the median.
assumptions.sample: ~50 per arm post-truncation for the clock itself; the data-quality comparison is readable from day one at any volume.

assumptions.change: Fix the three duration bugs in the shipped instrumentation before any speed claim is published: agent_test_ended sends `duration_sec: 30` as a literal with no timer; markBuildStart() writes its stamp only if absent so a returning user's time-to-live is measured from their first-ever builder mount in that browser; and timeToLiveMs() reads-and-clears in one call, so a failed dispatch or a StrictMode double-invoke loses the measurement with no retry.
assumptions.belief: Three of only three track() call sites in the entire builder are wrong or unreadable. Every A-row read before this lands is uninterpretable, so W0 cannot start on top of it. The measurement is not 'later' work — it is the gate.
assumptions.prediction: The corrected clock will read materially slower for returning users (whose current value can be days) and materially faster wherever the read-and-clear lost the event. Expect the published median to move by more than 3 standard deviations of week-to-week variation on the week the fix lands — which, by Twyman's law, must be attributed to the fix and not celebrated.
assumptions.metric: `agent_test_session{durationMs}` from a real useRef timestamp, ended from a useEffect cleanup in the component owning `testing` with `reason:'toggle'|'rail_closed'|'unmount'|'navigated'` (ng-console already ships this idiom at agent-detail-page.tsx:388). Build clocks stamped per attempt, keyed on agent id plus a session nonce, emitting `wallMs`, `activeMs` (visibility-aware, never a tick counter — background tabs throttle intervals to ≥1s) and `resumedCount`.
assumptions.test: Write a PostHog annotation on the fix date carrying the assumption id, then attribute any step change in the clock to it. Add `posthog-cli exp schema status` to CI so drift between the repo and the PostHog project fails the build — schema management is compile-time only and PostHog's own ingestion-side enforcement plugin was archived in July 2024 with a native replacement still unbuilt, so CI is the only real gate.
assumptions.risk: No product risk; the risk is to the ledger. If the fix ships in the same week as a design flag, the two are confounded and neither is readable — the fix must land alone, with a two-week clean window after it. Also note the property-casing split: ng-console's sanitizer enforces a 48-key camelCase allowlist and silently drops everything else, while studio_x_2 emits snake_case — `agent_id`, `duration_sec`, `preset`, `vendor` would all arrive as events with no properties at all.
assumptions.sample: n/a — a prerequisite, not a test. Two weeks of clean baseline after it lands.

assumptions.change: A pre-signup 'hear it talk' demo on the marketing surface, handing the visitor a pre-populated draft on signup.
assumptions.belief: The cheapest possible first answer is one that happens before the account exists. Bland puts a click-to-speak agent in front of anonymous visitors across four verticals; LiveKit's Agent Builder previews in-browser with zero local setup. Agora's nearest equivalent is behind a login. Every part already exists in the redesign — the TalkTab, a default managed stack, a default voice — so this is a routing and quota problem, not a build.
assumptions.prediction: Collapses signup-to-first-sound to zero for the anonymous cohort and should convert 10–20% of anonymous listeners into signups. It is the only instrument that can ever produce a zero-minute first answer, and it gives a first-answer distribution for people who never signed up — currently an entirely invisible population.
assumptions.metric: `agent_test_session_started{authState:'anonymous'}` → `agent_test_session_succeeded{turnCount≥1}` → signup, read as a funnel on the anonymous cohort with an anonymous-to-identified join at signup.
assumptions.test: Staged rollout on the marketing route with a hard minutes quota. Send the anonymous events with `$process_person_profile:false` — anonymous events are up to 4× cheaper in PostHog and the console today identifies before first render, so 100% of its events are identified and billed at the higher rate.
assumptions.risk: Abuse and quota: a free talking agent on an unauthenticated page is a minutes bill, and Agora's designed allowance is already the most generous in the set (300 min/month, 150 card-free). Second: if the anonymous-to-identified join is not wired at signup, the cohort cannot be followed and the conversion number is unknowable — which is the entire point of the change.
assumptions.sample: A 10–20% conversion rate on anonymous listeners is readable from ~200 anonymous sessions; marketing traffic makes this the highest-volume surface in the whole plan.

assumptions.change: A count-based canary on Go Live — 'watch the first N calls' with the statistical bound printed — plus an auto-rollback condition chosen at deploy time in the user's own words.
assumptions.belief: Hanley & Lippman-Hand's rule of three: zero failures in n independent trials bounds the true failure rate at 3/n with 95% confidence. So 20 clean calls only bound failure at 15%, 60 at 5%, 100 at 3%, 300 at 1%. Percentage canaries — which Retell and ElevenLabs both ship — are statistically meaningless at first-agent volumes, where Google Cloud's floor of ~50 data points per metric already fails; a 10% canary on an agent taking 30 calls a day yields 3 calls. Choosing the rollback condition before you deploy is the specific act that lets a builder flip the switch.
assumptions.prediction: Canary adopted on ≥40% of first deploys, and 24h rollback falls 1–2pp from an assumed 5% baseline. The printed bound ('No failures in 20 calls. That still allows a failure rate as high as 15%. Keep watching to 60 for 5%.') is the honest counter to LiveKit's 'zero to ringing in 60 seconds' — nobody in the category shows this.
assumptions.metric: `canary_started{n, rollbackCondition}`, `canary_completed{callsObserved, failures, boundPct}`, `agent_rolled_back{trigger:'auto'|'manual'}`; TCR as the tied guardrail.
assumptions.test: Monitored, with a stopping rule — TCR at 95% needs ~844 per arm to detect a fall to 92%, so it can never be a powered test. Read canary adoption as the primary and TCR as the deterioration metric.
assumptions.risk: A canary that asks the user to wait is in direct tension with the speed claim this whole redesign is built on — if adoption is below 20% the control is a tax nobody pays, and it should become an automatic background watch with a proactive signal ('your agent's first 20 live calls are ending worse than your tests predicted') rather than a gate. Second: for outbound agents this measures the wrong thing first — 86% of consumers do not answer calls from unknown numbers (Hiya, n>12,000), so answer rate belongs above every quality number on that panel.
assumptions.sample: Adoption rate at 40% with d=0.15 needs ~171 per arm; readable over a quarter. The rollback delta is monitored only.

backlog.name: W0 measurement gate: ship the test-session operation, fix the three duration bugs, extend the sanitizer allowlist
backlog.hypothesis: Nothing in this ledger is readable today. The whole builder emits three track() call sites; one reports a literal duration_sec: 30; time_to_live_ms is measured from the first-ever builder mount in that browser; and the three agent-builder events already firing in production (caller_first_selected, ai_disclosure_enabled, greeting_previewed) lose agentId and seconds to a 48-key camelCase allowlist that drops unknown properties silently. Until this lands, every speed claim is an opinion.

Cuts the sample needed to read the clock ~30× once server-anchored and truncated at 600s (Bing TimeToSuccess: skewness² 4.4 → 0.15; 1,550/arm → ~50/arm).
backlog.effort: S — one schema version, one allowlist edit, one timer, one useEffect cleanup, plus posthog-cli exp schema status in CI.
backlog.evidence: Repo: studio_x_2 components/wizard/agent-wizard.tsx toggleTest, lib/analytics.ts markBuildStart/timeToLiveMs; ng-console src/lib/observability/sanitize.ts and agent-opening-section.tsx:114,129,186. Dmitriev et al. KDD 2017 §5.3 (telemetry loss bias); Kohavi et al. KDD 2014 Rule #7; PostHog issue #24208 (funnel time-to-convert exposes median and mean only).

backlog.name: Immutable published versions with a one-click rollback that names what it restores
backlog.hypothesis: Agora wins the speed comparison and loses the trust one. Retell shipped A/B traffic splitting in March 2026 and Agent Versioning 2.0 with staging/production tags in May; ElevenLabs ships immutable version snapshots (agtvrsn_) and branches with deterministic routing; Bland runs draft/staging/production with per-call version targeting. Agora's Go Live has no version object, so 'undo to live' cannot say what it restores and config_drift_detected{ran_version, current_version} already implies a version concept that is unnamed.

backlog.name: Production scorers: reuse the §4 test rubric as live-call success criteria
backlog.hypothesis: ElevenLabs evaluates simulation results using the same criteria it applies in production — one rubric run offline and online. Only ~25% of eval-running teams do both (52.4% offline, 37.3% online), so this is rarer and more differentiating than it looks. In Agora's case it is nearly free: the assertions authored in Test become the production scorers behind one checkbox at Go Live.
backlog.expected: Turns a pre-launch artefact into the first-24-hours dashboard with zero new authoring, and makes 'proportion of agents with an eval suite' and 'proportion of live agents with production scorers' the same number. This is the concrete answer to the owner's 'how to build confidence in production'.
backlog.effort: M — one shared rubric object in the data model, plus a scoring hook on the runtime path.
backlog.evidence: ElevenLabs agent-testing docs (same criteria offline and online); Vapi Scorecards (artifactPlan.scorecardIds, points totalling 100, returned within seconds of call end); LangChain State of Agent Engineering n=1,340.

backlog.name: First-24-hours review built on the telephony and turn events Agora already emits
backlog.hypothesis: Three of the six barge-in signals and the entire call state machine are already in the runtime payload and are being thrown away. Event 112 carries start.type (voice_input / greeting / silence_timeout / api_speak / api_think), end.type (ok / error / ignored / interrupted) and interrupt_duration_ms; src/lib/latency-metrics.ts parses only agent_id, turn_id, start.start_at and metrics.*. Events 201/202 give START → CALLING → RINGING → ANSWERED → HANGUP with report_ms, so answer rate and post-dial delay are computable today.

The cheapest credible production panel Agora can build, and it closes the loop from the Advanced Speech Settings knob to its consequence.

Note: Agora emits no per-turn ASR confidence anywhere, so the 'ASR confidence below 80%' predictor is not instrumentable and must be dropped from the panel spec.

backlog.name: 20-participant moderated first-agent benchmark against today's console
backlog.hypothesis: At ~1,880 international active customers growing 0.4% YoY, the builder sees first agents in the tens per week. PostHog will not even render an experiment estimate below 100 exposures. A 20-participant timed benchmark resolves roughly the size of change this ledger predicts and does it in a week.
backlog.expected: Gives A0/B-row baselines a real number in one week instead of two-plus quarters of telemetry that may never accumulate. At n=20 a task time carries a margin of error under 20% at 95% confidence. Report as a geometric mean with a log-CI.

Note this replaces, and contradicts, any 5-user plan — five users is a problem-finding sample, not a measurement.

backlog.name: Timed competitive cold-start study, published with its method
backlog.hypothesis: Every competitor time claim is a scripted-happy-path documentation number with no definition, population, window, sample size or percentile — Retell ~3 min (docs) vs 'the 30 minute build is the floor' (its own blog), Vapi under 5 min, ElevenLabs 'minutes' vs 'within hours' in its own FAQ, LiveKit under 10 min after a CLI install, LiveKit Phone Numbers 'zero to ringing in 60 seconds'. Nobody publishes a measured distribution, so whoever measures first owns the claim.

backlog.effort: M — one cold account per platform, identical task, three trials each, screen-recorded, repeated quarterly.

backlog.name: End-reason taxonomy grouped by who can fix it
backlog.hypothesis: Vapi publishes 50+ end-reason values across ~10 categories and Retell ~30 across three status buckets, each with a per-reason fix instruction. Agora emits status STOPPED|FAILED plus a free-text message (event 102) and a loosely coupled errors array (event 110) — free text cannot be counted or charted.

Grouping by who can fix it (caller behaviour / your configuration, deep-linked to section N / Agora infrastructure / vendor credential) is directly enabled by the managed-key default, because the whole 401-429-quota class does not exist for default agents — and the Monitor screen should say so.
backlog.effort: M — a client-side synthesis over events 102, 110, 201 and 202.

backlog.hypothesis: Agora's revenue is expansion-led: Q2 2026 revenue $40.4M (+18% YoY) and dollar-based net retention 104% (from 94%), against active customers +0.4%. The builder header is a single non-wrapping 64px flex row with five shrink-0 controls; the lg:hidden strip that replaces it carries step chips and Deploy but no test control at all, and the test panel's Sheet fallback is never auto-opened. The audit records the builder at 390px as one ~5,000px column.

backlog.name: Post-deploy confidence micro-survey
backlog.hypothesis: Session Replay is disabled by policy, so §2.4's 'confidence in production' is entirely behavioural inference with no attitudinal check. HEART's own answer to a Happiness row with no log signal is a survey. PostHog Surveys can be triggered by a custom event and rendered through the product's own components via the API presentation type.

backlog.name: Tool mocking and deterministic rule assertions in the test case sheet
backlog.hypothesis: Agora's eval case sheet has a persona and plain-language assertions but no tool mocking and no dynamic variables. Without mocks, any agent with an MCP server or a connector cannot be tested safely — you would fire real bookings. Retell's four-field case makes mocks first-class; ElevenLabs offers mock-none / mock-all / mock-selected per test.

backlog.name: Scoped session-replay exception for the builder route
backlog.hypothesis: The blanket ban is stricter than PostHog's privacy model requires and is costing the design team the exact evidence the dwell budgets exist to produce. PostHog masks all inputs by default; maskTextSelector plus .ph-no-capture on credential rows closes the rest. Triggers are surgical: url_triggers on /agents/*/edit, event_triggers on the test-start event (name only — properties are not filtered), sample_rate 0.2, minimum_duration_milliseconds 5000.
backlog.expected: Turns 'we cannot watch a struggling user' into 'we watch the twenty sessions that blew the voice-picker budget'. Free tier covers 5,000 recordings a month, which at 20% sampling of test sessions is permanently free at Agora's volume. Also unlocks the two-click ritual: open the funnel, click the drop-off count at the Test step, watch five replays with 'Only show matching events' on.
